questions.stem: Five apples weigh the same as 24 eggs. Two pineapples weigh the same as 32 eggs. How many apples weigh the same as three pineapples?
questions.hint: Use eggs as the common unit. Find the weight of three pineapples in eggs, and the weight of one apple in eggs, then divide.

keyPoints.text: Five apples weigh the same as 24 eggs
keyPoints.note: 5 apples = 24 eggs, so 1 apple is 24 ÷ 5 eggs.

keyPoints.text: Two pineapples weigh the same as 32 eggs
keyPoints.note: 2 pineapples = 32 eggs, so 1 pineapple is 16 eggs.

steps.explain: Find the weight of one pineapple in eggs, then of three pineapples.
Find the weight of one apple in eggs.
How many apples weigh 48 eggs?
Check with the original numbers: 10 apples are 2 lots of 5 apples \(=2\times24=48\) eggs, and 3 pineapples are 48 eggs. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Tickets for a football game are available for \(\$29\) in advance or \(\$39\) if purchased on the day of the game. The organisers had a revenue of \(\$68,000\) for the game and they sold 2,000 tickets. How many tickets were sold in advance?
questions.hint: Suppose ALL 2000 tickets were sold in advance and see how much money that would raise. The real revenue is more, and each ticket sold on the day brings in \(\$10\) more than an advance ticket.

keyPoints.note: Advance tickets + tickets on the day = 2000.

keyPoints.text: How many tickets were sold in advance
keyPoints.note: The question asks for the number of ADVANCE tickets, not the day-of-game tickets.

steps.explain: If all 2000 tickets were sold in advance, the revenue would be:
The real revenue is \(\$68\,000\), so there is extra money. Find how much.
Each ticket sold on the day brings in \(39-29=\$10\) more than an advance ticket. So the number of tickets sold on the day is:
The rest of the 2000 tickets were sold in advance.

questions.stem: Two trains are 1 kilometre apart on a single track railway line. They set off towards one another at 1 metre/second. A bee sitting on the front of one of the trains starts to fly along the railway line at 3 metres/second. When the bee meets the other train it immediately turns around and flies towards the first train and so on. How far does the bee fly?
questions.hint: Do not try to add up all the back-and-forth flights of the bee! Find how long it takes the two trains to meet. The bee is flying all that time at 3 metres per second.

keyPoints.text: They set off towards one another at 1 metre/second
keyPoints.note: Each train travels at 1 m/s, so together they close the gap at 2 m/s.

keyPoints.text: How far does the bee fly
keyPoints.note: Distance = speed × time. The bee flies for exactly as long as the trains take to meet.

steps.explain: The trains are 1 km \(=1000\) m apart and each moves at 1 m/s towards the other, so the gap closes at \(1+1=2\) m/s.
(Each train travels half the distance: \(500\) m at 1 m/s takes \(500\) s.)
The bee flies for the whole 500 seconds at 3 m/s.
Change to kilometres.
Check: the bee flies 3 times as fast as one train, and each train travels 0.5 km. The bee flies \(3\times0.5=1.5\) km. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: There are two ways to add four odd numbers to get 8: \(5+1+1+1=8\) or \(3+3+1+1=8\). Changes in the order of numbers do not count as new solutions. How many ways can you add four odd numbers to get 12?
questions.hint: List the ways in an organised way: start with the BIGGEST odd number possible, then the next biggest, and so on, always keeping the numbers in order from biggest to smallest so you do not count the same way twice.

keyPoints.text: Changes in the order of numbers do not count as new solutions
keyPoints.note: 5 + 3 + 3 + 1 is the same solution as 3 + 5 + 1 + 3, so write each solution biggest first.
Each number is odd: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, ...

steps.explain: The smallest odd number is 1. Three 1s leave \(12-3=9\) for the largest number, which is allowed (9 is odd).
Largest number 7: the other three add to \(12-7=5\) (three odd numbers adding to 5): \(3+1+1\).
Largest number 5: the other three add to 7: \(5+1+1\) or \(3+3+1\).
Largest number 3: all four numbers must be 3, because \(3\times4=12\).

No other largest number is possible (11 would need three more odd numbers adding to 1, and a largest number of 1 gives a total of only 4). So the ways are: 9+1+1+1, 7+3+1+1, 5+5+1+1, 5+3+3+1 and 3+3+3+3.

questions.stem: There are 134 cars in a village of 30 families. Each family has either 4 or 5 cars. How many families have 5 cars?
questions.hint: Suppose EVERY family has 4 cars. How many cars would there be? The real total is bigger: each family with 5 cars adds exactly one extra car.

keyPoints.note: Every family has 4 cars, and some have 1 extra.
The number of families with 5 cars equals the number of extra cars.

steps.explain: If all 30 families had 4 cars, there would be:
The real number is 134, which is more. Find the number of extra cars.
Each family with 5 cars has exactly 1 extra car, so 14 extra cars means 14 families have 5 cars.
Check: 14 families with 5 cars \(=70\) cars, and 16 families with 4 cars \(=64\) cars. \(70+64=134\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: I sit in a seat which is third from the left, fourth from the right, fifth from the front and sixth from the back. How many seats are there?
questions.hint: Work out the number of seats in one ROW (using “from the left” and “from the right”) and the number of ROWS (using “from the front” and “from the back”). Your own seat is counted in both directions, so do not count it twice.

keyPoints.text: third from the left, fourth from the right
keyPoints.note: The seats in a row are: 2 on my left + me + 3 on my right (or 3 + 4 − 1).

keyPoints.text: fifth from the front and sixth from the back
keyPoints.note: The rows are: 4 in front + my row + 5 behind (or 5 + 6 − 1).

steps.explain: Seats along one row: my seat is third from the left and fourth from the right. My own seat is counted twice, so subtract 1.
Number of rows: my row is fifth from the front and sixth from the back, with my row counted twice.

questions.stem: Sam's dad pays him 70 cents for each correct answer he provides in his maths test and fines him 30 cents for each incorrect answer. Today Sam received \(\$19\) after completing 50 questions. How many problems did Sam answer incorrectly?
questions.hint: Pretend Sam got ALL 50 questions correct. Find how much money that would be. Each incorrect answer replaces a +70 cents by a \(-30\) cents, which is a loss of \(70+30=100\) cents compared with a correct answer.

keyPoints.text: fines him 30 cents for each incorrect answer
keyPoints.note: An incorrect answer loses 30 cents AND misses the 70 cents he would have earned: a difference of $1 each.
He ended with \(\$19\) after all 50 questions.

steps.explain: If all 50 answers were correct Sam would receive:
He actually received \(\$19\), which is less. Find the difference.
Each incorrect answer costs him \(0.70+0.30=\$1.00\) compared with a correct answer. So the number of incorrect answers is:
Check: 34 correct answers earn \(34\times0.70=\$23.80\), and 16 incorrect answers cost \(16\times0.30=\$4.80\). \(23.80-4.80=\$19\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A herd of cows drank \(\dfrac15\) of the water in a pond. After a break, they drank \(\dfrac14\) of the remaining water. After another break, they drank \(\dfrac13\) of the remaining water. After a final break, they drank \(\dfrac12\) of the remaining water. How much water is left in the pond, compared to the initial amount?
questions.hint: Follow the water step by step. Each time they drink a fraction of what is REMAINING, so what is left is \(1-\) that fraction of what was there before. Multiply the fractions that are left.

keyPoints.note: Each fraction is taken of the water that is LEFT at that moment, not of the starting amount.
Give the final amount as a fraction or percentage of the START amount.

steps.explain: After drinking \(\dfrac15\), the fraction left is:
They drink \(\dfrac14\) of the remaining water, so \(\dfrac34\) of it is left.
They drink \(\dfrac13\) of the remaining water, so \(\dfrac23\) of it is left.
They drink \(\dfrac12\) of the remaining water, so \(\dfrac12\) of it is left.
Change to a percentage.
Check by multiplying all the fractions left: \(\dfrac45\times\dfrac34\times\dfrac23\times\dfrac12=\dfrac{24}{120}=\dfrac15\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Three girls put \(\$40\), \(\$50\) and \(\$60\) in a piggy bank. How can they split the money in a ratio of 1:2:3?
questions.hint: First find the total amount of money in the piggy bank. The ratio 1 : 2 : 3 has \(1+2+3\) parts. Find the value of one part, then the three shares.

keyPoints.text: split the money in a ratio of 1:2:3
keyPoints.note: The shares are 1 part, 2 parts and 3 parts of the TOTAL money.

keyPoints.text: put \(\$40\), \(\$50\) and \(\$60\) in a piggy bank
keyPoints.note: The total is 40 + 50 + 60.

steps.explain: Total amount of money in the piggy bank.
The ratio \(1:2:3\) has \(1+2+3=6\) parts. Find one part.
The three shares are 1, 2 and 3 parts.

questions.stem: A plane figure which consists of three or more edges as its sides is called a(n):
questions.hint: Think about the general name for a flat shape made of straight sides. Some of the options name only ONE special kind of shape (for example triangles have exactly 3 sides).

keyPoints.text: three or more edges as its sides
keyPoints.note: The shape can have 3, 4, 5, 6, ... sides, so the name must cover all of them.

steps.explain: A scalene triangle and an isosceles triangle both have exactly 3 sides, so neither covers shapes with 4 or more sides.
An equilateral polygon is a polygon with all sides equal. Not every plane figure with 3 or more straight sides has equal sides.
A polygon is any closed plane figure made of 3 or more straight sides (edges).

questions.stem: John is driving a bus with 64 passengers. At each stop, half of the passengers get off. How many stops does he make until only 1 passenger is on the bus?
questions.hint: Halve the number of passengers at each stop and keep a count of the stops until you reach 1. Remember to count the stops, not the numbers in the list.

keyPoints.text: half of the passengers get off
keyPoints.note: The number on the bus is halved at each stop.
Count each halving as one stop.

steps.explain: Write the number of passengers after each stop, halving every time.
Count the stops: after the 1st stop 32 passengers remain, then 16, 8, 4, 2 and finally 1 after the 6th stop.
Check with powers of 2: \(64=2^6\), so it takes 6 halvings to reach \(2^0=1\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If \(a=3\), then what is \(2\times a^3\)?
questions.hint: The power applies only to \(a\). Do the power FIRST (\(a^3=a\times a\times a\)), then multiply by 2 (order of operations).

keyPoints.note: The index 3 belongs to a only, not to the 2. Do the power before the multiplication.

steps.explain: Substitute \(a=3\).
Work out the power first: \(3^3=3\times3\times3=27\).
Multiply by 2.
Check the trap: \((2\times3)^3=6^3=216\) is a different calculation, because the 3 is only on the \(a\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The ratio of the sides of a right-angled triangle is 3:4:5. If the shortest side is 6 cm, find the area of the triangle.
questions.hint: The shortest side is 3 parts of the ratio and equals 6 cm. Find one part, then the other two sides. In a right-angled triangle the two shorter sides are the base and the height, and the longest side (5 parts) is the hypotenuse.

keyPoints.text: ratio of the sides of a right-angled triangle is 3:4:5
keyPoints.note: The sides are 3, 4 and 5 parts. The longest side (5 parts) is the hypotenuse, so the base and height are the 3-part and 4-part sides.
The shortest side matches the smallest ratio number, 3.

steps.explain: The shortest side is 3 parts and is 6 cm. Find one part.
The other two sides are 4 parts and 5 parts.
The hypotenuse is the longest side (10 cm). The base and height are the two shorter sides, 6 cm and 8 cm. Area \(=\dfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}\).
Check: \(6^2+8^2=36+64=100=10^2\), so a triangle with sides 6, 8, 10 really is right-angled. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false?
options: In the fraction \(\dfrac12\), one is the numerator.
When 4.89 is rounded to the ones place, the answer is 5.
Ten thousandths place is located 5 places to the right of the decimal
\(\dfrac76\) is described as an improper fraction.
questions.hint: Check each statement one by one. Remember the place values after the decimal point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths, ten-thousandths. A fraction is improper when the numerator is bigger than the denominator.

keyPoints.text: Which of the following statements is false?
keyPoints.note: Three statements are true; find the ONE that is false.

steps.explain: Statement A: in \(\dfrac12\) the top number (1) is the numerator. TRUE.
Statement B: round 4.89 to the ones place. The tenths digit is 8, which is 5 or more, so round up to 5. TRUE.
Statement D: \(\dfrac76\) has a numerator bigger than the denominator, so it is an improper fraction. TRUE.
Statement C: the places to the right of the decimal point are 1st tenths, 2nd hundredths, 3rd thousandths, 4th ten-thousandths. So the ten-thousandths place is 4 places (not 5) to the right.
So statement C is false.

questions.stem: You need \(\dfrac45\) cups of water for a recipe. You accidentally put \(\dfrac13\) cups into the mixing bowl first. How many more cups of water do you need to add?
questions.hint: You need the difference between what the recipe needs and what is already in the bowl. Use a common denominator (15) to subtract the fractions.

keyPoints.text: How many more cups of water do you need to add
keyPoints.note: More needed = amount needed − amount already in the bowl.

steps.explain: The amount still needed is \(\dfrac45-\dfrac13\). Write both fractions with denominator 15 (the lowest common multiple of 5 and 3).
Subtract the numerators and keep the denominator.
Check: \(\dfrac{5}{15}+\dfrac{7}{15}=\dfrac{12}{15}=\dfrac45\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a whole number followed by its square?
questions.hint: The square of a number is the number multiplied by itself. Work out the square of the first number in each pair and see if it matches the second number.

keyPoints.text: not a whole number followed by its square
keyPoints.note: Three pairs are “number, square”. One pair is wrong.

steps.explain: \(1^2=1\times1=1\), so \(1,\ 1\) is correct.
\(11^2=11\times11=121\), not 144. (144 is \(12^2\).) So \(11,\ 144\) is NOT a number followed by its square.
The pair that does not fit is 11 and 144.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly identifies 4 consecutive odd integers where the sum of the middle two integers is equal to 24?
questions.hint: Consecutive odd integers go up by 2. The “middle two” of four numbers are the 2nd and 3rd. Add the 2nd and 3rd number in each option.

keyPoints.text: sum of the middle two integers is equal to 24
keyPoints.note: Add only the 2nd and 3rd numbers of each list.
Each option is a list of four numbers going up by 2.

steps.explain: Option A: the middle two are 7 and 9.
Option B: the middle two are 9 and 11.
Option C: the middle two are 11 and 13.
Option D: the middle two are 13 and 15, which add to 28. So only option C works.

questions.stem: What is 1230.932567 rounded to the nearest hundredths place?
questions.hint: The hundredths place is the 2nd digit after the decimal point. Look at the digit AFTER it (the thousandths digit): if it is 5 or more, round up, otherwise leave the hundredths digit alone.

keyPoints.note: Hundredths = 2 decimal places. Keep 2 digits after the decimal point.

steps.explain: Write out the decimal places: 1230.932567 has tenths 9, hundredths 3, thousandths 2, ...
Keep two decimal places: 1230.93. The next digit (thousandths) is 2, which is less than 5, so the 3 stays the same.
So the number rounded to the nearest hundredth is:
Check: the option 1230.9326 keeps 4 decimal places (nearest ten-thousandth), and 1230 is rounded to the ones place. \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Which of the following values is NOT equal to \(34\times(58+9)\)?
questions.hint: First find the value of \(34\times(58+9)\). Then test each option. Use the distributive law: \(a\times(b+c)=a\times b+a\times c\), but be careful that the SAME number multiplies both parts.

keyPoints.note: Three options equal the given expression and ONE does not.

steps.explain: Work out the bracket first: \(58+9=67\), so the given expression is \(34\times67\).
Option A is exactly \(34\times67\). Equal.
Option C uses the distributive law correctly: \(34\times58=1972\) and \(34\times9=306\), and \(1972+306=2278\). So options C and D are equal.
Option B: \(58\times(34+9)=58\times43=2494\). It multiplies 58 by the sum of 34 and 9, which is a different calculation.
So option B is not equal.

questions.stem: How many cubed pieces of fudge that are 3 cm on each side can be packed into a Christmas tin that is 9 cm deep by 12 cm wide by 8 cm high with the lid still being able to be closed?
questions.hint: Count how many cubes fit along each edge of the tin. Careful: the lid must still close, so the pieces cannot stick up above the top. Only WHOLE cubes count (no cutting).

keyPoints.text: with the lid still being able to be closed
keyPoints.note: The cubes must stay inside the 8 cm height. A stack of 3 cubes would be 9 cm, which is too tall.
Each cube measures 3 cm in every direction.

steps.explain: Along the 9 cm depth: \(9\div3=3\) cubes fit exactly.
Along the 12 cm width: \(12\div3=4\) cubes fit exactly.
Along the 8 cm height: \(8\div3=2\) remainder 2, so only 2 layers of cubes fit (3 layers would be 9 cm, which is more than 8 cm, so the lid would not close).
Multiply the numbers of cubes along the three edges.
Check: if you divided the volumes, \(\dfrac{9\times12\times8}{27}=32\), but the cubes cannot be cut, so only 24 whole cubes fit. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: In a writing competition, first place receives \(\dfrac12\) of the prize money. The runner up receives \(\dfrac14\) of what the first place won. What was the total amount of prize money distributed if the runner up receives \(\$6,000\)?
questions.hint: Work backwards. The runner up gets \(\dfrac14\) of the FIRST prize, so find the first prize. The first prize is \(\dfrac12\) of ALL the prize money, so double it.

keyPoints.text: \(\dfrac14\) of what the first place won
keyPoints.note: The quarter is a quarter of the FIRST prize, not of the total.

keyPoints.text: total amount of prize money distributed
keyPoints.note: The total is bigger than the first prize: first prize is only half of it.

steps.explain: The runner up has \(\dfrac14\) of the first prize, so the first prize is 4 times as much.
First place receives \(\dfrac12\) of the total prize money, so the total is double the first prize.
Check: first place \(=\dfrac12\times48\,000=24\,000\), runner up \(=\dfrac14\times24\,000=6000\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The cost to ride on a ferry is \(\$5.00\) per vehicle and driver with an additional cost of 50 cents per passenger. If the charge to get on the ferry was \(\$6.50\), how many people were in the vehicle?
questions.hint: The driver is included in the \(\$5.00\) vehicle charge. Take that away from \(\$6.50\) to find what was paid for PASSENGERS. Then remember to count the driver too when answering “how many people”.

keyPoints.note: The \(\$5.00\) already covers the vehicle AND the driver.

keyPoints.text: how many people were in the vehicle
keyPoints.note: People = passengers + the driver.

steps.explain: Take the vehicle-and-driver charge from the total.
Each passenger costs 50 cents, \(\$0.50\).
The driver is also a person in the vehicle, so add 1.
Check: \(5.00+3\times0.50=\$6.50\). \(\checkmark\) The option 3 forgets the driver.

questions.stem: Sue receives a base salary of \(\$90\) weekly plus a 12% commission on all sales. Sue made \(\$3,000\) in sales this week. How much did she make in total?
questions.hint: Her total pay is the base salary PLUS the commission. Find 12% of the sales for the commission.

keyPoints.note: Commission = 12% of \(\$3,000\).

keyPoints.text: How much did she make in total
keyPoints.note: Total = base salary + commission.

steps.explain: Find the commission: 12% of \(\$3000\). 1% is \(\$30\), so 12% is 12 times that.
Add the base salary of \(\$90\).
Check: the option \(\$360\) (not offered) would be the commission only. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Two angles in a triangle equal \(55^\circ\). What is the measurement of the third angle?
questions.hint: The three angles of a triangle always add up to \(180^\circ\). The two angles together are \(55^\circ\), so the third angle is what is left.

keyPoints.text: Two angles in a triangle equal
keyPoints.note: The two angles TOGETHER make 55°, so subtract that total from 180°.

steps.explain: The angles of a triangle add up to \(180^\circ\).
The two angles together equal \(55^\circ\).
Subtract from \(180^\circ\) to find the third angle.

Check: \(55^\circ+125^\circ=180^\circ\). \(\checkmark\) The third angle is bigger than \(90^\circ\), so the triangle is obtuse. (If each of the two angles were \(55^\circ\) the third would be \(70^\circ\), but the question gives \(55^\circ\) for the pair together.)

questions.stem: Pipe A can fill a tank in 3 hours. If pipe B can fill the same tank in 2 hours, how many minutes will it take both pipes to fill \(\dfrac23\) of the tank altogether?
questions.hint: Work with the part of the tank each pipe fills in ONE hour, and add them. Then find how long \(\dfrac23\) of the tank takes. Change hours to minutes at the end.

keyPoints.text: fill the same tank in 2 hours
keyPoints.note: Pipe B fills 1/2 of the tank each hour; pipe A fills 1/3 each hour.
You only need to fill two thirds of the tank, not the whole tank.

steps.explain: In one hour pipe A fills \(\dfrac13\) of the tank and pipe B fills \(\dfrac12\) of the tank. Together:
Time to fill \(\dfrac23\) of the tank \(=\) amount \(\div\) rate.
Change \(\dfrac45\) of an hour into minutes.

Check: in 48 minutes (\(\dfrac45\) h) pipe A fills \(\dfrac13\times\dfrac45=\dfrac{4}{15}\) and pipe B fills \(\dfrac12\times\dfrac45=\dfrac{6}{15}\). Together \(\dfrac{10}{15}=\dfrac23\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Which angle from the following is an obtuse angle?
questions.hint: An obtuse angle is bigger than \(90^\circ\) and smaller than \(180^\circ\). Change each option into degrees: a right angle is \(90^\circ\) and a full revolution is \(360^\circ\).

keyPoints.note: Obtuse: more than 90° but less than 180°.

steps.explain: Option A: \(\dfrac{12}{21}\) of a right angle is less than one right angle, so it is acute.
Option B: \(\dfrac{11}{21}\) of a revolution is just over half a turn (\(180^\circ\)), so it is a reflex angle.
Option C: \(\dfrac{8}{20}=\dfrac25\) of a revolution.
\(144^\circ\) is between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), so it is obtuse. Option D: \(\dfrac{8}{20}\) of a right angle is \(36^\circ\), which is acute.

questions.stem: Three single squares are placed side by side to form a single rectangle whose perimeter is 56 cm. What is the area of each square?
questions.hint: Let the side of each square be \(s\). The rectangle is \(3s\) long and \(s\) wide. Write the perimeter in terms of \(s\) and solve, then find the area of ONE square.

keyPoints.text: Three single squares are placed side by side
keyPoints.note: The rectangle is 3 squares long and 1 square high: 3s by s.
The answer is the area of ONE square (s × s), not of the rectangle.

steps.explain: Let the side of each square be \(s\). The rectangle has length \(3s\) and width \(s\).
Perimeter \(=2\times(\text{length}+\text{width})\).
Divide by 8.
Area of one square.
Check: the rectangle is 21 cm by 7 cm, and its perimeter is \(2(21+7)=56\) cm. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Each fortnight 20% of Steven's pay goes to home loan repayments and 28% to tax. This leaves him with \(\$416.00\). What is his weekly pay?
questions.hint: A fortnight is TWO weeks. The percentages and the \(\$416\) refer to ONE fortnight of pay. First find his pay for a fortnight, then halve it to get his weekly pay.

keyPoints.note: A fortnight is 2 weeks (14 days). The deductions are taken from the pay for a fortnight.
The question asks for the pay per WEEK, so divide the fortnightly pay by 2.

steps.explain: 20% goes to the loan and 28% to tax. Find the percentage that is left.
The \(\$416\) is 52% of his fortnightly pay. Find 1%, then 100%.
So his pay for a fortnight is \(\$800\). A fortnight is 2 weeks, so his weekly pay is half of that.
Check: weekly pay \(\$400\) gives a fortnightly pay of \(\$800\); 52% of \(\$800\) is \(\$416\). \(\checkmark\) (The option \(\$800\) is his pay for a whole fortnight.)

keyPoints.text: at an average speed of 80 km/h for 60 km
keyPoints.note: Two different speeds (80 and 100 km/h): calculate each time on its own.

keyPoints.text: How long does it take to travel the 100 km
keyPoints.note: Add the two times.

steps.explain: Time for the first 60 km at 80 km/h.
Time for the other 40 km at 100 km/h.
Add the two times.

keyPoints.note: Adam = 2 × George.

questions.stem: Greg normally earns \(\$950\) for a 38-hour week. For how many hours of overtime would he have worked in a week where his total pay is \(\$1150\), if all overtime is paid double times?
questions.hint: Find his normal hourly rate first. Double time means TWICE that rate. The extra money above his normal \(\$950\) is all overtime pay.

keyPoints.note: Hourly rate = 950 ÷ 38.
Each overtime hour pays 2 × the normal hourly rate.

steps.explain: Normal hourly rate.
Overtime rate is double time.
Overtime pay is the money above his normal pay.
Hours of overtime.
Check: \(950+4\times50=950+200=\$1150\). \(\checkmark\) The option 42 hours would be his total hours (\(38+4\)).

questions.stem: A box with 100 matches weighs 50 grams. The same box with 50 matches weighs 36 grams. Find the weight of the box.
questions.hint: The difference between the two weighings is the weight of the 50 matches that were taken out. Use it to find the weight of 50 matches, then take that away from the lighter weighing to find the box.

keyPoints.text: The same box with 50 matches weighs 36 grams
keyPoints.note: Both weighings use the same box; only the number of matches changes.

steps.explain: The box with 100 matches weighs 50 g and with 50 matches weighs 36 g. The difference is the weight of 50 matches.
The box with 50 matches weighs 36 g. Take away the 50 matches (14 g) to get the box.
Check: 100 matches weigh 28 g, and \(22+28=50\) g. Also 50 matches weigh 14 g and \(22+14=36\) g. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Fifteen students took part in a maths competition. The number of children who finished behind Jane was six times as large as the number of children who were more successful than her. In which place did Jane finish?
questions.hint: The 15 students are split into three groups: the students ahead of Jane, Jane herself, and the students behind Jane. Let the number ahead be \(x\), so the number behind is \(6x\).

keyPoints.note: Behind = 6 × (number ahead).

keyPoints.text: In which place did Jane finish
keyPoints.note: Place = (number of students ahead of her) + 1.

steps.explain: Let \(x\) students finish ahead of Jane. Then \(6x\) finish behind her, and Jane is 1 student.
Simplify and solve.
Two students finished ahead of Jane, so she finished in the next place.
Check: 2 ahead, Jane, and 12 behind: \(2+1+12=15\), and \(12=6\times2\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The area of the first page of a book is 600 square centimetres. What is the area, in square metres, of all the pages of a 50-page book laid side by side?
questions.hint: Find the total area in \(\text{cm}^2\) first (50 pages of 600 \(\text{cm}^2\)). Then change to \(\text{m}^2\): \(1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}\), so \(1\text{ m}^2=100\times100=10\,000\text{ cm}^2\).

keyPoints.note: Square metres: divide square centimetres by 10 000 (not by 100).
50 pages of the same area: multiply by 50.

steps.explain: Total area of the 50 pages.
Change to square metres. \(1\text{ m}^2=100\text{ cm}\times100\text{ cm}=10\,000\text{ cm}^2\).
Divide by 10 000.
Check: the option 30 comes from wrongly dividing by 1000, and 300 would come from dividing by 100. \(\checkmark\)

questions.hint: Solve each equation for \(p\) (collect the \(p\) terms on one side and the numbers on the other) and then compare the four values of \(p\).

keyPoints.note: You need to find p in EACH equation and compare the answers.

steps.explain: Option A: add \(p\) to both sides, then subtract 222.
Option B: add \(p\) and add 2 to both sides.
Option C: add \(p\) to both sides.
Option D: subtract \(21p\) and 2 from both sides.
Compare the values: 0, 3, 2 and 2. The largest is 3, from option B.

questions.stem: Apples are sold in bags of four that cost \(\$5\) per bag, or bags of six that cost \(\$6\) per bag. What is the smallest cost at which you can buy 74 apples?
questions.hint: Find which bag is cheaper per apple (the bag of 6 costs \(\$1\) per apple, the bag of 4 costs \(\$1.25\) per apple), so use as many bags of six as you can. Then make exactly 74 apples with the remaining bags.

keyPoints.note: Use the cheaper bag (6 apples for \(\$6\)) as much as possible.
You need at least 74 apples. Try combinations of 6-bags and 4-bags.

steps.explain: Price per apple: bag of 4 \(=5\div4=\$1.25\); bag of 6 \(=6\div6=\$1.00\). The bag of 6 is the better buy.

Try the biggest number of 6-bags that leaves a number of apples that 4-bags can make. \(74\div6=12\) remainder 2, but 2 is not a multiple of 4, so use 11 bags of six: \(66\) apples, leaving \(74-66=8\), which is exactly 2 bags of four.
Cost of 11 bags of six and 2 bags of four.
Check other ways to buy at least 74 apples: 13 bags of six (78 apples) cost \(\$78\), and 12 bags of six plus 1 bag of four (76 apples) cost \(\$77\). Both cost more than \(\$76\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Peter has an average of 60 marks on his first four Maths tests. He missed the last (fifth) test and got zero. What is the average score now?
questions.hint: Find his TOTAL marks on the first four tests (average \(\times\) 4). A zero adds nothing to the total but he now has 5 tests, so divide the same total by 5.

keyPoints.text: an average of 60 marks on his first four Maths tests
keyPoints.note: Total of the first four tests = 60 × 4.
The fifth test adds 0 marks but counts as a test, so divide by 5.

steps.explain: Total marks for the first four tests.
The fifth test is zero, so the total is still 240, but there are now 5 tests.
New average \(=\) total \(\div\) number of tests.
Check: the average has gone down from 60, so the answer must be less than 60. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem:
What whole number ‘X’ makes this statement not true?

\(\dfrac36\lt\dfrac{X}{9}\lt\dfrac56\)
questions.hint: Write all three fractions with the same denominator, 18, so you can compare the tops. Then X is allowed only if \(\dfrac{2X}{18}\) is strictly between the other two. Find the X that does NOT fit.

keyPoints.note: Three of the options make the statement TRUE; find the one that makes it false.

steps.explain: Use the common denominator 18: \(\dfrac36=\dfrac{9}{18}\), \(\dfrac{X}{9}=\dfrac{2X}{18}\), \(\dfrac56=\dfrac{15}{18}\).
So \(2X\) must be between 9 and 15, which means X is between 4.5 and 7.5.
The whole numbers that work are 5, 6 and 7.
X = 8 gives \(\dfrac{8}{9}=\dfrac{16}{18}\), which is bigger than \(\dfrac{15}{18}\), so the statement is NOT true.

questions.stem: John answers 25 multiple choice questions and receives a score of zero. Each correct answer is worth 3 points. Two points are deducted for each incorrect answer. How many questions does he answer correctly?
questions.hint: His score is zero, so the points won for the correct answers must exactly cancel the points lost for the incorrect answers. Let \(c\) be the number correct, and \(25-c\) the number incorrect. Or try each option.

keyPoints.note: Points for correct answers = points taken off for incorrect answers.

keyPoints.text: Two points are deducted for each incorrect answer
keyPoints.note: Each incorrect answer loses 2 points.

steps.explain: Let \(c\) be the number correct. Then \(25-c\) are incorrect. Points gained and points lost are equal.
Expand the bracket.
Add \(2c\) to both sides, then divide by 5.
Check: 10 correct earns \(30\) points and 15 incorrect loses \(30\) points. \(30-30=0\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The population of a certain town increases by 50 percent every 50 years. If the population in 1950 was 810, in what year was the population 360?
questions.hint: Work BACKWARDS in time. Going back 50 years divides the population by 1.5 (undo a 50% increase). Keep going until you reach 360.

keyPoints.note: Each 50 years the population is multiplied by 1.5. Going back, divide by 1.5.

keyPoints.text: in what year was the population 360
keyPoints.note: Go back one 50-year step at a time.

steps.explain: The 50 percent increase multiplies by 1.5. Going back 50 years from 1950 (to 1900), divide by 1.5.
Go back another 50 years (to 1850).
So the population was 360 in 1850.
Check forwards: \(360\times1.5=540\) (1900) and \(540\times1.5=810\) (1950). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Jerry walks half a distance at 4 km/h and runs the other half. If the total distance is 12 km and it takes 2 hours for the entire trip, how fast does he run?
questions.hint: Half of the distance is 6 km. Find how long the walking takes (time \(=\) distance \(\div\) speed), take it from the 2 hours to get the running time, and then find the running speed.

keyPoints.text: walks half a distance at 4 km/h
keyPoints.note: Half of 12 km = 6 km walked at 4 km/h.

keyPoints.text: it takes 2 hours for the entire trip
keyPoints.note: Walking time + running time = 2 hours.

steps.explain: Each half of the trip is 6 km. Time spent walking.
Time left for the running half.
Speed \(=\) distance \(\div\) time for the run.
Check: running 6 km at 12 km/h takes 0.5 h and walking takes 1.5 h, total 2 hours. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: What number is half way between 4.8 and 5.3?
questions.hint: The number half way between two numbers is their average: add them and divide by 2. Or find the gap between them, halve it and add that half to the smaller number.

keyPoints.note: Half way = the midpoint = the average of the two numbers.

steps.explain: Find the gap between the two numbers.
Half of the gap.
Add this to the smaller number.
Check with the average: \((4.8+5.3)\div2=10.1\div2=5.05\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If Ray is paid \(\$480\) for 10 hours, how much will he be paid for 12 hours work at the same rate?
questions.hint: Find how much Ray is paid for ONE hour (divide), then multiply by 12 hours. 12 hours is more than 10 hours, so the pay must be more than \(\$480\).

keyPoints.note: The same pay per hour: find the pay for 1 hour first.

steps.explain: Pay for one hour.
Pay for 12 hours.
Check: 12 hours is \(\dfrac{12}{10}=1.2\) times as long, so the pay is \(480\times1.2=576\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: What is the smallest number which is greater than 5000 and a multiple of 12?
questions.hint: Divide 5000 by 12 and look at the remainder. The next multiple of 12 above 5000 needs a few more to complete the last group of 12.

keyPoints.text: greater than 5000 and a multiple of 12
keyPoints.note: The number must be BIGGER than 5000 and divisible by 12 exactly.

steps.explain: Divide 5000 by 12.
\(416\times12=4992\), which is less than 5000. The next multiple of 12 is one more lot of 12.
Check: \(5004\div12=417\) exactly, and 5004 is greater than 5000 while 4992 is not. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem:
Find the four-digit number which fits all of the following criteria.

The tens digit is three times the units digit.
The thousands digit is twice the tens digit.
The hundreds digit is one more than the thousands digit.
The sum of the digits is seventeen.
questions.hint: Let the units digit be \(u\) and write every other digit using \(u\). The digits must be 0 to 9, which limits the possible values of \(u\). Then test the sum 17.

keyPoints.text: The tens digit is three times the units digit
keyPoints.note: Tens = 3 × units, so the units digit can only be 0, 1, 2 or 3.

keyPoints.text: The sum of the digits is seventeen
keyPoints.note: Check this last to choose the right value.

steps.explain: Let the units digit be \(u\). Then the tens digit is \(3u\), the thousands digit is \(2\times3u=6u\), and the hundreds digit is \(6u+1\).
All digits must be at most 9. The thousands digit \(6u\) is at most 9, so \(u=1\) (u = 0 would give a number starting with 0).
Put the digits in place: thousands 6, hundreds 7, tens 3, units 1.
Check the sum of the digits.
So the number is 6731.

questions.stem:
What could be the value of \(m\)?

\((m-2)^2=\dfrac14\)
questions.hint: If a number squared is \(\dfrac14\), the number itself is \(\dfrac12\) or \(-\dfrac12\). So \(m-2\) is one of these two values. Solve for \(m\) both ways and see which appears in the options.

keyPoints.text: What could be the value of
keyPoints.note: There may be two values of m; only one of them is an option.

steps.explain: Take the square root of both sides. A square can come from a positive or a negative number.
First case: add 2 to both sides.
Second case: add 2 to \(-\dfrac12\).
\(1\dfrac12\) is one of the options.
Check: \(\left(1\dfrac12-2\right)^2=\left(-\dfrac12\right)^2=\dfrac14\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A container holds 7.2 litres when half full. How much more liquid is needed to make it \(\dfrac23\) full?
questions.hint: Find the capacity of the full container first (7.2 L is only half). Then find the amount in \(\dfrac23\) of the container and subtract the 7.2 L already there.

keyPoints.note: 7.2 L is HALF of the container, so the whole container holds 14.4 L.
More needed = (amount at 2/3 full) − 7.2 L.

steps.explain: 7.2 litres is half full, so the full container holds twice as much.
When \(\dfrac23\) full the container holds:
The extra liquid needed is the difference.
Check with fractions: \(\dfrac23-\dfrac12=\dfrac16\) of the container, and \(\dfrac16\times14.4=2.4\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A certain fraction has 1 added to both the numerator and denominator. If the new fraction is (or is equivalent to) \(\dfrac23\), which is not the possible starting fraction?
questions.hint: Add 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom of EACH option, then simplify. Three of them become \(\dfrac23\) (or an equivalent fraction); one does not.

keyPoints.text: which is not the possible starting fraction
keyPoints.note: Find the option that does NOT become 2/3 after adding 1 to numerator and denominator.

steps.explain: Option A: \(\dfrac{19+1}{29+1}=\dfrac{20}{30}\). Divide the top and bottom by 10.
Option B: \(\dfrac{13+1}{20+1}=\dfrac{14}{21}\). Divide by 7.
Option C: \(\dfrac{5+1}{8+1}=\dfrac{6}{9}\). Divide by 3.
Option D: \(\dfrac{6+1}{9+1}=\dfrac{7}{10}\), which is not equal to \(\dfrac23\) (\(0.7\ne0.667\)).
So \(\dfrac69\) is not a possible starting fraction.

questions.stem: What is the value of \(2^3\times(2^3-3)=\)?
questions.hint: Use the order of operations: brackets first, and inside the bracket do the power before the subtraction. \(2^3\) means \(2\times2\times2\).

keyPoints.note: Brackets first. Work out each power (2³ = 8) before subtracting or multiplying.

steps.explain: Work out the power: \(2^3=2\times2\times2=8\).
Replace both powers by 8.
Brackets first, then multiply.
Check: the common mistake \(8\times8-3=61\) forgets the bracket. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Box P contains 4 yellow and 8 red marbles, while Box Q contains 15 yellow and 9 red marbles. How many red marbles should be transferred from Box Q to Box P so that the fraction of yellow marbles in box P equals the fraction of red marbles in Box Q?
questions.hint: Try each option: move that many red marbles from Q to P and work out BOTH fractions (yellow in P over all marbles in P, and red in Q over all marbles in Q). Look for the option where they are equal.

keyPoints.text: the fraction of yellow marbles in box P equals the fraction of red marbles in Box Q
keyPoints.note: Fraction yellow in P = yellow ÷ total in P. Fraction red in Q = red ÷ total in Q.

steps.explain: Box P has \(4+8=12\) marbles and Box Q has \(15+9=24\) marbles. Moving red marbles changes the totals. Test 1 red marble: P has 13 marbles, Q has 23.
steps.work: \(\dfrac{4}{13}\text{ yellow in P},\quad\dfrac{8}{23}\text{ red in Q}\ \ (\ne)\)

steps.explain: Test 2 red marbles: P has 14 marbles, Q has 22 marbles.
Test 3 red marbles: P has 15 marbles, Q has 21 marbles.
Test 4 red marbles: P has 16 marbles, Q has 20 marbles and 5 red marbles.
The two fractions are equal when 4 red marbles are moved.

questions.stem: 20% of a number is equal to \(\dfrac{p}{30}\) of the same number. What is the value of \(p\)?
questions.hint: Write 20% as a fraction (out of 100) and simplify. Then make its denominator 30 so that you can compare the numerators.

keyPoints.text: 20% of a number is equal to
keyPoints.note: 20% of the number and p/30 of the number are the same, so 20% = p/30.

steps.explain: 20% means 20 out of 100. Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 20.
We need \(\dfrac15=\dfrac{p}{30}\). Make the denominator 30 by multiplying the top and bottom by 6.
Check: \(\dfrac{6}{30}=0.2=20\%\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If the base of a triangle is increased by 10% while the height is decreased by 10%, what is the percentage change in the area?
questions.hint: Use easy numbers such as base 10 and height 10. Work out the original area and the new area (110% of the base and 90% of the height), then compare.

keyPoints.text: increased by 10% while the height is decreased by 10%
keyPoints.note: Base becomes 110% (1.1 ×) and height becomes 90% (0.9 ×).
Compare the new area with the ORIGINAL area.

steps.explain: Let the base and the height both be 10. The original area is \(\dfrac12\times10\times10\).
New base: 10% more than 10 is 11. New height: 10% less than 10 is 9.
New area.
The area went from 50 to 49.5, a decrease of 0.5, which is 1% of 50.
Check with multipliers: \(1.1\times0.9=0.99=99\%\) of the original area. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of boxes measuring 0.3m x 0.2m x 1m that can be packed into a container measuring 1.01m x 2m x 3m?
questions.hint: Whole boxes must fit along each edge of the container. Try to match the box edges to the container edges so that as little space as possible is wasted: the 1 m edge of the box fits across the 1.01 m edge of the container.

keyPoints.note: Choose the way of turning the boxes that wastes the least space.
Divide each container edge by a box edge and use whole numbers only.

steps.explain: Put the 1 m edge of the box along the 1.01 m edge of the container: 1 box fits (1 m is less than 1.01 m).
Put the 0.2 m edge along the 2 m edge: \(2\div0.2=10\) boxes fit.
Put the 0.3 m edge along the 3 m edge: \(3\div0.3=10\) boxes fit.
Multiply the numbers along the three edges.

Check by volume: the container is \(1.01\times2\times3=6.06\text{ m}^3\) and each box is \(0.06\text{ m}^3\), so at most \(6.06\div0.06=101\) would be possible by volume, but only 100 whole boxes fit. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: How many 200 mL glasses of juice are needed to completely fill a 4 litre bottle?
questions.hint: The bottle is in LITRES and the glasses are in MILLILITRES. Change both to millilitres first (1 litre = 1000 mL). Then divide.

keyPoints.note: Glass size is in millilitres.
Change litres to millilitres: multiply by 1000.

steps.explain: Change the bottle size into millilitres.
How many 200 mL glasses fit into 4000 mL?
Check: 5 glasses make 1 litre (\(5\times200=1000\) mL), so 4 litres need \(4\times5=20\) glasses. \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Which number is halfway between \(\dfrac14\) and \(\dfrac18\)?
questions.hint: Halfway means the average. Change both fractions to eighths (a common denominator) before adding, then halve the sum.

keyPoints.note: Halfway = the average of the two numbers: add and divide by 2.

steps.explain: Use the common denominator 8: \(\dfrac14=\dfrac28\).
Divide the sum by 2.
Check with sixteenths: \(\dfrac14=\dfrac{4}{16}\) and \(\dfrac18=\dfrac{2}{16}\). The number halfway between 4 and 2 is 3, so \(\dfrac{3}{16}\). \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Which number cannot be the result of the multiplication of an integer and 3?
questions.hint: A number that is 3 times an integer is a multiple of 3. Use the divisibility test for 3: add the digits (ignore the minus sign); the digit sum must be a multiple of 3.

keyPoints.text: cannot be the result of the multiplication of an integer and 3
keyPoints.note: The numbers that CAN be made are the multiples of 3, including negative ones.

steps.explain: Test 7767: \(7+7+6+7=27\), a multiple of 3.
Test 6533: \(6+5+3+3=17\), which is not a multiple of 3. So it is not 3 times an integer.
So 6533 cannot be the result.

questions.stem: What is the week's wages earned by a person who gets \(\$380\) per week plus 2% commission on the sale of goods in excess of \(\$10,000\), if his sales total \(\$26,000\)?
questions.hint: The 2% commission is paid only on the sales ABOVE \(\$10,000\) (the “excess”). Find the excess first, then 2% of it, then add the weekly \(\$380\).

keyPoints.note: Only the sales above \(\$10,000\) earn commission: 26,000 − 10,000.
Commission = 2% of the excess sales.

steps.explain: Sales above \(\$10\,000\).
Commission: 2% of \(\$16\,000\).
Add the weekly wage of \(\$380\).
Check: the option \(\$900\) would come from 2% of ALL the sales (\(0.02\times26\,000=520\), \(380+520\)). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The dimensions of a rectangular box are in the ratio of 4:2:5 and its volume is \(1080\text{ cm}^3\). What could not be one of the dimensions of the box?
questions.hint: Let the dimensions be \(4k\), \(2k\) and \(5k\) for some number \(k\). Their product is the volume. Find \(k\), then the three dimensions, and see which option is not one of them.

keyPoints.note: The dimensions are 4 parts, 2 parts and 5 parts, so write them as 4k, 2k and 5k.

keyPoints.text: What could not be one of the dimensions
keyPoints.note: Three options are real dimensions of the box; one is not.

steps.explain: Write the dimensions as \(4k\), \(2k\) and \(5k\). The volume is the product.
Divide by 40, then find the number that multiplies by itself three times to give 27.
Find the three dimensions.
The dimensions are 12 cm, 6 cm and 15 cm. So 27 cm cannot be one of them.
Check: \(12\times6\times15=1080\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: What is the total cost of cementing a backyard 0.5 metres long and 0.7 metres wide at \(\$85\) per square metre?
questions.hint: Find the area of the backyard in square metres (length \(\times\) width), then multiply by the cost per square metre. Be careful with the decimal point.

keyPoints.note: Area = 0.5 × 0.7 square metres (a number smaller than 1).
Cost = area × 85.

steps.explain: Area of the backyard: \(5\times7=35\), and there are two decimal places in total, so \(0.5\times0.7=0.35\).
Cost \(=\) area \(\times\) price per square metre.
\(35\times85=2975\), and with two decimal places the answer is \(29.75\).
Check: the backyard is small (a bit more than a third of a square metre), so the cost should be a bit more than a third of \(\$85\), which is about \(\$29\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Which one is the best value for money?
questions.hint: Compare the price for the SAME amount in every option: find the price of 1 kg for each (divide the price by the number of kilograms). The smallest price per kilogram is the best value.

keyPoints.note: Best value = the lowest price per kilogram.

steps.explain: Option A: 1 kg costs \(\$6.90\).
Option B: \(\$10.50\) for 3 kg.
Option C: \(\$23.80\) for 5 kg, and option D: \(\$79.60\) for 20 kg.
Compare the price per kilogram: 6.90, 3.50, 4.76 and 3.98. The lowest is 3.50, option B.

questions.stem: Density is calculated as \(\dfrac{mass}{volume}\). What is the mass, in grams, of a nugget of gold with a density of \(19\text{ g/cm}^3\) and volume of \(54\text{ cm}^3\)?
questions.hint: Rearrange the formula: if density \(=\dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\), then mass \(=\) density \(\times\) volume. Check that the answer should be a large number (gold is heavy).

keyPoints.note: Multiply both sides of the formula by the volume to get the mass.

steps.explain: Start with the formula and multiply both sides by the volume.
Substitute the numbers.
Calculate: \(19\times54=20\times54-54=1080-54\).
Check: dividing the mass by the volume gives the density back: \(1026\div54=19\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Perth in Western Australia is 8 hours ahead of Greenwich in England. Cape Town in South Africa is 2 hours ahead of Greenwich. What is the time in Cape Town when it is 1 pm in Perth?
questions.hint: Go through Greenwich in the middle. “8 hours ahead” means Perth's clock shows a LATER time. So to get to Greenwich time, SUBTRACT 8 hours from Perth's time. Then ADD 2 hours to get Cape Town's time.

keyPoints.note: Perth is ahead, so Perth's time = Greenwich time + 8 hours.
Cape Town's time = Greenwich time + 2 hours.

steps.explain: Perth is 8 hours ahead of Greenwich. When it is 1 pm in Perth, Greenwich time is 8 hours earlier.
Cape Town is 2 hours ahead of Greenwich, so add 2 hours.
Check: Perth is \(8-2=6\) hours ahead of Cape Town, and \(7\text{ am}+6\text{ h}=1\text{ pm}\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A square with an area of \(625\text{ cm}^2\) has 5 cm taken off its sides. Find the area of the remaining shape.
questions.hint: Find the side of the square (the number that multiplies by itself to give 625). Taking 5 cm off the sides means taking 5 cm off EACH of the four sides of the square, so the new square is 10 cm smaller in length and 10 cm smaller in width.

keyPoints.text: has 5 cm taken off its sides
keyPoints.note: 5 cm is removed from every side, so each dimension loses 5 cm + 5 cm = 10 cm.

steps.explain: Side of the original square.
Taking 5 cm off the sides (from both ends of each dimension) leaves a smaller square.
Area of the new square.
Check: the option \(400\text{ cm}^2\) is a \(20\times20\) square, which would only be 5 cm off ONE side of each dimension. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: What is the number if \(\dfrac34\) plus half of the number is equal to 35?
questions.hint: Read it as: three quarters of the number PLUS half of the number equals 35. Add the two fractions of the number to see what fraction of the number 35 is, then work backwards to the whole number.

keyPoints.note: Both parts are fractions of the same unknown number: 3/4 of it and 1/2 of it.
Together the two parts make 35.

steps.explain: Add the two fractions of the number: \(\dfrac34+\dfrac12=\dfrac34+\dfrac24=\dfrac54\).
So \(\dfrac54\) of the number is 35. Find one fifth of the number's worth: \(35\div5\) gives \(\dfrac14\) of the number.
The whole number is 4 quarters.
Check: \(\dfrac34\) of 28 is 21 and half of 28 is 14. \(21+14=35\). \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: If a car is driving at 90 kilometres per hour, how many metres does it go in one second?
questions.hint: Change kilometres to metres (\(\times1000\)) and hours to seconds (\(1\text{ h}=3600\text{ s}\)). A quick way: divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s.

keyPoints.note: 90 km in each hour. Convert km to m and an hour to seconds.
The answer is a distance in metres for ONE second.

steps.explain: 90 km in one hour is 90 000 metres in one hour.
One hour has 3600 seconds, so divide by 3600.
Check: 25 m in each second, \(25\times3600=90\,000\) m in an hour \(=90\) km. \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: What is the smallest positive integer by which 180 should be multiplied so that the product is a perfect square?
questions.hint: A perfect square has every prime factor appearing an EVEN number of times. Write 180 as a product of primes, see which prime appears an odd number of times, and multiply by that prime once.

keyPoints.note: Use the smallest possible multiplier: only add the missing prime factors.
Every prime in the prime factorisation must appear an even number of times.

steps.explain: Write 180 as a product of prime factors.
The primes 2 and 3 appear twice each (even), but 5 appears only once (odd). To make it appear twice, multiply by 5.
The product is \(900=30\times30\), a perfect square, and 5 is the smallest multiplier.
So the smallest integer is 5.

questions.stem: A baker makes a cake in \(\dfrac23\) of an hour. If he works for \(7\dfrac12\) hours, how many cakes will he fully bake working at the same rate?
questions.hint: Divide the total working time by the time for one cake. If the answer has a fraction left over, only count the WHOLE cakes (the last cake is not fully baked).

keyPoints.text: how many cakes will he fully bake
keyPoints.note: Only complete cakes count: round DOWN.
The total time is 7.5 hours.

steps.explain: Divide the total time by the time for one cake. Dividing by \(\dfrac23\) is multiplying by \(\dfrac32\).
Multiply the tops and the bottoms.
He can start 11 full cakes and a quarter of the next one, so only 11 cakes are fully baked.
Check: 11 cakes take \(11\times\dfrac23=7\dfrac13\) hours, which is less than \(7\dfrac12\) hours; 12 cakes would need 8 hours, which is more. \(\checkmark\)

Add the new step to O \((6,4)\).

questions.stem:
The charges for travelling in a taxi are as follows: the hiring of the taxi is \(\$4\) (called flagfall) and it costs \(\$2.50\) per kilometre travelled.

What is the cost for a journey of 28 km?
questions.hint: The cost has two parts: a fixed charge (flagfall) of \(\$4\) AND a charge for each kilometre. Find the cost of the kilometres, then add the flagfall.

keyPoints.note: The flagfall is paid once, at the start, whatever the length of the journey.
The distance part = number of km × \(\$2.50\).

steps.explain: Cost for the kilometres travelled.
Add the flagfall.
Check: the option \(\$70\) forgets the flagfall of \(\$4\), and \(\$112\) is \(28\times4\), which wrongly uses the flagfall as the price per kilometre. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem:
The charges for travelling in a taxi are as follows: the hiring of the taxi is \(\$4\) (called flagfall) and it costs \(\$2.50\) per kilometre travelled.

What is the length of the journey, in kilometres, if the taxi fare is \(\$59\)?
questions.hint: Take away the flagfall (paid once) from the fare. What is left pays for the kilometres at \(\$2.50\) each. Divide to find the number of kilometres.

keyPoints.note: The fare includes the \(\$4\) flagfall. Take it off first.

steps.explain: Take the flagfall from the total fare.
The remaining \(\$55\) pays for the kilometres at \(\$2.50\) each.

questions.stem: Kerrie keeps a rectangular garden that measures 14 m long by 12 m wide. How many bags of fertiliser will she need if each bag covers \(5\text{ m}^2\)?
questions.hint: Find the area of the garden. Divide by the area one bag covers. If there is something left over, she needs one more bag (you cannot buy part of a bag).

keyPoints.text: How many bags of fertiliser will she need
keyPoints.note: Bags are whole: if a part of a bag is needed, she must buy a whole extra bag.

steps.explain: Area of the garden.
Each bag covers \(5\text{ m}^2\).
33 bags cover only \(165\text{ m}^2\), so \(3\text{ m}^2\) is left. She needs one more bag.
Check: 34 bags cover \(34\times5=170\text{ m}^2\), enough for \(168\text{ m}^2\). \(\checkmark\)

steps.explain: Then he goes back from 25 km to 15 km: 10 km towards A. He stays at 15 km for a while (0 km travelled), then goes back to town A: 15 km.
Finally he goes from A to B, which is 50 km.
Add all the parts of the journey.
Check: the option 50 km is only the last stage, and 140 km would add the flat part wrongly. \(\checkmark\)

Change \(\dfrac{100}{3}\) to a mixed number.
Check: \(33\dfrac13\times1.5=50\) km. \(\checkmark\) The option 50 is the distance, not the speed.

questions.stem: What is the value of 6 less than the sum of 5 times 8.5 and two?
questions.hint: Work from the inside out: first 5 times 8.5, then add two, and only then take away 6. The words “6 less than” come last.

keyPoints.note: “6 less than” means subtract 6 from the whole result at the end.

keyPoints.text: the sum of 5 times 8.5 and two
keyPoints.note: Do the multiplication first, then add two.

steps.explain: Find “5 times 8.5” first.
“The sum of” that and two means add two.
“6 less than” this number means subtract 6.
Check the trap: if you added 2 before multiplying you would get \(5\times(8.5+2)-6=46.5\), which is option A – but the words say 5 times 8.5 first.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: What is the cost of 480 g of fish if its price is \(\$26.00\) per kilogram?
questions.hint: The price is per KILOGRAM but the fish is in GRAMS. Change 480 g into kilograms first (divide by 1000), then multiply by the price.

keyPoints.note: Convert to kilograms first: 1000 g = 1 kg.
The price is for 1 kg – make the units match before multiplying.

steps.explain: Change grams into kilograms. There are 1000 g in 1 kg, so divide by 1000.
Multiply the mass in kg by the price per kg. Split \(0.48\) as \(0.5-0.02\) to make the multiplication easy.
Subtract the two parts.

Check: 480 g is a little less than half a kilogram, so the cost should be a little less than half of \(\$26\), which is \(\$13\). \(\$12.48\) fits; \(\$1.248\) and \(\$124.80\) are far too small and too big.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.hint: Count the cubes that have NO paint instead: they form a smaller cube hidden in the middle. Take the unpainted ones away from the total number of cubes.

keyPoints.text: faces painted on any number of sides
keyPoints.note: Painted on 1, 2 or 3 sides all count – so count the cubes with no paint and subtract.
A 7×7×7 cube makes 343 small cubes.

steps.explain: Count all the small cubes: 7 along the length, 7 along the width and 7 along the height.

A small cube has no paint only if it is not on the outside. Remove the outer layer from every side: each edge loses 1 cube at each end, so \(7-2=5\) cubes remain along each edge of the hidden inner cube.

questions.stem: What is \(10\frac{3}{4}\%\) as a decimal?
questions.hint: Two jobs: change the fraction \(\frac{3}{4}\) into a decimal, then turn the percentage into a decimal by dividing by 100 (move the point 2 places left).

keyPoints.note: A percentage is “out of 100”, so divide by 100 to get a decimal.

steps.explain: Change the fraction part into a decimal.
So the percentage is 10.75 per cent.
Per cent means “out of 100”, so divide by 100. This moves the decimal point 2 places to the left.
Check: 10% is 0.1, and the extra 0.75% is a bit more, so the answer is just above 0.1. Options 10.34, 10.75 and 1.075 are all bigger than 1 or far too large – only 0.1075 fits.

questions.stem: Shilla is counting aloud backwards from 99 by sixes, saying 99, 93, and so on. What is the last positive number she says?
questions.hint: Every number she says is 99 minus a multiple of 6. Divide 99 by 6 and look at the remainder – that is the smallest positive number she can reach.

keyPoints.note: Each number is 99 minus a multiple of 6.
Stop just before the numbers go below zero.

steps.explain: Write the numbers she says: each time we subtract 6.
Find how many sixes fit into 99.
After subtracting 16 sixes (that is 96) from 99, we are left with the remainder.
The next number would be \(3-6=-3\), which is negative, so 3 is the last positive number.
Check: 3 is in the pattern because \(99-3=96\) is a multiple of 6. Numbers like 2, 1 and 4 are not, since \(99-2=97\), \(99-1=98\), \(99-4=95\) are not multiples of 6.

questions.stem: A rectangle is subdivided into 4 smaller rectangles, A, B, C and D. The area of A is \(12\ \text{cm}^2\), B is \(15\ \text{cm}^2\) and C is \(10\ \text{cm}^2\). Find the perimeter of the large rectangle. The diagram is not to scale.

questions.hint: A and B sit side by side so they have the same height; A and C sit one above the other so they have the same width. Use area = width × height to find simple side lengths that fit 12, 15 and 10.

keyPoints.note: A and B share the same height; A and C share the same width.

keyPoints.text: Find the perimeter of the large rectangle
keyPoints.note: Add all four outside sides: 2 × (total width + total height).

steps.explain: A and B have the same height, so their areas \(12\) and \(15\) are in the same ratio as their widths. A and C have the same width, so \(12\) and \(10\) are in the same ratio as their heights.
Pick the simplest side lengths: A is \(4\times3=12\) and B is \(5\times3=15\), so both have height 3 and the widths are 4 and 5.
C has the same width as A (4), so its height is its area divided by 4.
D then has width 5 and height 2.5, so its area is \(5\times2.5=12.5\ \text{cm}^2\) – consistent with the pattern \(12:15=10:12.5\).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false?
questions.hint: A statement is false if you can find ONE example that breaks it. Check each statement by thinking: does the first shape always have every property of the second shape?

keyPoints.text: Which of the following statements is false?
keyPoints.note: To show a statement is false, one counter-example is enough.

steps.explain: A rhombus has 4 equal sides; a rectangle has 4 right angles. A statement “all X are Y” is true only if every X has all the properties of Y.
Test B with a counter-example: a rectangle 6 cm long and 3 cm wide has 4 right angles, but its sides are not all equal, so it is not a rhombus.
So “All rectangles are rhombuses” is FALSE.

Check the others. A: a square has 4 right angles, so it is a rectangle (true). C: a parallelogram has 4 sides, so it is a quadrilateral (true). D: a rhombus has two pairs of parallel sides, so it has at least one pair, which is what a trapezium needs (true).

questions.hint: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at 90°. Look at the small triangle with angle \(x\), the \(71^\circ\) angle and the right angle at the centre – the angles in a triangle add to \(180^\circ\).

keyPoints.note: The diagonals of a rhombus also cross at right angles (90°).
Use the triangle: x + 71° + 90° = 180°.

steps.explain: The diagonals of a rhombus meet at right angles, so the angle at the centre of the figure is \(90^\circ\). Look at the triangle formed by the top vertex, the centre and the right vertex.

questions.stem: At Mr Troy's shop, his employees work 20 hours each week and earn \(\$17\) per hour. He uses an expression to find the total weekly payroll for \(x\) number of employees. Which is the correct expression to find the total weekly payroll?
questions.hint: First find what ONE employee earns in a week (rate × hours). Then, for \(x\) employees, multiply that amount by the number of employees.

keyPoints.note: One employee earns 20 hours × 17 dollars per hour each week.
Total = pay of one employee × number of employees.

steps.explain: One employee works 20 hours at \(\$17\) per hour. Pay of one employee in a week = rate × hours.
There are \(x\) employees and each is paid the same, so multiply by \(x\).
Test it with a real number. If \(x=2\) employees, the payroll should be \(2\times340=\$680\).
Check the other options with \(x=2\): A gives \(17\times10=170\), B gives \(20\times19=380\), and C uses the letter \(n\), which is not in the question. Only D gives 680.

questions.stem: Four times the difference between \(2\frac{1}{8}\) and \(1\frac{1}{4}\) is
questions.hint: “Difference” means subtract. Change both mixed numbers to eighths, subtract them, and only then multiply the result by 4.

keyPoints.note: Subtract first (the difference), then multiply by 4.

steps.explain: “Difference between” means subtract the smaller number from the larger. Change both mixed numbers into improper fractions with denominator 8.
Subtract the numerators; the denominator stays 8.
“Four times” that difference.
Simplify: \(28\div8=3\) remainder \(4\), so \(3\frac{4}{8}=3\frac{1}{2}\).
Check in decimals: \(2.125-1.25=0.875\) and \(4\times0.875=3.5\). \(\checkmark\) Option C, \(\frac{7}{8}\), is only the difference – it forgot to multiply by 4.

questions.stem: Alex wants to invest \(\$4{,}000\) at 6% simple interest rate for 5 years. How much interest will he receive?
questions.hint: Use the simple interest formula \(I=P\times r\times t\): principal times rate (as a decimal) times the number of years. Interest is earned every year for 5 years.

keyPoints.note: Simple interest: the same amount of interest is added every year.

steps.explain: Name the formula: simple interest \(I=P\times r\times t\), where \(P\) is the amount invested, \(r\) the rate per year and \(t\) the time in years.
Interest for ONE year = 6% of \(\$4000\).
The interest is the same each year, so multiply by 5 years.
Check with the formula in one line. Note \(\$240\) is only the first year’s interest (option B).

questions.stem: When the time is 5:23 pm in Honolulu, it is 11.23 pm in Miami. It takes 12 hours to travel from Honolulu to Miami. If you leave at 4.50 pm on Sunday, at what time will you arrive in Miami?
questions.hint: First work out the time difference between the two cities. Then change your leaving time to Miami time and add the 12 hours of travel.

keyPoints.text: 5:23 pm in Honolulu, it is 11.23 pm in Miami
keyPoints.note: Subtract the two times to get the time difference between cities.
This leaving time is in Honolulu time.

steps.explain: Find the time difference. When it is 5:23 pm in Honolulu it is 11:23 pm in Miami, so Miami is 6 hours ahead.
Leaving at 4.50 pm Sunday Honolulu time is the same moment as 6 hours later on Miami’s clock.
Add the 12 hours of travelling. From 10.50 pm Sunday, 2 hours reach 12.50 am Monday (just after midnight), then 10 more hours.
Check by adding the travel time first: \(4.50\text{ pm}+12\text{ h}=4.50\text{ am Monday}\) Honolulu time, then add 6 hours for Miami: \(10.50\text{ am Monday}\). \(\checkmark\)

Add the next groups one at a time.

How many families had more than 2 children?

steps.explain: List which columns are “more than 2 children”. The columns are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 children, so only 3 and 4 are bigger than 2.

questions.hint: Look at how the first row works: \(\Delta=5\) gives \(2\times\Delta=10\) and then \(2\times\Delta+3=13\). For (a), work backwards from \(14.2\): undo the \(+3\) and then undo the \(\times2\).

keyPoints.text: What could be the value of (a)?
keyPoints.note: Work backwards: undo +3 first, then undo ×2.

steps.explain: Read the rule from the first row: start with \(\Delta\), double it, then add 3.
For (a) the last column is \(14.2\), so \(2\times\Delta+3=14.2\). Undo the “plus 3” by subtracting 3.
Undo the “times 2” by dividing by 2.

questions.stem: Which one is in descending order?
questions.hint: Descending means biggest first, getting smaller each time. Write every number with 3 decimal places so they are easy to compare, then compare digit by digit from the left.

keyPoints.note: Descending = from the largest to the smallest.

steps.explain: Give every number three decimal places so the columns line up.
Compare the whole numbers first: only 11.009 has 11, so it is the largest and comes first.
Now the others all start 10. Compare the tenths digit: 10.981 has 9 tenths, the rest have 0 tenths. So 10.981 comes next.
Compare the remaining three: tenths are 0 for all; hundredths are 1, 0, 0; so 10.010 is next. Then thousandths: 8 and 1, so 10.008 then 10.001.
Put them in order from largest to smallest.
Check: each number is smaller than the one before it, which is exactly option D. Option A is ascending (smallest first).

questions.hint: Find the side length of the square that is easy to read (the one in the top right). Both squares are the same size, so ABCD has the same side. B is at \((1,1)\) and D is the opposite corner.

keyPoints.note: Both squares have the same side length – measure it on the easier square.
The corner of ABCD labelled B is at (1, 1).

steps.explain: Read the square in the top right: its left side is at \(x=1\) and its right side is above 5 on the \(x\)-axis; its bottom is at \(y=1\) and its top is at \(y=5\). So its side length is \(5-1=4\).
The squares are the same size, so ABCD also has side length 4. Its top right corner B is at the touching point \((1,1)\).
D is the corner opposite B. From B it is 4 units left (the side AB) and 4 units down (the side BC).

questions.stem:
Both squares are exactly the same size. They both touch each other at (1, 1).

Point M is the centre of the square ABCD. What are its co-ordinates?

questions.hint: Find the corners of ABCD first (each side is 4 long and B is at \((1,1)\)). The centre of a square is the midpoint of a diagonal, for example of B and D.

keyPoints.note: The centre is the midpoint of the diagonal BD (or AC).

steps.explain: The top right square has side \(5-1=4\), so ABCD has side 4. Its corner B is at \((1,1)\), so the opposite corner D is 4 left and 4 down.
The centre M is the midpoint of the diagonal BD. Midpoint = average of the \(x\)-values and average of the \(y\)-values.
Do the same for the \(y\)-values.

questions.stem:
Here are lengths of a sample of 15 bananas. All measurements are in centimetres.

Row 3: 21 yes, 23 yes, 20.3 yes, 53 yes, 9.4 no.
Add the favourable outcomes.
Probability = favourable ÷ total, then simplify by dividing top and bottom by 5.
Check: the 5 bananas that are not longer than 14 cm are 12, 14, 13.5, 14 and 9.4, and \(10+5=15\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Throughout a night the temperature decreased by \(3^\circ\text{C}\) every hour. At 4 am, the temperature was \(-14^\circ\text{C}\). What was the temperature 3 hours before midnight?
questions.hint: Going BACK in time the temperature was warmer. Find what time “3 hours before midnight” is, count the hours from then to 4 am, and add 3°C for each hour.

keyPoints.note: It gets 3°C colder each hour, so going backwards it gets 3°C warmer each hour.
3 hours before 12 midnight is 9 pm.

steps.explain: Find the time: 3 hours before midnight (12 am) is 9 pm.
Count the hours from 9 pm to 4 am: 3 hours to reach midnight, then 4 more hours to reach 4 am.
The temperature fell by \(3^\circ\text{C}\) in each of those 7 hours.
At 4 am it was \(-14^\circ\text{C}\) after falling 21 degrees, so at 9 pm it was 21 degrees warmer.

Check by counting forwards: 9 pm: 7, 10 pm: 4, 11 pm: 1, midnight: \(-2\), 1 am: \(-5\), 2 am: \(-8\), 3 am: \(-11\), 4 am: \(-14\). \(\checkmark\) Option A is the temperature at midnight and option D is the temperature at 10 pm.

questions.stem: Kathy wants to buy a DVD game costing \(\$150\) but she has saved \(\$17.50\) per week for 6 weeks. The shop starts a sale and announces a discount of 25% on all items. How much more money does she need now?
questions.hint: Three steps: (1) how much has she saved, (2) what is the SALE price after taking 25% off \(\$150\), (3) sale price minus savings.

keyPoints.text: a discount of 25% on all items
keyPoints.note: Take 25% (one quarter) off the price of the game.

keyPoints.text: How much more money does she need now
keyPoints.note: Sale price − money saved.

steps.explain: Money saved: \(\$17.50\) each week for 6 weeks. Split \(17.50\) as \(10+7.50\).
The discount is 25%, which is one quarter. Find the discount amount.
Subtract the discount from the original price to get the sale price.
She needs the sale price but has only saved \(\$105\).
Check: before the sale she needed \(150-105=\$45\) more (option C), but the discount made it cheaper by \(\$37.50\), and \(45-37.50=7.50\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If the ratio of boys to girls in a class is 5 to 3, which of the following could not be the number of students in the class?
questions.hint: In the ratio 5 to 3 the class is made of groups of \(5+3\) students. The total must be a whole number of these groups, otherwise there would be a part of a student.

keyPoints.text: could not be the number of students
keyPoints.note: Find the total that is NOT a multiple of the number of ratio parts.

steps.explain: Add the ratio parts to find how many students are in one “group”: 5 boys and 3 girls.
The number of students in the class must be a multiple of 8. Divide each option by 8.
36 is not a multiple of 8.
So a class of 36 would need \(4.5\) groups, which gives boys \(4.5\times5=22.5\) – not a whole number of students.
steps.work: \(\boxed{36}\text{ could not be the class size}\)

steps.explain: Check the others work: 32 gives 20 boys and 12 girls; 40 gives 25 boys and 15 girls; 48 gives 30 boys and 18 girls.

questions.stem: The average IQ of 4 people is 110. If three of these people each have an IQ of 105, what is the IQ of the fourth person?
questions.hint: Average = total ÷ number of people, so total = average × number of people. Find the total of all 4 IQs, then take away the IQs of the three known people.

keyPoints.text: The average IQ of 4 people is 110
keyPoints.note: Total of the 4 IQs = 4 × 110.

keyPoints.text: three of these people each have an IQ of 105
keyPoints.note: Their total is 3 × 105.

steps.explain: Reverse the average: total = average × number of people.
Total IQ of the three people who each have 105.
The fourth person has whatever is left of the total.
Check: the average of the four IQs is \((105+105+105+125)\div4=440\div4=110\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A petrol pump can hold enough petrol to supply 900 cars with 60 litres each. How many cars can it supply with 50 litres each?
questions.hint: First find how many litres the pump holds altogether (cars × litres each). Then divide that total by 50 litres per car. Since each car gets less, MORE cars can be supplied.

keyPoints.note: Total petrol = 900 × 60 litres.
Divide the total by 50 to find the number of cars.

steps.explain: Find the total amount of petrol the pump holds.
Each car now gets 50 litres, so divide the total by 50.
Check by reasoning: 50 litres is less than 60 litres, so more than 900 cars can be filled. Also \(\frac{60}{50}=1.2\) and \(900\times1.2=1080\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: How many hectares is the area of 500 metres long and 60 metres wide?
questions.hint: First find the area in square metres (length × width). Then convert: 1 hectare is a square 100 m by 100 m, which is \(10\,000\text{ m}^2\).

keyPoints.note: 1 hectare = 10 000 m² (a square of side 100 m).
Area of a rectangle = length × width.

steps.explain: Area of the rectangle in square metres.
One hectare is a square 100 m by 100 m.
Divide the area in square metres by the number of square metres in one hectare.

Check in hundreds of metres: \(500\text{ m}=5\) lots of 100 m and \(60\text{ m}=0.6\) lots of 100 m, so the area is \(5\times0.6=3\) hectares. \(\checkmark\) Option A, 30 000, is just the area in square metres.

questions.stem: If A#B = \(\sqrt{A\times B}\) then what is the value of 36#49?
questions.hint: The symbol # is a new operation defined by the rule. Replace A with the first number (36) and B with the second number (49), multiply them inside the square root sign, then take the square root.

keyPoints.note: The rule tells you what the # symbol means: multiply the two numbers, then take the square root.
A = 36 and B = 49.

steps.explain: Match the numbers to the rule: in \(36\#49\) the first number is \(A=36\) and the second is \(B=49\).
Multiply inside the square root first. \(36\times49=1764\).
Find the square root. Since \(40\times40=1600\) and \(42\times42=1764\), the root is 42. (Easier way: \(\sqrt{36}\times\sqrt{49}=6\times7\).)
Check: \(42\times42=1764\). \(\checkmark\) Option A, 1764, forgets the square root and option C, 13, comes from adding \(6+7\) instead of multiplying.

steps.explain: Read the calcium row for “60 g alone”: the cereal contains 38 mg of calcium, and this is 5% of the daily allowance.

steps.explain: Find 1% by dividing both sides by 5.
The whole daily allowance is 100%, so multiply by 100.
Check: 5% is one twentieth, and \(760\div20=38\). \(\checkmark\) The 38 mg of option A is only the cereal’s share, not the total allowance.

questions.hint: Use the “60 g alone contains” column, by weight: it tells you how many grams of protein are in 60 g of cereal. Work out how many times bigger 30 g is than that amount.

keyPoints.note: Use only the “60 g alone” column, not the milk columns.
Compare 30 g with the 12.0 g of protein that 60 g of cereal gives.

steps.explain: Read the protein row for “60 g alone”: 60 g of cereal contains 12.0 g of protein.

questions.stem: A square of area \(100\ \text{cm}^2\) is cut to make two rectangles, A and B. The ratio of area A to area B is \(3:1\). Find the ratio of the perimeter of A to perimeter of B.

questions.hint: Find the side of the square from its area. Share the area 3 : 1 to get the area of A and B. Both rectangles are 10 cm tall, so find each width and then each perimeter.

keyPoints.note: Side of a square = square root of its area.

keyPoints.text: ratio of area A to area B
keyPoints.note: Share 100 cm² in the ratio 3 : 1, which is 4 equal parts.

steps.explain: The square has area \(100\ \text{cm}^2\), so its side is the square root of 100.
Share the area in the ratio \(3:1\). There are \(3+1=4\) parts, so each part is \(100\div4=25\ \text{cm}^2\).
The cut runs from top to bottom, so both rectangles are 10 cm tall. Width = area ÷ height.

steps.explain: Check the widths add up to the side of the square.
Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 × (width + height).
Write the ratio and simplify by dividing both by 5.
Check the trap: option B, \(3:1\), is the ratio of the AREAS. Perimeters do not share in the same ratio as areas.

questions.hint: C is in the X column of the last row, where the last column is 55. Work backwards from 55, or try the options in the rule \(\frac{X+X^2}{2}\).

keyPoints.text: What will be the value of C?
keyPoints.note: C is the X-value that gives 55 in the last column.

steps.explain: For C the last column is 55, so \((C+C^2)\div2=55\). Multiply both sides by 2.
\(C+C^2\) is \(C\times(C+1)\): two numbers side by side that multiply to 110. Think of numbers near the square root of 110, which is a little over 10.
Try \(C=10\): \(10\times11=110\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: George is a delivery man. He begins the day with a full tank of diesel. By lunchtime he has half of a tank left. In the afternoon, he uses \(\frac{2}{5}\) of the remainder of the tank. What fraction of the tank is left at the end of the day?
questions.hint: “\(\frac{2}{5}\) of the remainder” means \(\frac{2}{5}\) of what was left at lunchtime (half a tank), NOT \(\frac{2}{5}\) of a whole tank. Find how much is used, then subtract.

keyPoints.note: The remainder at lunchtime is 1/2 of a tank.

keyPoints.text: of the remainder of the tank
keyPoints.note: Take 2/5 of the half tank – not of the full tank.
