questions.stem:
A bag contains counters that are red, black or green. 6 counters are red, 6 counters are green and \(\frac{1}{5}\) of the counters are black.

How many black counters are in the bag?
questions.hint: If \(\frac{1}{5}\) of the counters are black, then \(\frac{4}{5}\) are NOT black. The red and green counters together are those \(\frac{4}{5}\).

keyPoints.note: 1/5 are black, so the other 4/5 are red or green.

keyPoints.text: 6 counters are red, 6 counters are green
keyPoints.note: Red + green = 12 counters make up 4/5 of the bag.

steps.explain: Add the red and green counters.
Since \(\frac{1}{5}\) are black, the red and green counters make up the other \(\frac{4}{5}\) of the bag.
So \(\frac{4}{5}\) of the counters is 12. Find \(\frac{1}{5}\) by dividing 12 by 4.
\(\frac{1}{5}\) of the bag is black, so there are 3 black counters (and the bag has \(5\times3=15\) counters).

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
A bag contains counters that are red, black or green. 6 counters are red, 6 counters are green and \(\frac{1}{5}\) of the counters are black.

Before I take a counter out of the bag, I put one extra black counter into the bag. What effect does this have on the probability that I take out a red counter?
options: The probability has stayed the same.
questions.hint: Probability of red = number of red counters ÷ total number of counters. Work out the bag first (from the black counter fraction), then see what changes when one more black counter is added.

keyPoints.note: The number of red counters stays the same, but the total goes up by 1.

keyPoints.text: probability that I take out a red counter
keyPoints.note: P(red) = red ÷ total.

steps.explain: Find the bag first. The 12 red and green counters are \(\frac{4}{5}\) of the bag, so there are 3 black counters and 15 counters in total.
Probability of red BEFORE adding the black counter.
After adding one black counter there are still 6 red counters but 16 counters in total.
Compare the two probabilities using a common denominator of 40.
\(\frac{15}{40}\) is less than \(\frac{16}{40}\), so the probability has decreased. In words: red stays at 6 but the total gets bigger, so each draw is less likely to be red.

questions.hint: Imagine each move on the N. A reflection gives a mirror image; a rotation turns the shape around O. Check which move puts the two stems AND the diagonal back exactly where they started.

keyPoints.note: Test each move: do both stems and the diagonal land back on the original N?
A rotation turns the letter about O; a reflection flips it into a mirror image.

steps.explain: Rotation of \(90^\circ\): a quarter turn makes the two upright stems horizontal, so the N looks like a Z. It does not land on itself.

Reflections: the diagonal of the N goes from top left to bottom right. A reflection in the vertical line (or in the horizontal line) swaps this to a diagonal from top right to bottom left, giving a backwards N. So neither reflection works.

questions.hint: Read the height of each bar to find how many students are in each group, and check the total is 50. Then test each statement: is it definitely true, or could it be false because the graph only gives groups of hours?

keyPoints.text: Which of these statements must be true?
keyPoints.note: “Must be true” – it has to be certain from the graph, not just possible.
The five bars must add up to 50; use this to check your readings.

steps.explain: Read the bars: 1–5 hours has 7 students, 6–10 hours has 9, 11–15 hours has 12, 16–20 hours has 17 and 21–25 hours has 5. Check the total.
Test A. More than 15 hours means the 16–20 group AND the 21–25 group.
Test B. The 7 students are in the 1–5 hours group – we only know they watched between 1 and 5 hours, not exactly one hour.
Test C. The smallest the average could be uses the lowest hours in each group, and the largest uses the highest hours in each group.
Largest possible average. Since \(15.4\) is less than 16, an average of 16 is impossible.
Test D. Fewer than 11 hours means the groups 1–5 and 6–10 only: every student in those groups watched at most 10 hours.

questions.stem: Stephen was born in August 1961. How old will he be in July 2017?
questions.hint: Subtract the years first, then ask: has Stephen had his birthday yet in that year? His birthday is in August, but the question stops at July.

keyPoints.note: His birthday is in August.
July comes BEFORE August, so he has not had his 2017 birthday yet.

steps.explain: Subtract the years to find the age he would be if his birthday had already happened in 2017.
His birthday is in August, but we are asked in July, which is one month earlier. So he has not turned 56 yet.
So he is still one year younger.
Check: he turned 55 in August 2016 (\(2016-1961=55\)) and turns 56 in August 2017, so in July 2017 he is 55. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A car travels 369 kilometres in 4.5 hours. What is the average speed of the car?
questions.hint: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. To divide by 4.5, double both numbers so you divide by a whole number.

keyPoints.note: Average speed = distance ÷ time.

steps.explain: Use the formula for speed.
Dividing by 4.5 is awkward, so multiply both numbers by 2 (the answer does not change).
Divide: \(9\times80=720\), and \(738-720=18\), which is \(9\times2\).
Check by multiplying back: \(82\times4.5=82\times4+82\times0.5=328+41=369\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If 84 players split themselves into teams, how many more teams can they form by splitting into teams of 4 instead of teams of 6?
questions.hint: Find the number of teams in each case by dividing 84 by the team size, then subtract. Smaller teams means MORE teams.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: (teams of 4) − (teams of 6).

keyPoints.text: teams of 4 instead of teams of 6
keyPoints.note: Divide 84 by 4, then divide 84 by 6.

steps.explain: Number of teams if each team has 6 players.
Number of teams if each team has 4 players.
The question asks how many MORE teams, so subtract.
Check the traps: 21 and 14 are the two team counts themselves, not the difference.

questions.stem: Which one is equivalent to two divided by eight?
questions.hint: Write “two divided by eight” as \(2\div8\). Dividing by a number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal (flip it upside down).

keyPoints.note: Write it as 2 ÷ 8, then compare the value of each option.

steps.explain: Write the expression with symbols.
Dividing by 8 is the same as multiplying by \(\frac{1}{8}\), the reciprocal of 8.
Test the others. A divides by \(\frac{1}{8}\), which is the same as multiplying by 8, so it is 16. C is \(8\div2=4\) and D is 16.
Only B equals 0.25.

questions.stem: Decrease 50 by half the square of 5.
questions.hint: Build the number step by step: first the square of 5, then half of that, and finally take that amount away from 50.

keyPoints.note: Square 5 first (5 × 5), then take half.
Decrease means subtract from 50.

steps.explain: The square of 5 means 5 times itself.
Half of the square.
Decrease 50 by this amount, which means subtract it from 50.
Check the traps: \(50-25=25\) forgets to halve; \(50-5\div2\) would use half of 5 instead of half of the square.

questions.stem: The average of six numbers is 6. If 3 is subtracted from four of the numbers, what is the new average?
questions.hint: Find the TOTAL of the six numbers first (average × how many). Subtracting 3 from four numbers takes 3 four times from the total. Then divide by 6 again.

keyPoints.text: The average of six numbers is 6
keyPoints.note: Total = 6 × 6.

keyPoints.text: 3 is subtracted from four of the numbers
keyPoints.note: The total goes down by 3 four times.

steps.explain: Total of the six numbers.
3 is taken from each of four numbers, so the total falls by \(4\times3\).
New total.
Still six numbers, so divide the new total by 6.
Check: the average falls by \(12\div6=2\), from 6 to 4. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: What is the cost of 45 litres of petrol if its price is 118.9 cents per litre to the nearest cent?
questions.hint: Multiply 45 by 118.9 to get the cost in CENTS, change cents to dollars by dividing by 100, and round to the nearest cent (2 decimal places).

keyPoints.note: The price is in cents – convert to dollars at the end.
Round to 2 decimal places in dollars.

steps.explain: Total cost in cents: 45 litres at 118.9 cents each. Use \(45\times118.9=45\times100+45\times18.9\).
Change cents to dollars: divide by 100.
Round to the nearest cent. The third decimal place is 5, so round up.
Check: petrol costs about \(\$1.19\) per litre, and \(45\times1.19\approx\$53.55\), so about \(\$53\). Options B and C are 100 times too big, A is 10 times too big.

questions.stem: Three men, Alex, Ben and Chris, invested money in the ratio 1:4:7 in their small business. Their profits were distributed according to their investment. After one year, Chris's share of profit was \(\$63{,}000\). How much was the total profit?
questions.hint: Chris has 7 of the ratio parts. Find the value of ONE part, then multiply by the total number of parts.

keyPoints.note: Total number of parts = 1 + 4 + 7.
Chris owns the 7 part.

steps.explain: Add the ratio parts to find the total number of parts.
Chris has 7 parts, and his share is \(\$63{,}000\). Divide to find one part.
The total profit is all 12 parts.
Check: Alex gets \(\$9000\), Ben \(4\times9000=\$36{,}000\), Chris \(\$63{,}000\), and \(9000+36000+63000=108000\). \(\checkmark\) Option A is just one part.

questions.stem:
Neil bought a car for \(\$19\,200\). After paying a deposit of 10%, he borrowed the rest of the money at a flat rate with interest of 5% p.a. to be repaid over 2 years.

How much does he still owe after his 10% deposit?
questions.hint: After paying 10% he still owes the other 90%. Find 10% of the price first, then subtract it – or find 90% straight away.

keyPoints.note: The deposit is 10% of the price; he still owes the remaining 90%.

steps.explain: Find the deposit: 10% of \(\$19\,200\) is one tenth of it.
Subtract the deposit from the price of the car.
Check: 90% of \(\$19\,200\) is \(0.9\times19200=17280\). \(\checkmark\) Option B is only the deposit.

questions.stem:
Neil bought a car for \(\$19\,200\). After paying a deposit of 10%, he borrowed the rest of the money at a flat rate with interest of 5% p.a. to be repaid over 2 years.

How much interest does he have to pay over 2 years?
questions.hint: He borrows what is left after the deposit (90% of the price). “Flat rate” means the interest is 5% of the amount borrowed EVERY year for 2 years.

keyPoints.text: flat rate with interest of 5% p.a.
keyPoints.note: Flat rate: 5% of the original loan for each year (simple interest).
Multiply the yearly interest by 2.

steps.explain: The amount borrowed is what he still owes after the deposit.
Interest for one year: 5% of the loan (p.a. means per year).
The rate is flat, so the same interest is charged each year. Multiply by 2 years.
Check with the formula \(I=P\times r\times t\): \(17280\times0.05\times2=1728\). \(\checkmark\) Option A is only one year of interest.

questions.stem: Two 240 ml bottles contain water and orange juice in the ratio 3:1 and 2:1 respectively. If the contents of the two are mixed, what will be the new ratio of water to orange juice?
questions.hint: You cannot add ratios directly. Find the actual amount of water and of juice in each bottle (in ml), add the water together and the juice together, then write the new ratio.

keyPoints.note: Bottle 1 is 3:1 and bottle 2 is 2:1 – work each out separately.

keyPoints.text: new ratio of water to orange juice
keyPoints.note: Total water : total juice.

steps.explain: Bottle 1 has ratio \(3:1\), so 4 parts in 240 ml. Each part is \(240\div4=60\) ml.
Bottle 2 has ratio \(2:1\), so 3 parts in 240 ml. Each part is \(240\div3=80\) ml.
Add the water together and the juice together.
Write the ratio and divide both by 20 to simplify.
Check: total \(340+140=480\) ml, which is the two bottles. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: 5 pens cost the same as 2 pens and 6 pencils and 7 pens cost the same as 6 sharpeners and 2 pencils. How many pencils cost same as 1 sharpener?
questions.hint: Use letters: \(p\) for a pen, \(c\) for a pencil, \(s\) for a sharpener. Write each sentence as an equation, find a pen in pencils first, then a sharpener in pencils.

keyPoints.text: 5 pens cost the same as 2 pens and 6 pencils
keyPoints.note: First equation: 5 pens = 2 pens + 6 pencils.

keyPoints.text: 7 pens cost the same as 6 sharpeners and 2 pencils
keyPoints.note: Second equation: 7 pens = 6 sharpeners + 2 pencils.

steps.explain: First sentence as an equation. Take 2 pens from both sides.
Divide both sides by 3: one pen costs the same as 2 pencils.
Second sentence as an equation, then replace each pen by 2 pencils.
Take 2 pencils from both sides, then divide by 6.
Check with numbers: pencil \(\$1\), pen \(\$2\), sharpener \(\$2\). Then 5 pens \(=\$10=2\times2+6\times1\) and 7 pens \(=\$14=6\times2+2\times1\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If an item costs \(\$800\) after a 20 percent discount, what was the amount of the discount?
questions.hint: \(\$800\) is the SALE price, not the original. After a 20% discount you pay 80% of the original price. Find the original price first.

keyPoints.note: The ‘$800’ is 80% of the original price.
Discount = original price − sale price.

steps.explain: Paying 20% less means paying 80% of the original price. So \(\$800\) is 80% of the original.
Find 10% by dividing by 8, then 100% by multiplying by 10.
Discount = original price − sale price.
Check: 20% of \(\$1000\) is \(\$200\). \(\checkmark\) Option C wrongly takes 20% of \(\$800\) (\(\$160\)).

questions.stem: Which number does not have exactly 6 factors?
questions.hint: List ALL the factors of each number in pairs that multiply to give it, then count. A factor is a number that divides exactly.

keyPoints.note: Count every factor, including 1 and the number itself.

steps.explain: Factors of 32 in pairs.
Factors of 18 in pairs.
Factors of 75 in pairs.
Factors of 36 in pairs: there are more pairs.
The pair \(6\times6\) gives one factor (6) only, so 36 has \(4\times2+1\) factors.

In the narrow middle the same water fills a small area, so the level rises quickly: the graph gets much steeper.
In the wide top the level rises slowly again: the graph flattens off. So the shape is gentle, steep, gentle.

questions.stem:
Which set of numbers below does not make the following statement true?

\(\square\div\square\lt1\)
questions.hint: Put the first number in the first box and the second in the second box. A fraction or division is less than 1 only when the first number is SMALLER than the second.

keyPoints.text: does not make the following statement true
keyPoints.note: You are looking for the set that makes the statement FALSE.

steps.explain: The statement is first box \(\div\) second box \(\lt1\). Try option A: \(2\div3\).
Try B and D the same way: the first number is smaller than the second.
Try C: the first number 11 is bigger than the second number 10.
So C is the set that does not make the statement true.

questions.stem: The faces on a 10-sided die are numbered 1 to 10. What is the probability of not rolling a 5?
questions.hint: Count the outcomes that are NOT a 5 and divide by all possible outcomes. Or find P(5) and subtract it from 1.

steps.explain: There are 10 equally likely faces, and only one of them is a 5.
The probability of an event NOT happening is 1 minus the probability that it happens.
Subtract using a common denominator.
Check by counting: the faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 are not a 5, which is 9 faces out of 10. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Pedro's rate of pay is \(\$18\) per hour. When he works overtime, his rate of pay is at time-and-a-half. What is his pay for two hours of overtime work?
questions.hint: Time-and-a-half means the pay rate is 1½ times the normal rate. Find the overtime rate per hour first, then multiply by 2 hours.

keyPoints.note: Overtime rate = normal rate × 1.5.
Multiply the overtime rate by 2.

steps.explain: Half of the normal rate.
Time-and-a-half is the normal rate plus half of it.
Pay for 2 hours of overtime.
Check: \(18\times1.5\times2=18\times3=54\). \(\checkmark\) Option B is only ONE hour of overtime.

questions.stem: In a mail sorting centre, one machine can read and sort 120 envelopes per minute. Another machine can sort 180 envelopes per minute. Using both machines, how long will it take to sort 36 000 envelopes?
questions.hint: Working together the machines sort the envelopes of BOTH machines each minute. Add their rates, then divide the total number of envelopes by the combined rate.

keyPoints.note: Add the two rates to get the combined rate.
Time = total envelopes ÷ envelopes per minute.

steps.explain: Combined rate of the two machines working together.
Time = total ÷ rate.
Cancel two zeros from both numbers: \(36000\div300=360\div3\).
Check: in 120 minutes, \(300\times120=36000\). \(\checkmark\) A single machine alone would take longer (the 120-per-minute machine needs \(36000\div120=300\) minutes).

questions.stem:
Look at the information below. Find the true statement.

Two numbers multiply to make zero.
options: Exactly one number must be zero.
At least one number must be zero.
questions.hint: A product is zero only if one of the numbers is zero. Test each statement with examples: can you find two numbers that multiply to zero and break the statement?

keyPoints.text: Two numbers multiply to make zero
keyPoints.note: At least one of the numbers has to be zero.

steps.explain: Try \(0\times5=0\): only one number is zero. So “both numbers must be zero” (A) is false.
Try \(0\times0=0\): both numbers are zero. So “exactly one number must be zero” (B) is false.
Option C says neither number can be zero, but \(0\times5=0\) shows a zero is allowed. Two numbers that are both NOT zero never multiply to zero (for example \(2\times3=6\)).
So the product is zero only when the first, the second or both numbers are zero. That is “at least one number is zero”.

questions.stem: The glass gauge on a cylindrical coffee maker shows that there are 45 cups left when the coffee maker is 36% full. How many cups of coffee does it hold when it is 100% full?
questions.hint: 45 cups is 36% of the full amount. Find 1% by dividing by 36 (or find 4% first), then multiply by 100.

keyPoints.text: 45 cups left when the coffee maker is 36% full
keyPoints.note: 45 cups = 36% of the total.
Scale up from 36% to 100%.

steps.explain: Write what we know.
Divide both sides by 36 to find 1%. Use 4%: \(36\%\div9=4\%\) and \(45\div9=5\).
100% is 25 times as much as 4%.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: As a percentage \(\frac{7}{100}+\frac{3}{10}\) is
questions.hint: Give both fractions the same denominator (100), add them, and read the numerator as a percentage – percent means “out of 100”.

keyPoints.note: Percent means out of 100: a fraction over 100 is that many per cent.

steps.explain: Change \(\frac{3}{10}\) into hundredths by multiplying top and bottom by 10.
Add the two fractions.
\(\frac{37}{100}\) means 37 out of 100, which is 37 per cent.
Check in decimals: \(0.07+0.3=0.37\), and \(0.37\times100=37\%\). \(\checkmark\) Option B comes from adding \(7\) and \(3\) wrongly as \(73\).

questions.stem: There are two trains leaving Central Station to go to Melbourne. One train leaves at 8.32 am and arrives at 7.25pm. The second train leaves at 9.20 pm and arrives at 6.45am the next day. What is the difference in time taken between the two trains?
questions.hint: Find the travel time of each train separately, then subtract. Use a convenient stopping point (noon, midnight, or the same minutes) to make each time easy to count.

keyPoints.note: Work out each journey time, then subtract the shorter from the longer.

steps.explain: Train 1: from 8.32 am to 7.32 pm is exactly 11 hours. The train arrives at 7.25 pm, which is 7 minutes earlier.
Train 2: from 9.20 pm to midnight is 2 hours 40 minutes. From midnight to 6.45 am is 6 hours 45 minutes.
Add: 40 + 45 = 85 minutes = 1 hour 25 minutes, so the total is \(2+6+1=9\) hours 25 minutes.
Subtract the shorter journey from the longer one.
steps.work: \(10\text{ h }53\text{ min}-9\text{ h }25\text{ min}=\boxed{1\text{ h }28\text{ min}}\)

steps.explain: Check in minutes: \(653-565=88\) minutes \(=1\) hour \(28\) minutes. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A castle is 9 km 68 m from the forest. There is a waterfall between the castle and the forest. It is 2456 metres nearer to the castle than to the forest. How far away is the waterfall from the castle in metres?
questions.hint: Change 9 km 68 m into metres first. The two distances (castle to waterfall and waterfall to forest) add up to this total and differ by 2456 m. Take the difference away from the total and share what is left equally.

keyPoints.note: Change to metres: 9 km = 9000 m.

keyPoints.text: 2456 metres nearer to the castle than to the forest
keyPoints.note: (distance to forest) − (distance to castle) = 2456 m.

steps.explain: Change the total distance into metres. 1 km is 1000 m.
Let the waterfall be \(c\) metres from the castle and \(f\) metres from the forest. The two parts make up the whole distance, and \(f\) is 2456 m longer than \(c\).
Take away the extra 2456 m from the total. What remains is two equal distances of \(c\).
Divide by 2.
Check: \(f=3306+2456=5762\) and \(3306+5762=9068\). \(\checkmark\) Option D, 5762, is the distance from the FOREST.

questions.stem: A family car can travel approximately 100 km on 11 litres of fuel. About how far will it travel on 68 litres of fuel?
questions.hint: Find how many times 68 litres is bigger than 11 litres, then multiply 100 km by that number. The answer only needs to be approximate, so pick the option closest to your result.

keyPoints.note: The same distance for every 11 litres of fuel.
Choose the closest option.

steps.explain: How many lots of 11 litres are in 68 litres?
Each lot of 11 litres gives 100 km.
The closest option to 618 km is 620 km.
Check: \(11\times6=66\) litres gives 600 km, and the remaining 2 litres give about \(\frac{2}{11}\times100\approx18\) km, so about 618 km. 680 km would need about 74.8 litres.

questions.stem: Tim makes \(\$200\) per week plus \(\$16\) per hour. Pat makes \(\$125\) per week plus \(\$17\) per hour. What is the total amount that Tim and Pat earned if they worked 20 hours each?
questions.hint: Work out Tim’s earnings and Pat’s earnings separately (weekly amount plus hourly rate times 20 hours), then ADD them – the question asks for the total.

keyPoints.note: Each earns a fixed weekly amount PLUS pay for the hours worked.

keyPoints.text: total amount that Tim and Pat earned
keyPoints.note: Add Tim’s and Pat’s earnings together.

steps.explain: Tim: the hourly part for 20 hours.
Tim’s total = weekly amount + hourly part.
Pat: the hourly part for 20 hours.
Pat’s total = weekly amount + hourly part.
The total earned by both of them.
Check the traps: \(\$520\) is Tim alone, \(\$465\) is Pat alone, and \(\$55\) is the difference \(520-465\), not the total.

questions.stem: On Saturday Joseph read 60% of a book. On Sunday he read 20% of the remaining pages of the book. What percentage of the whole book was not read by Sunday night?
questions.hint: The 20% on Sunday is 20% of what was LEFT after Saturday, not 20% of the whole book. Find what percentage of the whole book that is.

keyPoints.note: Take 20% of the remaining 40%, not of 100%.
100% minus everything he read on both days.

steps.explain: After Saturday, the part of the book left is the rest of 100%.
On Sunday he read 20% of those remaining pages, which is 20% of 40% of the whole book.
Total read by Sunday night.
The part not read is what is left of the whole book.
Check another way: after Sunday he has \(80\%\) of the remaining \(40\%\) left, and \(0.8\times40\%=32\%\). \(\checkmark\) Option D, 68%, is the amount that WAS read.

questions.stem: Express \(\frac{1}{100}+\frac{33}{1000}\) as a decimal.
questions.hint: Change each fraction into a decimal (the denominator tells you the number of decimal places), line up the decimal points, and add.

keyPoints.note: 100 = 2 decimal places (hundredths); 1000 = 3 decimal places (thousandths).

steps.explain: \(\frac{1}{100}\) is one hundredth, which is 2 decimal places.
\(\frac{33}{1000}\) is 33 thousandths, which is 3 decimal places.
Line up the decimal points and add.
Check by using a common denominator: \(\frac{10}{1000}+\frac{33}{1000}=\frac{43}{1000}=0.043\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length 9 cm and area \(72\ \text{cm}^2\).
questions.hint: Area = length × width, so you can find the width. Then perimeter = 2 × (length + width).

keyPoints.note: Width = area ÷ length.
Perimeter = 2 × (length + width).

steps.explain: Area = length × width. Put in the known numbers.
Divide both sides by 9.
Perimeter = 2 × (length + width).
Check the traps: 8 cm is just the width and 17 cm is only half the perimeter.

questions.stem: Ten years ago, the sum of the ages of Terry and his twin brother Tom was 22. How old is Terry now?
questions.hint: Twins are the same age. Split the sum equally to find each twin’s age ten years ago, then remember to add the ten years.

keyPoints.note: Twins have the same age, so each was 22 ÷ 2 years old.
Add 10 years to get the age now.

steps.explain: Terry and Tom are twins, so they have the same age. Split the sum of 22 into two equal ages.
That was ten years ago, so now each twin is 10 years older.
Check: ten years ago the ages were \(11+11=22\). \(\checkmark\) Option A, 16, subtracts instead of adds.

questions.stem: The ratio of boys to girls who voted for the SRC is 3:2. If 10 more boys and 5 more girls voted, the ratio would have been 5:3. How many students voted for the SRC?
questions.hint: Write the numbers of boys and girls as \(3k\) and \(2k\) (ratio 3:2). After adding 10 boys and 5 girls the new numbers are in the ratio 5:3 – use that to find \(k\).

keyPoints.note: Boys = 3k and girls = 2k for some number k.
New numbers: 3k + 10 boys and 2k + 5 girls.

steps.explain: Boys and girls are in the ratio 3:2, so call them \(3k\) and \(2k\). After the extra voters they are \(3k+10\) and \(2k+5\), in the ratio 5:3.
Cross-multiply.
Expand both sides.
Subtract \(9k\) and \(25\) from both sides.
So there were \(3k=15\) boys and \(2k=10\) girls. The number of students who voted is the total.
Check: with the extra voters it is \(25\) boys and \(15\) girls, and \(25:15=5:3\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The product of two fractions is \(\frac{4}{5}\). If one fraction is \(\frac{2}{3}\), what is the second fraction?
questions.hint: “Product” means multiply. To undo multiplying by \(\frac{2}{3}\), divide by \(\frac{2}{3}\) – which means multiply by its flip, \(\frac{3}{2}\).

keyPoints.note: Product = the answer when you multiply.
Second fraction = product ÷ first fraction.

steps.explain: Write the question as an equation with the unknown fraction \(x\).
Divide both sides by \(\frac{2}{3}\).
Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by the flipped fraction.
Simplify \(\frac{12}{10}=\frac{6}{5}\), then change to a mixed number.
Check: \(\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{6}{5}=\frac{12}{15}=\frac{4}{5}\). \(\checkmark\)

The middle number in the ratio, which is B’s share.

steps.explain: Multiply every part of the ratio by 2 so there are no fractions.
Total number of parts.
One part of the money.
The middle share is B’s share, which is 4 parts.

questions.stem: Jennifer left her house at 8.28 am to walk to her school. She walks at a constant speed of 4.5 km per hour. If the school is 3.75 km from her house, when will she arrive at her school?
questions.hint: Use time = distance ÷ speed. The answer will be in hours – change it to minutes before adding it to 8.28 am.

keyPoints.text: constant speed of 4.5 km per hour
keyPoints.note: Time = distance ÷ speed.
Distance = 3.75 km.

steps.explain: Time = distance ÷ speed.
Multiply top and bottom by 4 to clear the decimals: \(\frac{15}{18}\), which simplifies to \(\frac{5}{6}\).
Change hours to minutes. One hour is 60 minutes.
Add 50 minutes to 8.28 am. 8.28 + 32 minutes is 9.00, and 18 minutes remain.
Check: in 50 minutes she walks \(4.5\times\frac{50}{60}=3.75\) km. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Water flows from a hose at a rate of 300 mL/min. How many litres of water would have flowed out in two and half hours?
questions.hint: Change the time into minutes (to match mL per minute), multiply by the rate, and then change mL into litres (divide by 1000).

keyPoints.note: The rate is per MINUTE, so use the time in minutes.
1 litre = 1000 mL.

steps.explain: Change 2½ hours into minutes. 1 hour is 60 minutes.
Water flowed out in mL.
Change millilitres to litres: divide by 1000.
Check: 300 mL per minute is 18 000 mL = 18 L per hour, and \(18\times2.5=45\). \(\checkmark\) Option A forgot to change mL to litres.

questions.stem: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio of 4:7:25. What is the difference in magnitude between the smallest and the largest angles?
questions.hint: The angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\). Share \(180^\circ\) in the ratio 4:7:25, find the smallest and largest angles, and subtract.

keyPoints.note: They add up to 180°.

keyPoints.text: difference in magnitude between the smallest and the largest
keyPoints.note: Largest − smallest.

steps.explain: Add the parts of the ratio.
The angles add to \(180^\circ\), so one part is
Smallest and largest angles.
Difference between the largest and smallest.
Check: the three angles are \(20^\circ+35^\circ+125^\circ=180^\circ\). \(\checkmark\) Options A and D are the angles themselves.

questions.stem:
How many whole numbers could be in the box so that the expression has a value between 1 and 2?

\(1\lt\frac{\square+3}{8}\lt2\)
questions.hint: Multiply every part of the inequality by 8 to remove the fraction, then take away 3. Then list the whole numbers that fit, being careful with the end points.

keyPoints.text: whole numbers could be in the box
keyPoints.note: List every whole number that makes the statement true.
‘Between’ does not include 1 or 2 themselves.

steps.explain: Multiply all three parts by 8.
Subtract 3 from all three parts.
The box must be bigger than 5 and smaller than 13 (5 and 13 are not allowed). List the whole numbers.
Count them.
Check the end points: 5 gives \(\frac{8}{8}=1\) and 13 gives \(\frac{16}{8}=2\), neither is strictly between 1 and 2.

questions.stem: What time is 6 hours before 6 minutes after noon?
questions.hint: First write “6 minutes after noon” as a clock time. Then go back 6 hours and decide whether you cross noon or midnight (am or pm).

keyPoints.note: Noon is 12.00 pm, so this time is 12.06 pm.
Subtract 6 hours; the minutes stay the same.

steps.explain: Noon is 12 pm. Six minutes after noon is 12.06 pm.
Go back 6 hours: the minutes stay the same, the hour goes from 12 back to 6. Going back from noon means we move into the morning, so it is am.
Check: 6.06 am plus 6 hours is 12.06 pm. \(\checkmark\) Options C and D take away 12 minutes instead of 6.

questions.stem: René lost 80% on her share investments. After a period of time her shares increased in value to their previous value. What is this increase expressed as a percentage?
questions.hint: Pick a starting value like \(\$100\). After the loss find what is left, then work out how much it must grow to get back to \(\$100\) and write that growth as a percentage of what she had at the START of the increase, not of the original.

keyPoints.note: She only has 20% of the original value left.
Percentage increase = increase ÷ value before the increase.

steps.explain: Start with \(\$100\). She loses 80% of it.
The shares then increase back to their previous value, \(\$100\). The increase in dollars is
A percentage increase is the increase divided by the value BEFORE the increase (\(\$20\)).
Check: increasing \(\$20\) by 400% adds \(4\times20=\$80\), giving \(\$100\). \(\checkmark\) Option C, 80%, wrongly compares with the original \(\$100\).

questions.stem: Which of the following scales would be the most appropriate to make a scale drawing of a police car on a piece of paper the same size as this page?
questions.hint: A police car is about 5 metres long and an A4 page is about 30 cm long. Divide the real length (in cm) by the scale number and see which drawing fits the page nicely.

keyPoints.note: A car is roughly 4–5 m long, which is 400–500 cm.

keyPoints.text: the same size as this page
keyPoints.note: The drawing should fill most of a page about 30 cm long.

steps.explain: Change the real length of the police car into centimetres: about 5 m.
A scale of \(1:25\) means 25 cm in real life is 1 cm on paper. Divide the car’s length by 25.
20 cm nearly fills the 30 cm page. Try the others: 1:100 gives 5 cm, 1:250 gives 2 cm and 1:1000 gives 0.5 cm, which are too small.
So the most appropriate scale is 1:25.

questions.stem: A square has an area of \(450\ \text{cm}^2\). A small square is cut from the large square. All the sides of the new square are one third of the large square. What is the area of the small square?
questions.hint: If every side is one third as long, the area is not one third. Area uses length × length, so the area is \(\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{1}{3}\) of the large area.

keyPoints.text: sides of the new square are one third of the large square
keyPoints.note: Sides × 1/3 means area × 1/9.
Small area = large area ÷ 9.

steps.explain: Let the large square have side \(s\). The small square has side \(\frac{s}{3}\).
So the small area is one ninth of the large area.
Divide 450 by 9.
Check: the large side is \(\sqrt{450}\approx21.2\), the small side is about \(7.07\), and \(7.07^2\approx50\). \(\checkmark\) Option B, 150, is one third of the area, which is the trap.

questions.stem: A Quadratfrei is the name given to square-free numbers, numbers that are not divisible by any perfect squares, except 1. Perfect squares are the squares of any number. For example, 10 is square-free but 18 is not, as it is divisible by \(9=3^2\). Which number is not the quadratfrei (square-free numbers) between 20 and 30?
questions.hint: List the perfect squares that could divide numbers below 30: 4, 9, 16, 25. A number that is divisible by any of these (other than 1) is NOT square-free. Test each option.

keyPoints.text: not divisible by any perfect squares, except 1
keyPoints.note: Test divisibility by 4, 9, 16 and 25.
You want the number that is NOT square-free.

steps.explain: Perfect squares that are less than 30 (apart from 1).
Test 21: it is not divisible by 4, 9, 16 or 25 (\(21=3\times7\)). Test 22: \(22=2\times11\), not divisible by any. Test 23: a prime number, not divisible by any.
Test 24: it is divisible by 4 because \(24\div4=6\). A perfect square (4) divides 24, so 24 is not square-free.
So the number that is not a quadratfrei number is 24.

questions.stem: Tom's Hat Corner increased all original prices by 25%. Now the shop is having a sale where all prices are 20% off these increased prices. Which statement best describes the sale price of an item?
options: The sale price is 5% higher than the original price.
The sale price is higher than the original price, but by less than 5%.
The sale price is lower than the original price.
The sale price is the same as the original price.
questions.hint: Pick an easy original price like \(\$100\). Increase it by 25%, then take 20% off the NEW price (not the original), and compare.

keyPoints.note: Price after the increase is 125% of the original.
The 20% is taken off the NEW (increased) price.

steps.explain: Start with an original price of \(\$100\). Increase it by 25%.
The sale takes 20% off this increased price of \(\$125\).
Sale price.
The sale price equals the original price. In general \(1.25\times0.80=1\), so this works for any price.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: How many whole numbers are between \(\sqrt{8}\) and \(\sqrt{80}\)?
questions.hint: Estimate each square root using the nearest perfect squares, then list the whole numbers strictly between them.

keyPoints.note: Count whole numbers bigger than the first root and smaller than the second.

steps.explain: \(\sqrt{8}\) lies between \(\sqrt{4}=2\) and \(\sqrt{9}=3\), so it is about 2.8.
\(\sqrt{80}\) lies between \(\sqrt{64}=8\) and \(\sqrt{81}=9\), so it is just under 9.
The whole numbers bigger than 2.8 and smaller than 8.9 are
Count them.
Check: 3 is above \(\sqrt{8}\approx2.83\), and 8 is below \(\sqrt{80}\approx8.94\), but 9 is above 8.94 and 2 is below 2.83.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: If A # B means \(\frac{A+B}{2}\), then what value is 8 # (3 # 5)?
questions.hint: Do the brackets first: the symbol # means “add the two numbers, then halve”. Work out \(3\#5\), then use that answer with 8.

keyPoints.note: # means add the two numbers then divide by 2.
Brackets first: 3 # 5.

steps.explain: Brackets first. \(3\#5\) means add 3 and 5, then halve.
Now the question becomes \(8\#4\). Add and halve again.
Check the trap: if you did \((8\#3)\#5\) you would get \(5.5\#5=5.25\), so the order and brackets matter.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Let \(P\) be an odd whole number and let \(N\) be any whole number. Which of the following statements about the whole number \((P^2+N\times P)\) is always true?
options: it is even only if N is even
it is odd only if N is odd
it is odd only if N is even
questions.hint: Use odd and even rules: odd × odd is odd, odd × even is even, odd + odd is even, odd + even is odd. Work out the parity of each part, then test a few numbers.

keyPoints.note: P is odd, so ‘P²’ is odd too.
Test each statement with an example; one counter-example makes it false.

steps.explain: \(P\) is odd, so \(P^2=P\times P\) is odd × odd, which is odd.
\(N\times P\): if \(N\) is even the product is even; if \(N\) is odd the product is odd (odd × odd).
steps.work: \(N\times P\text{ has the same type as }N\)

steps.explain: Add the two parts. Odd + even gives odd, and odd + odd gives even. So the whole number is odd when \(N\) is even and even when \(N\) is odd.

Test with \(P=3\): \(N=2\) gives \(9+6=15\) (odd, \(N\) even); \(N=1\) gives \(9+3=12\) (even, \(N\) odd). So A is false (12), B is false (12 is even with \(N\) odd), and C is false (15 is odd with \(N\) even).
The expression is odd exactly when \(N\) is even, which is statement D.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: A picture 3 metres across is hung in the centre of a wall that is 19 metres wide. How many metres from the end of the wall is the nearest edge of the picture?
questions.hint: The picture is in the centre, so the empty wall is shared equally on the two sides. Take the picture width away from the wall width and halve what is left.

keyPoints.text: hung in the centre of a wall
keyPoints.note: Equal gaps on the left and right.
The gap from the end of the wall to the picture.

steps.explain: Take the picture off the wall width: this is the bare wall.
The picture is in the centre, so half of the bare wall is on each side.
Check: \(8+3+8=19\). \(\checkmark\) Option C, 9.5, is the distance to the centre of the wall.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Martians measure angles in clerts. There are 500 clerts in a full circle. How many clerts are there in three right angles?
questions.hint: A right angle is a quarter of a full circle. Find how many clerts are in a quarter circle, then take three of them.

keyPoints.note: A full circle is 500 clerts, so a right angle is a quarter of 500.
Multiply one right angle by 3.

steps.explain: A right angle is one quarter of a full turn (\(90^\circ\) out of \(360^\circ\)).
Three right angles.
Check: three right angles are three quarters of a circle, \(\frac{3}{4}\times500=375\). \(\checkmark\) Option A is only ONE right angle.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Half the people in a room left. One third of those remaining started to dance. There were then 12 people who were not dancing. What was the original number of people in the room?
questions.hint: Let the original number be \(N\). Half stay; one third of those dance, so two thirds of those who stayed are NOT dancing. That group is 12 people – work backwards.

keyPoints.text: One third of those remaining started to dance
keyPoints.note: Two thirds of the people who stayed are not dancing.
These 12 are 2/3 of the people who stayed.

steps.explain: Half the people left, so half stayed. Of those who stayed, one third dance, so two thirds do not.
The 12 who are not dancing are two thirds of those remaining. One third is 6.
The 18 people remaining were half of the original group, so double it.
Check: 36 people, 18 leave, 18 remain; \(\frac{1}{3}\) of 18 is 6 dancing, so \(18-6=12\) not dancing. \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: If the length of a rectangular prism is 3 times its height and 2 times its breadth, the total length of edges is 44 cm. How long is the breadth?
questions.hint: A rectangular prism has 4 edges of each size: length, breadth and height. Write the length and the height using the breadth \(b\), then add all edges.

keyPoints.text: length of a rectangular prism is 3 times its height and 2 times its breadth
keyPoints.note: length = 2 × breadth, and height = length ÷ 3.

keyPoints.text: total length of edges is 44 cm
keyPoints.note: 4 × (length + breadth + height) = 44.

steps.explain: Let the breadth be \(b\). The length is 2 times the breadth, and the height is one third of the length.
A prism has 12 edges: 4 of each length. So the total length of edges is 4 times the sum.
Add inside the bracket using thirds: \(2b+b=3b=\frac{9b}{3}\), so the sum is \(\frac{11b}{3}\).
Divide 44 by 4, then multiply by 3 and divide by 11.

questions.hint: Start with the 12 edges of the prism. Cutting off a corner removes a vertex and adds a small triangle. Count the new edges of that triangle and multiply by 8 corners.

keyPoints.text: Each corner of a rectangular prism is cut off
keyPoints.note: There are 8 corners; each cut makes one triangular face.
Original edges (shortened) + new edges.

steps.explain: A rectangular prism has 12 edges and 8 corners. After the cuts, all 12 original edges are still there (just shorter).

Total number of edges.

Which of the following is NOT shown in the diagram?

questions.hint: Recall the meaning of each word: a radius joins the centre to the edge, a diameter passes through the centre from one side of the circle to the other, an arc is part of the circumference and a sector is a slice with two radii and an arc.

keyPoints.text: P is the centre of a circle
keyPoints.note: Lines from the centre P to the circle are radii.

keyPoints.text: Which of the following is NOT shown
keyPoints.note: Check each term against the diagram.

steps.explain: PQ and PR join the centre P to points on the circumference, so they are radii. Radius is shown.

The slice bounded by the radii PQ, PR and the arc QR is a sector. Sector is shown.
A diameter must pass through the centre and join two points on the circle. No such line is drawn: QR does not go through P.

questions.stem: How many kilograms of seeds will be needed to mark the perimeter of a rectangular play area 110 metres long by 80 metres wide if 200 grams of seeds are needed for every 10 metres?
questions.hint: Build the calculation in stages: the perimeter, then how many lots of 10 m it contains, then how many grams, then change grams to kilograms.

keyPoints.note: Perimeter = 2 × (length + width), not the area.

keyPoints.text: 200 grams of seeds are needed for every 10 metres
keyPoints.note: Divide the perimeter by 10, multiply by 200 g, and convert grams to kilograms.

steps.explain: Perimeter of the play area. Perimeter, not area, because the seeds mark the edge.
Seeds are used for every 10 m, so find how many lots of 10 m there are.
Each lot needs 200 grams.
The question asks for kilograms, so divide by 1000.
Put the stages in one expression: this is option C. A uses the area. B stops at grams (no \(\div1000\)). D multiplies by 10 instead of dividing.

questions.hint: Use the order of operations: brackets first (the innermost bracket, then the square bracket), and inside it work left to right with ÷ and ×. Multiply by 2 last.

keyPoints.note: Brackets first, then divide and multiply from left to right.

steps.explain: Innermost bracket first.
Inside the square bracket, ÷ and × are done from left to right: first \(18\div6\).
Then multiply by 3.
Finally multiply the bracket by 2.
Check the trap: doing \(6\times3=18\) before dividing gives \(18\div18=1\), which is wrong because ÷ comes before × when reading left to right.

questions.stem: Two numbers have a difference of 11 and their product is 60. What is their sum?
questions.hint: List pairs of numbers that multiply to 60 (factor pairs) and find the pair whose difference is 11. Then add that pair.

keyPoints.note: Subtract the two numbers: the answer must be 11.
Multiply the two numbers: the answer must be 60.

steps.explain: List the factor pairs of 60 and their differences.
The pair \(4\) and \(15\) has difference \(15-4=11\) and product \(4\times15=60\).
Their sum.
Check the other pairs: \(5\times12\) has difference 7 and \(6\times10\) has difference 4, so no other pair works.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: What is the numeral for three hundred, two thousand and forty-two?
questions.hint: Read the words in groups of thousands: “three hundred and two thousand” is the thousands group, and “forty-two” is the last group.

keyPoints.note: ‘Three hundred and two’ followed by ‘thousand’ is the thousands group: 302 thousand.

steps.explain: The thousands group is “three hundred and two thousand”, so it is 302 thousands.
The last group is “forty-two”, written as 042 (hundreds digit is 0).
Put the groups together.
Check by place value: 3 hundred-thousands, 0 ten-thousands, 2 thousands, 0 hundreds, 4 tens, 2 ones.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Which of the following has the largest value?
questions.hint: Write every number with 3 decimal places so they line up, then compare the digits from the left: first the ones, then tenths, then hundredths.

keyPoints.note: Compare tenths first: the biggest tenths digit wins.

steps.explain: Write all with 3 decimal places.
All have 1 one. Compare the tenths digits: 1, 2, 0, 1. The biggest tenths digit is 2.
So 1.2 is the largest. 1.12 is a common mistake because 12 looks bigger than 2, but \(1.12\) means 1 tenth and 2 hundredths.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: How many faces and edges does an octagonal pyramid have?
questions.hint: Count the faces and the edges separately, then ADD them together because the question asks for faces and edges. An octagon has 8 sides.

keyPoints.note: The question asks for faces plus edges together.

steps.explain: Faces: the base is an octagon (1 face) and each of its 8 sides has a triangle going up to the top point (8 faces).
Edges: the base has 8 edges and there are 8 sloping edges going up to the apex.
Faces and edges together.
Check the traps: 9 is only the faces and 16 is only the edges.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Find the value of \(0.378\div20\).
questions.hint: Dividing by 20 is dividing by 2 and then by 10. Divide by 2 first, then move the decimal point one place to the left.

keyPoints.note: Split ÷ 20 into ÷ 2 then ÷ 10.

steps.explain: Divide by 2 first.
Divide by 10: move the decimal point one place left.
Check by multiplying back: \(0.0189\times20=0.378\). \(\checkmark\) The answer must be much smaller than 0.378, because 0.378 is shared into 20 parts.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Which is the smallest value?
questions.hint: Change every option into a decimal so you can compare them. Remember \(\frac{3}{8}=3\div8\) and \(25\%=\frac{25}{100}\).

keyPoints.note: Convert all four to decimals first.

steps.explain: Option A: multiply.
Option B: divide. Multiply top and bottom by 10 to get \(\frac{5.5}{11}\).
Option C: divide 3 by 8.
Option D: a percentage is out of 100.
Compare: 0.36, 0.5, 0.375, 0.25. The smallest is 0.25.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: If 5 notebooks cost \(\$9.75\), what will be the price of 9 notebooks?
questions.hint: Find the price of ONE notebook first (divide by 5), then multiply by 9. 9 notebooks cost a bit less than twice the price of 5.

keyPoints.note: Divide by 5 to find the cost of 1 notebook.

steps.explain: Price of one notebook.
Price of 9 notebooks. Use \(1.95\times9=2\times9-0.05\times9\).
Check: \(\$1.95\) is the price of one notebook (option A), and \(\$48.75\) is 25 notebooks. 9 notebooks is a bit less than 2 lots of 5, \(2\times9.75=\$19.50\). \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: How many millilitres are in \(6\frac{1}{8}\) litres?
questions.hint: 1 litre is 1000 mL. Find the mL in 6 litres and the mL in \(\frac{1}{8}\) of a litre, then add.

steps.explain: Millilitres in 6 whole litres.
Millilitres in \(\frac{1}{8}\) of a litre: divide 1000 by 8.
Add them.
Check: \(6\frac{1}{8}=6.125\) litres, and \(6.125\times1000=6125\). \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: How long will it take to finish a job if it took \(2\frac{1}{3}\) days to complete \(\frac{1}{3}\) of the job?
questions.hint: If one third of the job takes \(2\frac{1}{3}\) days, the whole job takes 3 times as long (there are 3 thirds in a whole). Change the mixed number to an improper fraction to multiply.

keyPoints.note: One third of the job takes this long; the whole job is 3 thirds.

steps.explain: There are 3 thirds in the whole job, so multiply the time by 3.
Change \(2\frac{1}{3}\) to an improper fraction.
Multiply: the 3s cancel.
Check: \(7\div3=2\frac{1}{3}\) days for each third. \(\checkmark\) (The answer is the time for the WHOLE job, 7 days; the time still left after the first third would be \(4\frac{2}{3}\) days.)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: A man, his wife and three children stayed one night in a hotel where the rate was \(\$50\) for an adult and half that rate for a child. If breakfast cost \(\$15\) per person, how much was the total payment for the family?
questions.hint: Build the family’s cost in three parts: the 2 adults, the 3 children at HALF the adult rate, and breakfast for all 5 people. Then match each part to the expression.

keyPoints.text: half that rate for a child
keyPoints.note: Child rate = 50 ÷ 2 = $25 each.
Breakfast is for all 5 people.

steps.explain: Two adults pay \(\$50\) each.
Each child pays half of \(\$50\), so three children pay \(50\div2\) each.
Breakfast for 5 people at \(\$15\).
Add the parts: this matches option D. (Total \(100+75+75=\$250\).)
Check the others: A charges all 5 people the adult rate, B adds 3 for no reason, and C divides 3 by \(\frac{1}{2}\), which doubles the children’s rate instead of halving it.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Two quantities P and Q are in the ratio 2:3. If P is reduced by 1, the ratio becomes 1:2. What could be the values of P and Q?
questions.hint: Test each option twice: first check that P : Q is 2 : 3, then reduce P by 1 and check the new ratio is 1 : 2. Only one option passes both tests.

keyPoints.note: P : Q must simplify to 2 : 3.
Then (P − 1) : Q must simplify to 1 : 2.

steps.explain: Test A (\(6:4=3:2\)) and B (\(3:2\)): neither is \(2:3\), so they fail the first test.
Test C: \(8:12=2:3\). It passes the first test. Reduce P by 1: \(7:12\), which is not \(1:2\).
Test D: \(4:6=2:3\). It passes the first test. Reduce P by 1: \(3:6=1:2\). It passes the second test too.
Check by algebra: \(P=2k\) and \(Q=3k\) with \(\frac{2k-1}{3k}=\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(4k-2=3k\), so \(k=2\), \(P=4\), \(Q=6\).

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Zac has a stationery shop. He is going to put a 20% profit margin and a further 10% GST on every item in the shop. What is the overall percentage increase?
questions.hint: Pick an easy starting price like \(\$100\). Add 20%, then add 10% of the NEW price (not of the original). Compare the final price with \(\$100\).

keyPoints.note: The 10% is taken of the price AFTER the 20% increase.
Final price − original price, as a percentage of the original.

steps.explain: Start with an item that costs \(\$100\). Add the 20% profit margin.
Now add 10% GST on this new price of \(\$120\).
The overall increase from \(\$100\) to \(\$132\).
Check with multipliers: \(1.2\times1.1=1.32\), which is a 32% increase. The trap is adding \(20\%+10\%=30\%\).

steps.explain: The common multiple of 6 and 8 is 24. Multiply the first exchange by 4 so it gives 24 mangoes.

16 pineapples is 4 lots of 4 pineapples.
Check the other way: \(16\) pineapples \(=\frac{16}{5}\times6=19.2\) mangoes, and \(19.2\times\frac{15}{8}=36\). \(\checkmark\)

steps.explain: Right face: 4 shaded squares (the middle of each edge). The left face is the same.
Top face: only the centre square is shaded. The bottom face is the same.

No cube is counted twice: the front and back shaded cubes are corner or face-centre cubes, the left and right ones are edge-middle cubes, and the top and bottom ones are face-centre cubes of the top and bottom layers.
Check the cube has \(27\) small cubes in total, so \(20\) cubes with a shaded face and \(7\) with none is possible.

questions.stem:
A list of 8 numbers is formed by beginning with two given numbers. Each new number in the list is the product of the two previous numbers. Find the first number if the last three are shown:

\(\_\_,\ \_\_,\ \_\_,\ \_\_,\ \_\_,\ 16,\ 64,\ 1024\)
questions.hint: Work BACKWARDS. Each number is the product of the two before it, so any number divided by the number just before it gives the number two places before it.

keyPoints.text: product of the two previous numbers
keyPoints.note: Term = (previous term) × (term before that).

steps.explain: The 7th number is 64 and the 8th is 1024; the 6th number is 16. Since \(64=\text{5th}\times16\), find the 5th number.
The 6th number is \(16=\text{4th}\times\text{5th}=\text{4th}\times4\).
The 5th number is \(4=\text{3rd}\times4\), so the 3rd number is 1. The 4th number is \(4=\text{2nd}\times1\), so the 2nd number is 4.
The 3rd number is \(1=\text{1st}\times\text{2nd}=\text{1st}\times4\).

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

<text x="150.0" y="242.0" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#ea580c">48 + 24 = 72 m²</text>
</svg>

steps.explain: Inside: from each face the tunnel goes in 1 m before it reaches the middle cube. That is 6 short tunnels (3 holes × 2 ends), each with 4 walls of \(1\times1\ \text{m}^2\).
Add the outside and inside surfaces.
Check: a solid cube has \(54\ \text{m}^2\). The holes remove 6 and add 24, so \(54-6+24=72\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Adding 10 from 6 times a number gives the same result as multiplying the number by 7 and subtracting 6. What is the number?
questions.hint: Call the number \(n\). Write each sentence as an expression, set the two expressions equal and solve. Or test the four options.

keyPoints.note: Write it as 6n, then add 10.

keyPoints.text: multiplying the number by 7 and subtracting 6
keyPoints.note: Write it as 7n − 6.

steps.explain: First expression: 6 times the number, plus 10. Second expression: 7 times the number, minus 6. They are equal.
Subtract \(6n\) from both sides.
Add 6 to both sides.
Check: \(6\times16+10=106\) and \(7\times16-6=106\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem:
The length of the diagonals for two shapes are:

Rhombus: diagonal 1 = 3 cm, diagonal 2 = 5 cm
Kite: diagonal 1 = 3 cm, diagonal 2 = 5 cm

Which of the following is true?
options: The rhombus has a larger area.
The kite has a larger area.
More information is needed to determine the areas of each shape.
Both of the areas are equal.
questions.hint: The diagonals of both a rhombus and a kite cross at right angles. That gives the same area formula for both shapes: half the product of the diagonals.

keyPoints.note: Both shapes have the same two diagonals.

keyPoints.text: Which of the following is true?
keyPoints.note: Check the area formula for each shape.

steps.explain: In a rhombus the diagonals cross at \(90^\circ\). Area = \(\frac{1}{2}\times d_1\times d_2\).
In a kite the diagonals also cross at \(90^\circ\), so the same formula works.
Both areas are \(7.5\ \text{cm}^2\), so they are equal.
Check why no more information is needed: the side lengths and angles can differ, but with perpendicular diagonals the area depends only on the diagonals.

questions.stem: A cylindrical container has a circular cross-sectional area of \(70\ \text{cm}^2\). The tank is partially filled with water. Blocks are then placed into the water, hence making the water level rise. If the volume of the blocks is \(392\ \text{cm}^3\), by what level does the water rise?

questions.hint: The blocks push the water up. The extra volume of water in the rise equals the volume of the blocks. A rise is a slice with the cross-sectional area as its base: volume = area × height.

keyPoints.note: The base of the extra slice of water.
Extra volume of water = volume of the blocks.

steps.explain: The rise in water level is a cylinder-shaped slice. Its volume equals the volume of the blocks.

steps.explain: Put in the cross-sectional area.
Divide both sides by 70.
Check: \(70\times5.6=392\). \(\checkmark\)

Check with the trapezium formula (parallel sides BO = 2 and CA = 4.5, distance 4 apart): \(\frac{1}{2}\times(2+4.5)\times4=13\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Seven consecutive integers are listed. The sum of the smallest three is 33. What is the sum of the largest three?
questions.hint: Three consecutive numbers add to 33, so the middle one is the average. Write out all seven numbers, then add the last three.

keyPoints.note: They go up by 1 each time.

keyPoints.text: sum of the smallest three is 33
keyPoints.note: The middle of those three is 33 ÷ 3.

steps.explain: The middle of three consecutive numbers is their average.
So the smallest three are 10, 11 and 12. Continue the list up to seven numbers.
The largest three are 14, 15 and 16.
Check: the largest three are each 4 more than the smallest three, so the sum is \(33+3\times4=45\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: One mile is about \(1\frac{3}{5}\) kilometres. How many kilometres is 15 miles?
questions.hint: Multiply the number of miles by the number of kilometres in one mile. Change the mixed number to an improper fraction or a decimal first.

keyPoints.note: 1 mile ≈ 1 3/5 km = 1.6 km.
Multiply 15 by 1.6.

steps.explain: Change the mixed number to a decimal: \(\frac{3}{5}=0.6\).
15 miles is 15 times as far.
Check with fractions: \(\frac{8}{5}\times15=8\times3=24\). \(\checkmark\) Option A divides instead of multiplying.

questions.stem:
Brian wants to buy a cup of instant noodles from the school canteen at lunch time. He will decide what to buy based on the recommendation from his friends. There are three products.

• Fantastic Bowl: $2.80, recommended by 4 of his friends.
• Super Chicken Noodles: $3.50, recommended by 3 of his friends.
• Beef Oodles: $5.20, recommended by 2 of his friends.

If the noodles are cheap, then they don't have to be recommended by many people.
If the noodles are expensive, then they have to be recommended by many people.

Which product should Brian buy and why?
options: Fantastic Bowl because it's the cheapest and reasonably recommended.
Super Chicken Noodles because it is reasonably priced and least recommended.
Beef Oodles because it is the most expensive and most highly recommended.
questions.hint: Check each reason against the facts. A cheap item needs few recommendations; an expensive item needs many.

steps.explain: Compare price and number of recommendations for each product.
steps.work: Fantastic Bowl: cheapest ($2.80), most recommended (4). Super Chicken: $3.50, 3 friends. Beef Oodles: most expensive ($5.20), fewest recommendations (2).

steps.explain: Beef Oodles is expensive, so by the rule it would need many recommendations — but it has the fewest. So C is wrong (it is also not 'most highly recommended').
Super Chicken Noodles is not the least recommended (Beef Oodles is), so B's reason is false.
Fantastic Bowl is cheap, so it doesn't need many recommendations — and it still has the most. It is the best choice.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
One of the largest impacts TV has on teenagers is violence. When someone sees a lot of violence on TV or video games, it can desensitize the viewer and make them feel almost immune to it when it is happening to them.

Sandra: “Children should reduce their TV time to less than 30 minutes a day.”

Which one of these statements, if true, most weakens Sandra's argument?
options: Studies have shown that violence in young adults has been steadily increasing over the years.
Television has both positive and negative effects on children.
The average child watches TV about 14 hours each week.
There are channels on TV that are both fun and educational.
questions.hint: Sandra limits ALL TV time because of violent content. Which option shows that some TV time is actually good for children?

steps.explain: Sandra's reasoning: TV shows violence, which is harmful, so children should cut ALL TV time to under 30 minutes.
steps.work: Claim: less TV time → less harm.

steps.explain: A weakener must show that cutting TV time would lose something valuable, or that TV time is not the real problem.
A supports the concern about violence. C just states how much TV is watched. B is too general — it does not say what the benefit is.
D shows there is TV content that is fun AND educational and has nothing to do with violence. Cutting all TV time would also cut this useful content, so a blanket limit is not the best answer.

keyPoints.text: reduce their TV time to less than 30 minutes a day
keyPoints.note: Sandra limits all TV, not just violent shows.
Look for a reason the limit would be a bad idea.

questions.stem:
David has four cars. No one else in his company has four cars. There are 50 people in his company.

If the information in the box is true, which one of the following must be also true?
options: All employees in the company have less than four cars each.
Everybody in the company has cars.
Some of the employees have more than four cars.
Forty-nine people in the company don't have 4 cars.
questions.hint: The box only tells you who has EXACTLY four cars.

steps.explain: Only David has exactly four cars. Everyone else (49 people) has some number other than four.
A is not certain — others could have 5 or more cars (and David himself has 4, not fewer). B and C are not certain either — we know nothing about who has more or fewer cars.
D must be true.

questions.stem:
The Cinema Club has three categories of cinema memberships, as below.

• Gold membership – annual subscription $80
• Silver membership – annual subscription $40
• Bronze membership – annual subscription $20

The gold membership entitles members a 20% off discount on tickets.
The silver membership entitles members a 10% off discount on tickets.
The bronze membership entitles members a 5% off discount on tickets.

John is planning to watch one movie each month for a year and has decided to join one of the membership categories.

Which membership is the best deal for John?
questions.hint: Work out how expensive a ticket would have to be for a bigger discount to cover a bigger subscription fee.

steps.explain: John sees 12 movies. Compare how much more each dearer membership costs with how much extra it saves.
Silver costs $20 more than Bronze and gives 5% more off. To save $20 with 5% on 12 tickets, each ticket would need to cost more than $33.
Gold costs $40 more than Silver and gives 10% more off — again the ticket would need to cost more than $33 to be worth it.
A normal movie ticket costs much less than $33, so the extra fees are never paid back. The cheapest subscription is the best deal.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
The children Kerry, Sam, Ethan, Lee and Susan are all in one family.

Lee is 1 year younger than Ethan.
Sam and Ethan are twins.
Kerry is 3 years older than Lee.
Sam is 9 years old.
Susan is older than Ethan, but younger than Kerry.

If all of the statements are correct, which of the following must also be true?
options: Kerry is 2 years older than Susan.
All the children are 9 or older.

steps.explain: Sam is 9 and Ethan is his twin, so Ethan is 9.
Lee is 1 year younger than Ethan, and Kerry is 3 years older than Lee.
Susan is older than Ethan (9) but younger than Kerry (11), so Susan is 10.
Check: A is false (Ethan is 9), B is false (11 − 10 = 1 year), C is false (Lee is 8). D is true.

questions.stem:
I am hiding in one of three rooms. On the door of each room I have written two statements, some true, some false. However, no more than one statement on each door is false.

Room 1: “My name is Kerry.” / “I am not in this room.”
Room 2: “I am not in this room.” / “I am in Room 1 or 3.”
Room 3: “My name is Luke.” / “I am not in Room 1.”

Which one of the following statements must be true?
questions.hint: Start with Room 2 — what do its two statements have in common?

steps.explain: Look at Room 2. Its two statements say the same thing: ‘not in Room 2’ means ‘in Room 1 or 3’. If one were false, the other would be false too — but a door can have at most one false statement.
So both statements on Room 2's door are true.

Checking the others: if I were in Room 1, door 1 and door 3 would each have one false statement, forcing both ‘My name is Kerry’ and ‘My name is Luke’ to be true — impossible. So B is false, and my name could be Kerry, Luke or neither (A and D are not certain).

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests
meta.note: Source option B ('I am not in Room 1') is also always true; replaced with 'I am in Room 1' so the book's answer C is the only correct one.

questions.stem:
Terry bought some small notebooks for $3 each and some big notebooks for $5 each, spending a total of $55.

He bought three more big notebooks than small notebooks.

How many big notebooks did Terry purchase?

steps.explain: Let the number of small notebooks be s. Then there are s + 3 big notebooks.
Solve.

questions.stem:
There are three brothers who all play different sports and different instruments. All of them are a different age.
We know that:

• The person who plays soccer is the youngest
• Andrew plays violin
• The oldest child plays cello
• The person who plays tennis is younger than the person who plays football
• James plays football
• Joshua is the youngest
• The person who plays tennis is the middle child

Who plays tennis as a sport?

steps.explain: Joshua is the youngest, and the youngest plays soccer.
Tennis is played by the middle child, and James plays football — so James is not the middle child or the youngest. James is the oldest.
That leaves Andrew as the middle child, who plays tennis. (Check: the oldest plays cello, and Andrew plays violin — consistent.)

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Screens are everywhere we look. We use them for keeping in touch with friends and family, shopping, playing games and reading news and entertainment. But too much screen time is associated with negative effects on children.

Ryan: “Since excessive computer usage causes eye development issues in young children, they should stay off the computer as much as possible.”

Which of the following best strengthens the argument?
options: It is important to introduce our kids to new technology.
Children learn a lot from using the computer.
Young children's eyes are still developing, and the blue light delays their development.
Children can supplement their learning experiences through using the computer.

steps.explain: Ryan's reason: computer use harms young children's eye development. His conclusion: keep them off the computer.
A, B and D all give reasons FOR children using computers — they weaken the argument.
C explains HOW screens harm developing eyes (blue light delays development), which backs up Ryan's reason.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
George, Steve, Terry and Victor sell cars in a car dealer. When they sell more than $200,000 in a month, they get paid a bonus. Today, George was paid a bonus and Victor had sold $320,000 last month.

If the above statements are true, which one the following statements must definitely be true?
options: Steve was not paid a bonus.
Terry did not sell more than $500,000 last month.

steps.explain: Rule: sell more than $200,000 in a month → get a bonus.
Victor sold $320,000, which is more than $200,000, so Victor must get a bonus.
We only know George sold more than $200,000 — not exactly $500,000. We know nothing about Steve or Terry.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
There are 24 students in 6F. In 6S, there are 13 boys and 11 girls.

When the classes are combined, there are 2 more girls than boys.

How many girls are there in 6F?

steps.explain: Total students in both classes:
Girls are 2 more than boys, so girls + boys = 48 and girls − boys = 2.
Girls in 6F = all girls − girls in 6S.

questions.stem:
There are some cubes in a bag. The number of cubes in the bag is more than 5 but less than 15.

The cubes are either red (R) or black (B).

The teacher says:
If you take a cube at random out of the bag, the probability that it will be red is \(\frac{1}{5}\).

A pupil takes one cube out of the bag.
It is red.

What is the probability of choosing a black cube from the bag next time?

questions.stem:
James is a part time taxi driver. He is planning to collect passengers from the railway station only. He collects a passenger, drives them to their destination, and returns to the station to collect the next passenger.

For each journey James plans to charge a fixed fare of $20, plus $1 per kilometre of journey distance from the railway station to the passenger's destination. His fuel costs are $0.50 per kilometre that he drives his taxi (including the return journey to the station). His profit for that passenger is the difference between the fare he charges and his fuel costs.

How much profit does he earn for taking a passenger to a destination 15 km away and then returning to the station?
questions.hint: Fuel is paid for the return trip too, but the fare is only for the trip out.

steps.explain: Fare charged for a 15 km journey:
Fuel: he drives 15 km there and 15 km back.

steps.explain: The figure has 4 layers: 10 cubes on the bottom (rows of 4, 3, 2, 1), then 6, then 3, then 1 on top. It is a 'staircase' in a corner, so its back walls and bottom are flat.
Count the hidden (touching) faces of each cube. A cube has three orange faces when exactly three of its six faces touch another cube.

The step cubes on the outside have 4 or 5 painted faces; the edge cubes along the back walls have 2; the cubes buried inside have 1. Only two cubes have exactly 3: the back bottom corner cube (bottom + two back walls painted) and the cube in the middle of the second layer (its top and two front faces are exposed steps).
steps.work: back corner cube: 3   centre cube of layer 2: 3

questions.stem:
Louis thinks buying a dog is a much better option than adopting a dog from a shelter because you have the opportunity to choose your own puppy. Even though it can be expensive to buy and requires a lot of work to look after, it will motivate you to take care of it and keep the pet, rather than returning it to the shelter or abandoning it, as some owners do.

Which one of these statements, if true, most weakens Louis' argument?
options: More than 75% of dogs were rehomed or reclaimed from shelters.
Getting a pet has many unexpected responsibilities.
Untrained puppies quickly grow into out-of-control dogs.
Adopting a dog is like saving two lives. The life of the pet you're adopting and the other that can be placed in the shelter for care.

steps.explain: Louis claims buying is a much BETTER option than adopting.

B is true of both buying and adopting, so it doesn't change which is better. C is a reason against getting a puppy, but says nothing about shelters. A is about what happens at shelters, not why adopting is better.
D gives a strong benefit that only adopting has: it saves the adopted dog AND frees a space for another dog. This directly challenges the claim that buying is better.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
There are 2 ways to qualify for the Science Competition: by scoring a grade ‘A’ in the most recent school report or by getting more than 95% in the most recent test.

This year, 10 students from Sophie's school have qualified for the Science Competition.

Sophie: “I know that 5 students got more than 95% in the most recent test. That means that 5 students got an ‘A’ in their most recent school report.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Sophie has made?
options: Some of the students from Sophie's school may have gotten more than 95% in the most recent test but did not get ‘A’ in their report.
There may be an equal number of people who got ‘A’ in the report and got more than 95% in the recent test.
The number of students competing in the Science Competition is different every year.
Some of the students from Sophie's school may have gotten both ‘A’ in their report and scored more than 95% in the test.

steps.explain: Sophie assumes the two groups don't overlap: 10 qualified − 5 by test = 5 by report.
But a student could qualify both ways — an ‘A’ in the report AND more than 95% in the test. Then more than 5 students could have an ‘A’.
steps.work: e.g. if 3 of the test qualifiers also got an ‘A’: ‘A’ students = 5 + 3 = 8, not 5

steps.explain: D points out exactly this overlap.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
The International Morse Code uses dots and dashes (symbols) to represent letters. These are separated by gaps.

There are two letters using only one symbol: E and T.

A, I, M and N use two;

D, G, K, O, R, S, U and W use three;

and the rest of the letters use four.

The following combinations are not used.

• — • —
— — — •
— — — —
• • — —

A secret message with various letters was written down, unfortunately without the spaces between the letters:

• — • • — • • • — — — • • — • • • • — •

What is the minimum number of letters that this message could have?
questions.hint: Check whether the message can be cut into blocks of 4. If one block is a banned combination, you need more letters.

steps.explain: Count the symbols in the message.

Every 1-, 2- and 3-symbol combination is a letter (2 + 4 + 8 = 14 letters), and 12 of the 16 four-symbol combinations are letters. Each letter uses at most 4 symbols, so we need at least 20 ÷ 4 = 5 letters.
Five letters would mean five blocks of exactly 4, starting from the beginning. But the third block is ‘— — — •’, which is not used. So 5 letters is impossible.
Try six letters — for example:
All six blocks are allowed (none is in the not-used list), so the minimum is 6.

questions.stem:
Many apartment blocks have two to twenty-two floors. If an apartment has more than three floors, it has a lift.

If the information in the box is true, which one of these sentences must also be true?
options: You can't get to the second floor by using the lift.
All floors may be reached by lifts.
If you want to go to the first floor, you must use the stairs.
An apartment with ten floors has lifts.

steps.explain: The rule: more than three floors → it has a lift.
Ten floors is more than three, so that apartment must have a lift.
Nothing is said about which floors the lift stops at or whether stairs are needed, so A, B and C are not certain.

questions.stem:
The prices for passes for a tourist bus are shown in the table below.
Passes are valid for the number of days indicated after using it for the first time.

Pass for 1 day: $11 · Pass for 4 days: $33 · Pass for 7 days: $50

Sandy needs a pass on the following days of the month:

2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16.

How much is the cheapest valid combination she could use?

steps.explain: Days 2 to 7 (6 days): a 7-day pass costs $50; a 4-day pass + two 1-day passes costs $33 + $22 = $55.
Days 10, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 all fit inside one 7-day pass (days 10–16) for $50. Other ways cost more: e.g. 4-day ($33) + three 1-day ($33) = $66.
Could one 7-day and one 4-day pass ($83) work? A 7-day pass covers at most one of the two groups, and a 4-day pass can't cover the other group (each spans 6–7 days).
