questions.stem:
What causes the periods of strong and widespread stormy weather that Earth sometimes suffers? The answer is sunspots. Every now and then, the sun develops cool dark areas known as sunspots. Scientists have found that high sunspot activity happens at the same time as stormy weather on Earth.

Which one of these statements, if true, most strengthens the above argument about sunspots?
options: Storms are the result of low-pressure systems in the Earth's atmosphere.
Low sunspot activity happens at the same time as calm weather on Earth.
There is always a storm somewhere on Earth.
There are stormy periods in some areas but not in others while there is sunspot activity.
questions.hint: The argument says sunspots CAUSE storms because they happen at the same time. Evidence that fits the link in BOTH directions makes the link stronger.

steps.explain: Find the claim: high sunspot activity goes together with <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">stormy weather</mark>, so sunspots cause storms.
To strengthen a link like this, show it works the other way too: when sunspots are low, the weather should be calm.

A names a different cause of storms (low pressure) — that competes with sunspots ✗. C says there is always a storm somewhere — it doesn't connect to sunspots ✗. D says storms happen in some areas but not others, even with sunspots — that weakens the claim ✗.
B: low sunspot activity happens at the same time as calm weather — the weather follows the sunspots both ways, which makes a cause-and-effect link much more believable.

keyPoints.text: high sunspot activity happens at the same time as stormy weather on Earth
keyPoints.note: The evidence in the passage: a link between sunspots and storms.

keyPoints.text: most strengthens the above argument about sunspots
keyPoints.note: Add evidence for the link.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Cars should be restricted after dark as they can be very noisy. Although it is unlikely car noise will wake heavy sleepers, it is possible that it would wake light sleepers, especially in cities. This leads to annoyed and irritated residents who will complain about the noise. People need sleep in order to go to work the next day.

Which one of the following statements, if true, most weakens the above argument?
options: Some people work late at night when public transport is not available.
People can just catch public transport at night, which is much quieter.
Even if cars are banned, people can always walk.
A majority of people work during the daytime.
questions.hint: The conclusion: cars should be restricted after dark. A good weakening statement shows that some people NEED their cars after dark.

steps.explain: Find the conclusion: <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">cars should be restricted after dark</mark> because of the noise.
To weaken it, show a strong reason why people still need to drive at night.

B says people can use quiet public transport — that SUPPORTS the restriction ✗. C says people can walk — also supports it ✗. D says most people work in the daytime — so few need cars at night, which supports it ✗.
A: some people work late at night when public transport is not available. They would have no way to get home if cars were restricted, so a restriction would cause a real problem.

keyPoints.text: Cars should be restricted after dark
keyPoints.note: The conclusion to be weakened.
Choose a reason people need cars at night.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
X-rays have been used to show a painting in our local museum was not the work of a famous artist as previously thought. This has caused its value to drop from millions to almost nothing. Yet no art experts were able to detect that it was not 'the real thing'. This means that the value of a painting is determined by who painted it rather than the actual artistic elements.

Which of these statements, if true, most strengthens the above argument?
options: The works of some forgers of art now sell for very large amounts of money.
Many artists changed their style during their career.
In controlled tests, art experts have been shown to be very good at identifying the painters of works they have not seen before.
Until its true origin was discovered, the painting in our museum was widely regarded as a masterpiece.
questions.hint: The argument: the painting itself did not change, only the belief about who painted it — and the value collapsed. Find the option that shows the painting was valued highly BEFORE the discovery.

steps.explain: Find the argument: the value dropped from millions to almost nothing <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">only when</mark> it was found to be by someone else. No expert could tell the difference by looking, so the artistic elements were the same before and after.
steps.work: same painting, different painter → value fell

steps.explain: The conclusion: value depends on WHO painted it, not on how it looks.

A says forgeries can be valuable — that goes against the idea that the painter matters ✗. B (artists changed styles) and C (experts are good at identifying painters) don't support the conclusion — C even weakens it ✗.

D: until its origin was discovered, the painting was widely regarded as a masterpiece. People loved it for its artistic elements until the painter was found to be different, then valued it at almost nothing — so value really did depend on the painter.

keyPoints.text: no art experts were able to detect that it was not 'the real thing'
keyPoints.note: The painting looked the same before and after.

keyPoints.text: the value of a painting is determined by who painted it rather than the actual artistic elements
keyPoints.note: The conclusion to be supported.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
There are six towns A, B, C, D, E and F in a region.

• Town C is north of Town D and northeast of Town B.
• Town D is north of Town E and west of Town F.
• Town A is east of Town F.

Which one of the following is not possible?
options: Town B is west of Town E.
Town E is southwest of Town A.
Town A is southwest of Town C.
Town F is east of Town B.
questions.hint: Draw a map with North at the top. Put D in the middle: C straight above it, E straight below, F to the right. Then add A and B.

steps.explain: Start with D. Town C is NORTH of D (straight above) and Town E is SOUTH of D (straight below).
steps.work: C above D;  E below D

steps.explain: Town F is EAST of D (to the right), and Town A is east of F, so A is even further right, on the same level.
steps.work: D — F — A  from left to right

steps.explain: Town C is NORTHEAST of B, which means B is SOUTHWEST of C: B is below and to the left of C.

questions.stem:
This is part of a tiled wall in my house that has a regular, repeating pattern. One tile has fallen off the wall and broken, leaving a square space.

Which one of the following tiles could be used to replace the space?
questions.hint: The wall repeats: every 2 tiles across and down the same star pattern comes back. Look at the lines that reach the EDGES of the gap — the new tile must continue every one of them.

steps.explain: Find the gap (red outline). It is one square tile: the new tile must fit its four edges exactly.
The pattern is made of eight-pointed stars and dark diamonds that repeat. A line or a shaded corner that touches an edge of the gap has to carry straight on into the new tile.
steps.work: match: lines at the top, bottom, left and right edges

steps.explain: Compare the four tiles. Each tile has three white corner triangles and one dark wedge system pointing in a different direction. The shaded pieces in A, B and C leave a break where they would meet the neighbouring pieces around the gap ✗.
Tile D continues the star and diamond shapes on every side with no gap and no change of direction — this is the tile of the book's solution.

keyPoints.note: The same shapes return at regular distances — copy the surrounding lines.

keyPoints.text: Which one of the following tiles could be used
keyPoints.note: The correct tile continues every line meeting the gap.

questions.stem:
Dogs need the space and freedom to run around and fully exercise their body. They are able to run three times as fast as humans but this is not possible when they are held on a leash. When a dog tries to run but its owner is too slow, there is a risk of choking. Thus, leashes should not be used when walking a dog.

Which one of the following statements, if true, most weakens the above argument?
options: Some unrestrained dogs can be aggressive and bite humans.
Owners can try to keep fit by running with their dogs everyday.
Dogs are social creatures and need to interact with other dogs so taking dogs to a dog park is important for their mental and physical wellbeing.
Keeping a dog on a leash does not restrict their legs.
questions.hint: The conclusion: don't use leashes (so dogs can run freely). Which option gives a good reason a dog should NOT run free?

steps.explain: Find the conclusion: <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">leashes should not be used</mark> when walking a dog, because dogs need freedom to run.
To weaken it, show a serious problem with a dog being off the leash.

B says owners can run with dogs — that actually helps the dog run freely, so it supports the argument ✗. C (dog parks) is about interaction, not about leashes ✗. D says a leash does not restrict the legs — this is a weak attack on the claim that dogs can't run on a leash, but it doesn't give a reason to use leashes ✗.
A: unrestrained dogs can be aggressive and bite humans — a real danger to people, which is a strong reason to keep dogs on a leash.

keyPoints.text: leashes should not be used when walking a dog
keyPoints.note: The conclusion to attack.
Choose a reason FOR using leashes.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Mr Wilson, the language teacher, would like to find out the number of senior students who do a language elective. In a group of 28 students, 7 take French, 10 take Spanish, and 4 take both languages. The students taking both French and Spanish are counted in the 7 taking French or the 10 taking Spanish.

June: “That means there are only 3 people who only take French.”

Alex: “That means there are 14 people who either take French or Spanish.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: The 4 students who take BOTH are already inside the 7 and the 10. Draw two overlapping circles and put the 4 in the overlap first.

steps.explain: Draw two overlapping circles: one for French and one for Spanish. The 4 students who take both go in the overlap.

Check June: 'only 3 people only take French' matches the French-only part ✓. Check Alex: 'there are 14 people who either take French or Spanish'. Count the students in the circles: French or Spanish (or both) is 3 + 4 + 6 = 13; those who take just one of the two is 3 + 6 = 9. Neither equals 14, so Alex is wrong ✗.
Only June's reasoning is correct.

keyPoints.text: The students taking both French and Spanish are counted in the 7 taking French or the 10 taking Spanish.
keyPoints.note: Subtract the 4 from each group before finding 'only' numbers.
Check June and Alex separately.

questions.stem:
Sandra's class wanted to choose which sport to play for their class. They decided to have a vote. Students could vote for soccer, volleyball or basketball.
Students had to cast two votes, but they could not vote for the same sport twice. Every sport got at least one vote.

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?

Karl: “If everyone had to cast two votes, I am sure soccer got the most votes because all my friends like soccer.”

Sandra: “Every student had to vote for either basketball or volleyball or both.”
questions.hint: List every pair of sports a student could vote for. Three sports, two different votes each: how many pairs are there, and does each pair include basketball or volleyball?

steps.explain: A student votes for two DIFFERENT sports out of three. List every possible pair.
steps.work:
soccer + volleyball
soccer + basketball
volleyball + basketball

steps.explain: Sandra: 'every student voted for basketball or volleyball or both.' Look at each pair: the first has volleyball, the second has basketball, the third has both. Soccer can never be voted for twice, so nobody can avoid both basketball and volleyball ✓.
steps.work: every pair contains basketball or volleyball ✓

steps.explain: Karl: 'soccer got the most votes because all my friends like soccer.' His friends are only some of the class — we don't know how the others voted. Soccer could easily get fewer votes than the others ✗.
Only Sandra's reasoning is correct.

keyPoints.text: they could not vote for the same sport twice
keyPoints.note: Every student's two votes are two different sports.
Friends are only part of the class — not proof soccer won.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
In the end-of-year test at Smart High School, the following results were achieved by students.

• All students received a grade A in science.
• No student in the school received a grade B in mathematics.

To become a member of the Mathematics Olympiad and represent the school next year, a student has to have a grade A in both mathematics and history.

Patrick received a grade A in history but did not get into the Mathematics Olympiad team.

What could be the reason?
options: He received a grade B in science.
He received a grade A in mathematics.
He did not receive a grade A in science.
He received a grade C in mathematics.
questions.hint: To join the team Patrick needs A in BOTH maths and history. He has history, so look at maths. Then check each option against the two facts about the school.

steps.explain: List the entry rule: grade A in <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">both mathematics and history</mark>. Patrick has A in history, so he failed to get in because of mathematics.
Check each option against the school facts. A: a grade B in science — but ALL students got A in science ✗. C: no grade A in science — again everyone got A ✗.
B: a grade A in mathematics — then he would have both As and would have got in ✗.
D: a grade C in mathematics. This is not an A, so he doesn't qualify, and no student got a B in maths so a C (or lower) is the kind of result he must have.

keyPoints.text: a student has to have a grade A in both mathematics and history
keyPoints.note: Both grades must be A.

keyPoints.text: No student in the school received a grade B in mathematics.
keyPoints.note: Patrick's non-A in maths must be C or lower.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
In the following pairs of numbers, the right-hand number is the result of applying a certain rule to the left-hand number. This rule is applied to both numbers in the table.

I applied the same rule to a new number.
What is the number if the code is 5713?

questions.stem:
Four friends are counting their money in their wallets to see who has the highest amount.

• Only two people had a lower amount than Tom.
• Ben has a lower amount of money than Harry.
• Silvia did not have the least amount of money.

Based on the information above, which one of the following must also be true?
options: Ben has more money than Silvia.
Tom has more money than Harry.
Silvia has less money than Harry.
Tom has more money than Ben.
questions.hint: Tom has exactly two people below him, so Tom is 2nd out of 4. Only ONE person has more money than Tom. Work out who it could be.

steps.explain: Only two people had less than Tom, so exactly one person has MORE than Tom: Tom is second richest.
Ben has less than Harry, and Silvia is not the lowest. Try the person who is first. If Harry is first, then Ben and Silvia are third and fourth; Silvia is not last, so Silvia is 3rd and Ben is 4th.

steps.explain: If Harry is NOT first, then Harry and Ben are both below Tom, so the person above Tom must be Silvia. Then Harry is 3rd and Ben is 4th (Ben < Harry).

steps.explain: Check the options in BOTH orders. A: Ben more than Silvia — no, Ben is last ✗.  B: Tom more than Harry — fails in Order 1 ✗.  C: Silvia less than Harry — fails in Order 2 ✗.  D: Tom more than Ben — true in both orders ✓.
Ben is last in both orders, so Tom always has more than Ben.

keyPoints.text: Only two people had a lower amount than Tom.
keyPoints.note: Tom is 2nd of the four.
It has to be true in EVERY possible order.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
As they prepare for the state championships, one gymnast must be moved from the Level 2 team to the Level 1 team. The coaches will move the gymnast who has won the biggest prize and has the most experience.

In the last competition, Roberta won a bronze medal and has competed seven times before. Jamie has won a silver medal and has competed fewer times than Roberta. Beth has won a higher medal than Jamie and has competed more times than Roberta. Michelle has won a bronze medal and it is her third time competing.

Who will be moved to the Level 1 team?
questions.hint: Two things count: the BIGGEST medal and the MOST competitions. Make a small table with both facts for each gymnast, then find the gymnast who is top in both.

steps.explain: Write down what we know about each gymnast. Medals rank gold > silver > bronze.
steps.work:

Jamie: silver, fewer than 7 times
Michelle: bronze, 3 times

Small and large rowing boats can be hired out for different lengths of time at different rates (cost per hour). Each person is required to wear a life jacket, so one life jacket must be hired for each person. Extra charges are made for oars and cushions as shown in the table below.

Sally and six friends take a large rowing boat with four oars for five hours. Each person has a cushion.

What is the total cost?

questions.stem:
The diagram below is the net of a shape.

Which one of the shapes below is the solid that can be folded from the net shown?
questions.hint: Count and describe the faces in the net: how many are rectangles and what shape are the other faces? Then find the solid with exactly those faces.

steps.explain: Look at the net. There are two bigger faces shaped like the letter L, one on each side of the central rectangle.

Count the rectangles: the column of three squares-and-rectangles on the right (the blue one is one of them), the long central rectangle, and the small rectangles joined to the L-shapes. Altogether there are six rectangles.
So the solid has 8 faces: two L-shaped faces (the ends) and six rectangular faces. This is a prism with an L-shaped end — the L has six sides, so it has six rectangular sides.
Compare with the options: A, C and D have ends that are NOT an L (arrow-shaped, zig-zag and sloping shapes). Only B is a step-shaped prism with an L-shaped end.

keyPoints.note: A net shows every face of the solid laid flat — count the faces.

keyPoints.text: solid that can be folded from the net shown
keyPoints.note: Match the number and shapes of the faces.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests
meta.note: Figure vectorised from the book page (exact outlines, blue face colour matched). Book solution: only B has 2 L-shapes and 6 rectangles.

questions.stem:
The world urgently needs sufficient distribution of food so that everyone gets enough food and nutrition. Medicine and medical facilities also need to be distributed across the world to ensure people in developing countries can get proper medical care.

Which one of these statements, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: Food and medicine production is slow in developing countries.
Studies have found that people in developing countries don't seek medical attention even when they are sick.
Most of the people in developing countries are not getting enough food and medical care.
There is sufficient food and medicine manufactured for everyone.
questions.hint: The conclusion: medicine and medical facilities should be distributed so people in developing countries can get care. Which option says distributing more would not help?

steps.explain: Find the conclusion: medicine and facilities <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">need to be distributed</mark> so that people in developing countries can get proper medical care.
To weaken it we want a statement that shows distribution would not lead to better care.

A and C describe the problem (slow production, people not getting enough) — they support the need ✗. D says there is enough made for everyone — then the problem is distribution, which supports the argument ✗.
B: people in developing countries don't seek medical attention even when they are sick. Then more medicine and facilities would not be used, so distributing them would not improve their care.

keyPoints.text: Medicine and medical facilities also need to be distributed across the world
keyPoints.note: The claim to weaken.
Find a reason distribution would not help.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Mathematics tells us about economic trends, patterns of disease, and the growth of populations. Mathematics is all around us and helps us understand the world better. Mathematics is good at exposing the truth, but it can also perpetuate misunderstandings and untruths. Figures have the power to mislead people.

Which of the following statements, if true, most strengthens the above argument?
options: Students should spend more hours at school studying mathematics as it will help them in future.
Companies recruit people who are good at mathematics since they are good at problem solving.
Mathematics can be helpful for balancing your budget because you will have a good understanding of how to make sure where you can use your money.
A poorly conducted survey can mislead people to underestimate or overestimate the truth.
questions.hint: Notice the TWO sides of the argument: maths exposes the truth, but figures can also mislead. Choose the option that supports the 'mislead' side.

steps.explain: The passage says mathematics helps us understand the world — but its final point is that <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">figures have the power to mislead people</mark>.
A strengthening statement should give an example of numbers misleading people.
A, B and C only say that maths is useful (for the future, for jobs, for budgets) ✗ — they support the first half, not the 'mislead' point.
D: a poorly conducted survey can mislead people to underestimate or overestimate the truth — a clear example of figures misleading, so it strengthens the argument.

keyPoints.text: Figures have the power to mislead people.
keyPoints.note: The key idea to support.
Choose an example of numbers misleading people.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Plots of land within the community garden are allocated for people to grow fruit and vegetables. The plots come in a variety of sizes. The garden consists of seven plots as described in the table below.

Which one of the plans below could show the plots in the garden? (For each plot the length is the longest side and the width is the shortest side.)
questions.hint: Measure each rectangle in each plan in metres. A plan is correct only if its seven rectangles are exactly 8×3, 8×2, 5×4, 4×3, 3×3, 3×3 and 3×2. The two longest plots (8 m) make a good ruler.

steps.explain: Add the areas of the seven plots: this is the area of the whole garden.
All four plans have the same outline. The two long plots (8 m) in plan A lie side by side with the 5 × 4 plot (4 m wide) on their left, so the plan is 12 m wide, and 96 ÷ 12 = 8 m tall.

Measure plan A with this scale. Top: the 5 × 4 plot, the 8 × 3 plot and the 8 × 2 plot. Bottom row (3 m high): 3 × 3, 3 × 3, 4 × 3 and 2 × 3 (the 3 × 2 plot turned). These are exactly the seven plots in the table — each plot is used once.
Plan B contains rectangles of 6 × 4, 5 × 3, 4 × 2 and 5 × 2 — none is in the table.
Plan C contains 6 × 3 (twice), 5 × 2 and 3 × 5 — not in the table.
Plan D contains 3 × 6, 6 × 2 and 6 × 3 — not in the table. Only plan A works.

keyPoints.text: The garden consists of seven plots
keyPoints.note: Every plot is used exactly once.

keyPoints.text: the length is the longest side and the width is the shortest side
keyPoints.note: A plot 3 × 2 can be drawn turned (2 wide × 3 tall).

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests
meta.note: Plans vectorised from the book page (exact outlines). Dimensions in the solution come from measuring the plans, which are drawn to scale.

questions.stem:
When Jessica receives an email, her smart watch will receive an alert. Otherwise, nothing happens to the smart watch.

Jessica: “I received an alert on my smart watch so I checked my email. But I'm still getting the alert on my smart watch, so that means I haven't read the email.”

Whitney: “No, that's not right. The alert on the smart watch means that there is another email.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: The box says an alert comes WHEN an email is received — an alert is caused by an email arriving, not by an email being unread. Test each speaker against that.

steps.explain: The rule: email received → alert on the watch. 'Otherwise, nothing happens.' So every alert is caused by an email arriving.
steps.work: email arrives → alert;  no email → nothing

steps.explain: Jessica: 'I'm still getting the alert, so I haven't read the email.' But the alerts are about emails ARRIVING, not about reading them. Reading her email doesn't stop alerts, and still getting an alert doesn't show an unread email ✗.
Whitney: 'The alert on the watch means that there is another email.' If she is still getting an alert, something must be arriving — another email ✓.
steps.work: alert → an email arrived → another email

steps.explain: Only Whitney's reasoning is correct.

keyPoints.text: When Jessica receives an email, her smart watch will receive an alert.
keyPoints.note: Alert = an email has arrived.

keyPoints.text: Otherwise, nothing happens to the smart watch.
keyPoints.note: No alerts without a new email.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
There are five people in the queue.

1. Sue is ahead of Jessica.
2. Jessica is standing next to Alfred.
3. Ashley is in first place, just ahead of Fred.
4. Fred is two places ahead of Jessica.
5. Jessica is not standing next to Ashley.

If the information in the box is true, which two statements together prove that Jessica is not last in the queue?
questions.hint: Place the people one clue at a time. Which two clues alone are enough to fix Jessica's position (and show it is not 5th)?

steps.explain: Use statement 3 first: Ashley is first, and Fred is just behind her, so Fred is second.

questions.stem:
Shorter men tend to have larger feet.

Dean: “My dad is shorter than your dad so my dad's feet must be larger than your dad's feet.”

Tom: “I am taller than you so that must mean my feet are smaller than yours.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Look at the key word in the box: 'TEND to'. It describes a general pattern, not a rule that is always true for every pair of people.

steps.explain: The box says shorter men <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">tend to</mark> have larger feet. 'Tend to' means it is usually true — but there are exceptions.
Dean: 'my dad is shorter, so his feet MUST be larger.' A shorter man usually has larger feet, but it is not guaranteed for these two particular men ✗.
Tom: 'I am taller, so my feet MUST be smaller.' Same mistake — taller people usually (not always) have smaller feet ✗.
Both speakers turn 'tend to' into 'must'. Neither is correct.

keyPoints.text: Shorter men tend to have larger feet.
keyPoints.note: 'Tend to' is a general pattern with exceptions.
Check whether each speaker says 'must' when the box only says 'tends to'.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
The table below shows the marks scored by 3 students in each subject.

A prize is awarded to the student with the highest final score.
The total of the 3 best subjects is the final score for each student.

Each subject is scored out of 50.

If the final scores between students are equal, then the person who has the highest single mark wins the prize.

If student B won the prize, what is the minimum mark for Art that he/she must have scored?

steps.explain: The score to beat is Student A's 122. Student B's best two marks are History 42 and English 36, then the Art mark x (Art must be one of the three best).

If x = 44, B's total is 122 — equal to A's. Then the highest single mark decides: B's highest mark would be 44 and A's highest is also 44 — still equal, so B does NOT win clearly. B needs a total of at least 123.
Solve for x.

keyPoints.text: The total of the 3 best subjects is the final score for each student.
keyPoints.note: Add each student's three highest marks.

keyPoints.text: If the final scores between students are equal, then the person who has the highest single mark wins the prize.
keyPoints.note: A tie at 122 doesn't help B because the highest marks are also equal (44 and 44).

questions.stem:
One style of personalised number plates allows a mixture of letters and digits.
The rules applying to this style of number plates are:

• Both letters and digits must be used.
• The first symbol must be a letter, not a digit.
• The digits 1 – 9 are allowed, but not 0.
• A number plate can only have four, five or six symbols (letters and digits).

Note: this is the letter O and this is the digit 0.

How many of the following number plates are allowed under the rule?

steps.explain: List the four rules as a checklist.
steps.work:
1) letters AND digits   2) first symbol a letter
3) no digit 0 (1–9 only)   4) 4, 5 or 6 symbols

steps.explain: A3B6C9: letters and digits ✓, starts with a letter ✓, digits 3, 6, 9 (no zero) ✓, 6 symbols ✓.  Allowed.
MY320: it contains the digit 0, which is not allowed ✗. 24TEE: the first symbol is a digit ✗. XXX: only letters (no digit) and only 3 symbols ✗.
XY4GEN: letters and digit ✓, first symbol a letter ✓, digit 4 ✓, 6 symbols ✓.  B4MA: letters and digit ✓, first symbol a letter ✓, digit 4 ✓, 4 symbols ✓.

questions.stem:
When Jane's oven timer is sounding, it means there are 5 minutes before the potatoes are fully baked.

Kim: “The timer has stopped sounding. The potatoes are fully baked.”

Pam: “The timer only tells us that there is exactly five minutes left.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: The box says what the timer MEANS WHILE it is sounding. It tells us nothing about what happens after it stops.

steps.explain: What the box says: <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">while the timer is sounding</mark>, there are 5 minutes left. That is all.

Kim: 'the timer has stopped sounding, so the potatoes are fully baked.' The box says nothing about the timer stopping, so we can't conclude the potatoes are done — maybe the timer rang for just a few seconds, and there are still 5 minutes to go ✗.
Pam: 'the timer only tells us there is exactly five minutes left.' That is exactly what the box says: the timer is only a 5-minute warning ✓.
Only Pam's reasoning is correct.

keyPoints.text: When Jane's oven timer is sounding, it means there are 5 minutes before the potatoes are fully baked.
keyPoints.note: The timer is only a 5-minute warning.
Stopping tells us nothing about the potatoes.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
In the final Amateur Golf Tournament, ten competitors play for three days. The trophy, and a prize of $2,000, is won by the person with the lowest total score from over three days. There are also three $500 prizes for the lowest individual score on each day and three $200 prizes for the second lowest score on each day.

These are the results of the games played in each tournament.

Which person does not receive a $200 prize?

questions.stem:
A handful of countries dominate the lithium market – a metal that has grown in stature in recent years due to its use in rechargeable batteries in electronic devices and electric vehicles.

According to the latest figures, global lithium production in 2019 stood at 77,000 tonnes, and Australia was the world's top producer of lithium with an output of 42,000 tonnes.

The diagram below shows the 2019 production of lithium in metric tonnes by the world's major producers.

Which of the pie charts, if suitably labelled, would represent the same data?
questions.hint: A pie chart shows each bar as a slice. Describe the bar chart in words (which bars are equal, which are about half of another), then pick the pie whose slices follow the same pattern.

steps.explain: Read the bar chart from the left: Chile and Australia are the two tallest bars and are about equal; China is about half of those; Argentina is about half of China; Portugal, Zimbabwe and Brazil are three tiny bars of similar size.
steps.work: Chile ≈ Australia;  China ≈ 1/2;  Argentina ≈ 1/2 of China;  last three tiny and similar

steps.explain: Turn this into slices: two large, similar slices; a third slice about half their size; a fourth slice about half of the third; three tiny similar slices.
steps.work: slices:  big, big, 1/2, 1/4, tiny, tiny, tiny

steps.explain: Check the pie charts (sizes of the slices measured from the pictures). A: 42%, 23%, 19%, 11% — the second slice is much smaller than the first and the third is not about half ✗. B: 41%, 26%, 14%, 11% — the fourth slice is almost as big as the third ✗. C: 35%, 27%, 24%, 14% — three big slices; the third is not half of the first two ✗.
D: 44%, 33%, 17%, 5% and three tiny slices — two big slices, then about half, then about half again, then three tiny ones. This follows the bar chart.

keyPoints.text: The diagram below shows the 2019 production of lithium in metric tonnes
keyPoints.note: Compare the SHAPE of the bar chart with each pie chart.

keyPoints.text: Which of the pie charts, if suitably labelled, would represent the same data?
keyPoints.note: Match the relative sizes: equal, half, half of half, tiny.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
In a school function ceremony, seven students, Amy, Bob, Chad, Dom, Elisa, Fisher and Grant have to deliver their performances in seven consecutive slots, but not necessarily in that order.

The following information is known about the order in which the students perform:

• Chad performs immediately before Dom.
• Grant performs sometime after Chad.
• There are exactly two performances made between the performances of Amy and Elisa.
• Elisa performs immediately before Grant.

Dom: “That means Grant is right before Amy.”

Fisher: “Oh that means I have to perform third.”

Based on the information given above, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: 'Must' means true in EVERY possible order. To show a claim is wrong, you only need ONE order that fits all the clues but breaks the claim.

steps.explain: Link the clues into blocks: Chad–Dom (Chad immediately before Dom) and Elisa–Grant (Elisa immediately before Grant). Amy is three slots away from Elisa (two performances between them).
steps.work: block 1: Chad, Dom;  block 2: Elisa, Grant;  Amy 3 slots from Elisa

steps.explain: Try an order: put Chad and Dom first (slots 1–2), Amy third. Then Elisa must be three slots from Amy: slot 6, so Grant is slot 7. Fisher and Bob fill slots 4 and 5.
steps.work: Chad, Dom, Amy, Fisher, Bob, Elisa, Grant

questions.stem:
Good sleep is vital for a child's well-being and can cause more than just tiredness in the morning. Sleep is an essential part of everyone's routine and an indispensable part of a healthy lifestyle. Studies have shown that kids who regularly get an adequate amount of sleep have improved attention, behaviour, learning, memory, and overall mental and physical health. Not getting enough sleep can lead to high blood pressure, obesity, depression and contribute to long term chronic health problems. Four million Australians aren't sleeping properly and many of us will experience health issues as a result.

Which of the following statements, if true, most strengthens the above argument?
options: Researchers are reliable people since they always work with facts.
Sleeping problems is prevalent in adults and children and more than 25% of population don't get enough sleep.
Sleep deprivation has been strongly correlated with chronic heart diseases and strokes.
Ever since Jane has started to sleep more than 8 hours, she feels more relaxed and has been able to work longer.
questions.hint: The argument: not sleeping enough causes health problems. Which option gives NEW evidence of a health problem linked to lack of sleep?

steps.explain: Find the argument: <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">not getting enough sleep can lead to</mark> high blood pressure, obesity, depression and long-term chronic health problems.
steps.work: claim: lack of sleep → health problems

steps.explain: To strengthen it, add further evidence that sleep loss and health problems are linked.

A just praises researchers — no new link ✗. B says many people don't get enough sleep — that is about how common the problem is, not about health damage ✗. D is about one person feeling relaxed and working longer — not health problems from sleep loss ✗.
C: sleep deprivation is strongly correlated with chronic heart diseases and strokes — extra evidence of serious chronic health problems linked to lack of sleep.

keyPoints.text: Not getting enough sleep can lead to high blood pressure, obesity, depression
keyPoints.note: The cause-and-effect claim to support.
Choose NEW evidence linking lack of sleep to health problems.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

He gave 4 boxes to his sister with one statement written on each box.

Exactly one of these boxes contains the present, but only one of the four statements is true.

steps.explain: Rule: exactly one statement is true and the present is in exactly one box. Test each box in turn.

Present in Box 2: Box 1 false; Box 2 'not here' false; Box 3 'in box 1 or 4' false; Box 4 false. Zero true statements ✗.
Present in Box 3: Box 1 false; Box 2 'not here' TRUE; Box 3 'in box 1 or 4' false; Box 4 false. Exactly one true statement ✓.

questions.stem:
Sally and Tom want to use a code to send secret messages to each other. In the code, each letter of the alphabet is represented by a one-digit number as shown below:

For example, the word SORRY would be written in the code as 8-4-7-7-4.

To test the system, Sally writes four words using the code and sends them to Tom. Tom tries to decode them, and gets the following answers:

SHORT

HELLO

CLOWN

EVERY

Tom is confident that he has three of these words correct, but he is unsure about the other one.

Which word is Tom unsure about?

questions.hint: Several letters share the same digit (for example A, K and U are all 0), so one code can decode to more than one word. Write each word's code, then look for another real word with the same code.

steps.explain: Learn the code: each letter has a one-digit number, and the numbers repeat every 10 letters (A–J are 0–9, K–T are 0–9 again, U–Z are 0–5).
Write the code for each word.
Tom is sure about a word if no other real word has the same code. Look at HELLO = 7-4-1-1-4. Another word with the same digits: H(7) O(4) B(1) B(1) Y(4) = HOBBY.

questions.stem:
Annie, Mary, and Diana are three sisters of different ages. Whenever they are asked their names, each one states either her own name or the name of an older sister.

On one occasion, when all three were asked their names, two of them answered "Annie".

What is not possible?
questions.hint: The OLDEST sister can only give her own name (no older sister exists). The middle can give her own or the oldest's. The youngest can give any of the three. Now ask: could two of them say 'Annie' if Annie is the youngest?

steps.explain: Who can say what? The oldest sister has no older sister, so she can only say her OWN name. The middle sister can say her own name or the oldest's name. The youngest can say her own name or either older sister's name.
steps.work:
oldest: own only
middle: own or oldest
youngest: own, middle's or oldest's

steps.explain: Two answered 'Annie'. Suppose Annie is the OLDEST: she says 'Annie' herself, and either of the others can name her too. Two (or even three) can say 'Annie' ✓ possible.
Suppose Annie is the MIDDLE sister: she says 'Annie', and the youngest can say 'Annie' (older sister) ✓ possible.

Suppose Annie is the YOUNGEST. Only the youngest can say 'Annie' (her own name). The oldest says her own name and the middle says her own or the oldest's name — nobody older can name the youngest. So only ONE person can say 'Annie', but two did ✗.
So 'Annie is the youngest sister' is not possible. The other options (Diana or Mary in the middle, Mary the older one) all fit with Annie as the oldest or middle sister.

keyPoints.text: each one states either her own name or the name of an older sister
keyPoints.note: You can only name yourself or someone OLDER.
Two sisters said Annie: Annie must be old enough for another to name her.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Students spending too much time on online games every week tend to suffer from worsened learning ability, concentration problems, poor academic performance and decreased interactions with other people.

Max: “Susan doesn't play any online games, so her maths mark must be top of the class.”

Sean: “Peter plays so much games every day, so his maths mark must be very bad.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: 'TEND to suffer' describes a pattern, not a guarantee. And 'no games' does not mean 'top of the class'. Test both speakers for words like 'must'.

steps.explain: The box says too much gaming <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">tends to</mark> lead to poor performance. It does not say it ALWAYS does, and it says nothing about people who don't play.
steps.work: too many games → TENDS to lower results

steps.explain: Max: 'Susan doesn't play games, so her maths mark MUST be top of the class.' Not playing games does not make you top of the class — many other things affect marks ✗.
Sean: 'Peter plays so much, so his mark MUST be very bad.' 'Tend to' leaves exceptions: Peter might still do well ✗.
Neither reasoning is correct.

keyPoints.text: tend to suffer from worsened learning ability
keyPoints.note: 'Tend to' = usually, not always.
Both speakers use the strong word 'must'.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Dr Lee: “Just as the sun's rays can be focused by a magnifying glass to burn a piece of paper, High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound waves can be concentrated to burn human tissue. HIFU targets cancerous tissue precisely through high frequency sound waves. The waves are harmless until they converge at the focal point, so a surgeon can operate deep inside the body without harming the surrounding tissue.”

Which one of these statements, if true, most weakens the Dr Lee's argument?
options: HIFU requires no cuts to be made, and many operations don't even need an anaesthetic.
The patient can be in and out of hospital within a day.
Ultrasound waves can be too focused and cause damage.
It allows for very deep penetration into the body.
questions.hint: Dr Lee's key claim: HIFU can operate deep inside the body WITHOUT harming the surrounding tissue. Look for the option that says the waves CAN cause harm.

steps.explain: Find the claim: the waves are <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">harmless until they converge</mark>, so a surgeon can operate deep inside the body without harming the surrounding tissue.
steps.work: claim: HIFU is safe for surrounding tissue

steps.explain: To weaken it, show that HIFU may cause harm.
A and B are advantages of HIFU (no cuts, quick recovery) — they support it ✗. D says it reaches deep into the body — that is part of Dr Lee's claim ✗.
C: ultrasound waves can be too focused and cause damage — this directly contradicts the claim that the surrounding tissue is not harmed.

keyPoints.text: The waves are harmless until they converge at the focal point
keyPoints.note: The safety claim to weaken.

keyPoints.text: most weakens the Dr Lee's argument
keyPoints.note: Choose a statement showing possible harm.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Five students had a competition to see who could read the most books.

• Chris read more books than Bexley but fewer books than Elvis.
• David read two more books than Chris.
• Alex has an odd number of books read which is the average number of books that Chris and David read.
• Elvis read 8 books and Bexley read half as many as Elvis.

The five students read a total of 33 books together.

Which one of the following sentences must be true?
options: Elvis and David read same number of books.
Alex read more books than David.
Bexley read 3 more books than Alex.
Chris read more books than Elvis.
questions.hint: Start with the exact numbers: Elvis 8, Bexley 4. Then work out Chris, David and Alex in terms of Chris's number, and use the total 33 to check.

steps.explain: Elvis read 8 books and Bexley read half as many.
Chris read more than Bexley (4) but fewer than Elvis (8), so Chris read 5, 6 or 7. David read two more than Chris; Alex read the average of Chris and David, which is exactly one more than Chris.
Alex has an ODD number of books, so Chris + 1 is odd, which means Chris is even. Among 5, 6, 7 the only even number is 6.
Check the total: 8 (Elvis) + 4 (Bexley) + 6 (Chris) + 8 (David) + 7 (Alex).

questions.stem:
A sculpture is placed in a glass box and displayed in an exhibition as shown in the diagram below.

The sculpture can be viewed from all sides.

Which one of the following is not a possible view from one of the sides of the glass box?
questions.hint: Imagine walking round the glass box and looking from the front, side and top. Three of the drawings are real views of the sculpture; one has a shape that never appears.

steps.explain: Describe the sculpture: a solid bracket with a rounded U-shaped slot cut through it, and a small block sticking out at the left end.

Looking at it from the FRONT you see the arch-shaped slot with the small block on top: that is view A. Looking from the SIDE you see the block with a sloping corner: view B. Looking from ABOVE you see an L-shape: view D.
steps.work: front = A,  side = B,  top = D

steps.explain: The book's solution confirms that A, B and D are the top, side and front views of the sculpture.

C shows a rectangle with a round notch cut out of its upper corner. The slot in the sculpture goes right through it, so no side of the glass box ever shows a notch like that. C is not a view of the sculpture.

keyPoints.text: The sculpture can be viewed from all sides.
keyPoints.note: Top, bottom and the four sides all count as views.
Find the drawing that matches NO side.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests
meta.note: Figure vectorised from the book page. Book solution: views A, B and D are the top, side and front views.

questions.stem:
Last month in our town's annual dance competition, five competitors went to the final and were awarded marks out of 10 for five different disciplines.

The pie chart shows the marks awarded to one of the competitors.

This pie chart has been converted into a bar graph. The horizontal axis represents the types of discipline and the vertical axis represents the marks.

Which of these bar charts could represent this competitor's scores?
questions.hint: A bar's height is proportional to the size of its slice. Rank the five slices (smallest, middle, two equal, biggest) and find the bar chart with the same pattern in the same order.

steps.explain: Estimate the five slices of the pie (as a share of the whole circle), going round clockwise from the smallest slice on the right.
Describe them in words: one very small slice, then a medium one, then a bigger one, then the BIGGEST, then one about the same as the third.

So the bars should rise from a tiny bar up to the tallest bar, then drop slightly. Check the bar charts: A starts with the tallest bar and falls ✗. C is symmetric with a very tall middle bar and two tiny bars ✗. D has two equal tallest bars and its smallest bar is too big ✗.
B: heights in the ratio about 6 : 18 : 23 : 29 : 23 (per cent of the total) — exactly the pie chart's slices, in the same order.

keyPoints.text: The pie chart shows the marks awarded to one of the competitors.
keyPoints.note: Slice size = share of the marks.

keyPoints.text: Which of these bar charts could represent this competitor's scores?
keyPoints.note: Same pattern of sizes, same order.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests
meta.note: Figures vectorised from the book page. Slice sizes measured from the picture (5/18/24/29/24 %), B matches within 1 %.

questions.stem:
Above is a picture of two identical boxes. Below is a picture of three of these boxes placed next to each other.

What are the shapes on the end faces, face 1 and face 2?
questions.hint: Each box has six faces with six DIFFERENT symbols. The two identical boxes show five of the symbols — use them to find the symbols that are missing from the row of three boxes.

steps.explain: List the symbols seen on the two identical boxes: square (front), cross (side), crossed arrows (top), black dot, thick ring, thin circle (top of the second box).
steps.work: symbols: square, +, arrows, black dot, thick ring, thin circle

steps.explain: Look at the three boxes in a row. We see squares on the front faces, the arrows, the ring and the black dot on top. The boxes are identical, so every box has these same six symbols, with only the SQUARE shared along the front.
steps.work: front: square  |  top: arrows, ring, dot

steps.explain: Face 1 (left end) belongs to the first box: its top is the arrows, its front is the square, so the end face must be a symbol next to both of those — in the first picture the arrows and the square meet the thick ring.
Face 2 (right end) belongs to the last box: its top is the black dot and its front is the square, so the end face is the symbol next to the dot and the square — the white (thin) circle.
Face 1 is the thick ring and face 2 is the white circle.

keyPoints.note: Same six symbols on every box — use the first picture as a key.

keyPoints.text: What are the shapes on the end faces
keyPoints.note: Find the symbol that touches the two visible faces at each end.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests
meta.note: Figure vectorised from the book page. Answer follows the book solution (face 1: thick circle, face 2: white circle).

questions.stem:
Pilates is a popular form of exercise but it is not for everyone. Before you enrol yourself into a Pilates class, you should examine what you want from your fitness routine. If you are looking for an intense aerobic workout, a Pilates class will not fulfill your needs.

David: “Since Pilates is an intense workout, it will definitely provide both mental and health benefits.”

Peter: “Pilates must be less popular than aerobics.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Read what the box says AND what it does not say: it never calls Pilates 'intense', never lists its benefits, and never compares its popularity with aerobics.

steps.explain: What the box says: Pilates is popular but not for everyone, and if you want an <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">intense aerobic workout</mark> Pilates will NOT fulfil your needs.

David: 'Pilates is an intense workout and will definitely provide mental and health benefits.' The box says Pilates will not give an INTENSE aerobic workout — David's starting point contradicts the box, and the box never mentions mental or health benefits ✗.
Peter: 'Pilates must be less popular than aerobics.' The box says Pilates is a popular form of exercise but never compares it with aerobics ✗.
Neither speaker's reasoning follows from the box.

keyPoints.text: a Pilates class will not fulfill your needs
keyPoints.note: The box says Pilates is NOT an intense aerobic workout.

keyPoints.text: Pilates is a popular form of exercise but it is not for everyone
keyPoints.note: Nothing here compares Pilates with aerobics.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Some children were taking free throws at the school basketball court during lunch break. Below are some facts about how many baskets the children shot.

• George shot 8 baskets less than Alex.
• Alex and George together shot 40 baskets.
• Daniel and Richard together shot 37 baskets.
• Richard shot 1 less basket than Daniel.
• Jack shot 8 baskets more than Daniel.

Which of the following statements is true?
options: Richard and Jack together shot 45 baskets.
George shot 18 baskets and Richard shot 21 baskets.
Daniel shot 3 more baskets than Richard.
Alex and Jack together shot 50 baskets.
questions.hint: Solve two pairs. Alex + George = 40 with a gap of 8: find both. Daniel + Richard = 37 with a gap of 1: find both. Then Jack. Then test the options.

steps.explain: Alex and George together shot 40, and George shot 8 less than Alex. If George shot x, Alex shot x + 8.
So George shot 16 and Alex shot 16 + 8 = 24.
Daniel and Richard together shot 37, and Richard shot 1 less than Daniel. If Richard shot y, Daniel shot y + 1.
So Richard shot 18 and Daniel shot 19. Jack shot 8 more than Daniel.
Test the options. A: Richard + Jack = 18 + 27 = 45 ✓.  B: George shot 16, not 18 ✗.  C: Daniel shot 1 more than Richard, not 3 ✗.  D: Alex + Jack = 24 + 27 = 51, not 50 ✗.

keyPoints.text: George shot 8 baskets less than Alex.
keyPoints.note: George = Alex − 8.

keyPoints.text: Alex and George together shot 40 baskets.
keyPoints.note: Alex + George = 40.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Four pieces of puzzle are put together to make one shape. The diagrams are not to scale.

Which figure can be made from these shapes without resizing, nor overlapping?
questions.hint: Describe the four pieces (a right triangle, a flat hexagon, a long thin rectangle and a small square turned 45°) and look for the figure that can be built from ALL FOUR, with each piece at its own size.

steps.explain: Describe the pieces: a right-angled triangle, a flat hexagon, a long thin tilted rectangle and a small square standing on a corner (a diamond).

In figure A the pieces fit together exactly: the triangle forms the left tip, the hexagon sits on the right of it, and the long rectangle and the small square form the bottom — each at its own size, with no gaps or overlaps.
steps.work: A = triangle + hexagon + long rectangle + square

steps.explain: In B, C and D at least one of the pieces would have to be made bigger or smaller (or squeezed) to fill the figure, or the pieces would overlap, so they can't be built from these pieces at their given sizes.
Only figure A can be made.

keyPoints.note: Each piece keeps its own size and nothing can lie on top of another piece.
All four pieces must be used.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Mark is working with a real estate agent to find a location for the toy store he plans to open in his town. He is looking for a place that is either in, or not too far from the centre of town, and one that would attract the right kind of foot traffic.

Which of the following locations should Mark's real estate agent call to his attention?
options: A storefront in a new high-rise building near the train station in the centre of town whose occupants are mainly young, childless professionals who use the train to commute to their offices each day.
A little shop three blocks away from the town's main street, located across the street from a primary school and next door to an ice cream store.
A stand-alone storefront on a quiet residential street ten blocks away from the town's centre.
A storefront in a small shopping centre located on the outskirts of town that is also occupied by a pharmacy and a dry cleaner.
questions.hint: Check each place against BOTH of Mark's two needs: (1) in or not too far from the centre, and (2) the right kind of foot traffic for a TOY store (children and families).

steps.explain: Mark's two needs: <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">in, or not too far from the centre of town</mark> AND <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">the right kind of foot traffic</mark> — people who buy toys, such as children and parents.
steps.work: need 1: near the centre;  need 2: families / children

steps.explain: A is in the centre, but its occupants are young, CHILDLESS professionals who just pass through to the train — not toy buyers ✗.

C is ten blocks away from the centre — too far, and on a quiet street with little foot traffic ✗. D is on the outskirts of town, and its neighbours (a pharmacy and a dry cleaner) bring adult customers, not families ✗.
B is only three blocks from the main street (not too far), across from a primary school and next to an ice cream store — both attract many children and parents, exactly the toy-store customers.

keyPoints.text: not too far from the centre of town
keyPoints.note: Need 1: close to the centre.

keyPoints.text: attract the right kind of foot traffic
keyPoints.note: Need 2: for a toy store, children and families.

questions.stem:
Mr Smith's school collected books to donate to schools in Africa. They collected 40 boxes of books in total. Mr Smith has to transport all the boxes to the office 60 kilometres away where all the donations are collected. He has three vehicles he can use but he wants to spend as little money on petrol as possible.

The following is the cost of petrol for each type of vehicle.

• He can fit 8 boxes in his own car and each return journey will cost $14.
• He can fit 15 boxes in the school mini-bus and each return journey will cost $23.
• He can fit 18 boxes in his friend's van and each return journey will cost $28.

What is the lowest cost of transporting the 40 boxes, using any combination of these vehicles?
questions.hint: Compare the COST PER BOX of each vehicle (the car is the dearest per box), then try combinations that carry at least 40 boxes and add up the costs.

steps.explain: Find the cost per box of each vehicle when it is full.
A single type of vehicle: five cars carry 40 boxes ($70); three mini-buses carry 45 ($69); three vans carry 54 ($84).
Try to MIX the vehicles so that the total is at least 40 boxes without paying for too many trips. One of each: 8 + 15 + 17 (the van need not be full) carries all 40 boxes.
Add up the cost of one trip of each vehicle.
Check other mixes: 1 car + 2 vans = $70, 3 cars + 1 van = $70, 3 mini-buses = $69 — none is cheaper than $65. Options A and B ($56, $60) cannot carry 40 boxes.

questions.stem:
For companies looking to save money, the idea of being able to replace a human with a computer and robot is enticing. A robot can work 24/7 with little to no pay or benefits and is often faster than a human with fewer errors. Over the last few years, robots and computers have made tremendous leaps in their performances and capabilities and replaced more human jobs.
Up to 20 million manufacturing jobs around the world could be replaced by robots by 2030, according to the analysis firm Oxford Economics.

Tina: “Robots will replace human employment in the future especially in jobs that require manual labour and physical exertion. So all of us going to lose our jobs one day.”

Which one of these statements, if true, most weakens Tina's argument?
options: Robots have emotional capacity, so we no longer need humans to work.
In the future, robots may be able to learn human emotions.
Jobs that require more compassion, creativity and intelligence are likely to still be carried out by humans.
The productivity from automation will boost growth.
questions.hint: Tina's conclusion: ALL of us will lose our jobs. To weaken it, find a statement saying some jobs will stay with humans.

steps.explain: Find the conclusion: Tina says robots will replace human employment, so <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">all of us</mark> will lose our jobs one day.
A weakening statement says that some jobs WON'T be replaced.
A and B both say robots may become able to do human work (emotions) — they SUPPORT Tina ✗. D says automation boosts growth, which doesn't say jobs are safe ✗.
C: jobs that need compassion, creativity and intelligence are likely to still be carried out by humans — so not all jobs will be lost, which directly weakens 'all of us will lose our jobs'.

keyPoints.text: So all of us going to lose our jobs one day.
keyPoints.note: The strong conclusion ('all of us') is easy to weaken.
Pick a statement saying some jobs will remain.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
In a classroom survey, everyone who liked calculating liked mathematics.
Everyone who liked mathematics liked problem solving, but no one who liked mathematics liked history.

Simon: “If Susan doesn't like calculating, she likes history.”

Mike: “Amanda doesn't like history so she must dislike problem solving.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Write the rules as arrows: calculating → maths → problem solving, and maths → NOT history. Arrows only work forwards. Test each speaker.

steps.explain: Turn the sentences into arrows.
steps.work:
calculating → maths
maths → problem solving
maths → NOT history

steps.explain: Simon: 'if Susan does NOT like calculating, she likes history.' The arrows start from 'likes calculating'. They say nothing about someone who does NOT like calculating, so Susan could like history or not ✗.

Mike: 'Amanda doesn't like history, so she must dislike problem solving.' Not liking history doesn't tell us about problem solving — the arrow goes the other way (maths → not history). She could still like problem solving ✗.
Neither speaker's reasoning follows from the box.

keyPoints.text: everyone who liked calculating liked mathematics
keyPoints.note: Arrow: calculating → maths.

keyPoints.text: no one who liked mathematics liked history
keyPoints.note: Arrow: maths → NOT history.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
The Crowntown Community Centre has announced an expansion that will double its capacity along with an increase in the hire fee. Crowntown is a small town near the coast and the population of the town is not expected to increase dramatically in the next several years.

Melanie: “The expansion would allow the Crowntown Community Centre to stage larger and more popular performances for the residents.”

Which one the following sentences strengthens Melanie's statement?
options: A larger community centre will attract more people to move into the community.
Many young people like to live near the coast.
There will also be an increase in the budget for new performances.
The stagnation of the population increase will not help to profit the community.
questions.hint: Melanie's statement is about PERFORMANCES: a bigger centre can stage larger, more popular shows. Which option helps the centre actually afford and put on bigger shows?

steps.explain: Find the claim: the expansion allows <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">larger and more popular performances</mark> for the residents.
To strengthen it, show that the centre will be able to pay for and run larger shows.
A and B talk about people moving to the town — but the population is NOT expected to grow, and neither says anything about performances ✗. D is about profit from population, not performances ✗.
C: there will also be an increase in the budget for new performances, so the larger centre will have money to put on bigger and more popular shows.

keyPoints.text: stage larger and more popular performances for the residents
keyPoints.note: The claim is about performances.
Choose what makes bigger shows more likely.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
The plan below shows an office block with six offices, A, B, C, D, E and F.

• Both B and C occupy offices to the right of the corridor (as one enters the office block) and A occupies one office to the left of the corridor.
• E and F occupy offices on opposite sides of the corridor but their offices do not face each other.
• The offices of C and D face each other.
• Office E is not in the corner.
• Office F is further down the corridor than office A, but they are on the same side.

Which office is opposite office A?
questions.hint: Draw the corridor with three offices on each side. Standing at the entrance and looking along the corridor, the RIGHT-hand side is the lower row. Put the sure things in first: B and C on the right, A on the left.

steps.explain: Set up the plan: three offices on the left of the corridor (top row) and three on the right (bottom row). B and C are on the right (bottom row) and A is on the left (top row).
steps.work:
top row (left side): A, ?, ?
bottom row (right side): B, C, ?

steps.explain: C and D face each other, so D is on the left side (top row), opposite C. That leaves E and F: F is on the same side as A (the left), so F is also on the left, and E must go on the right.
steps.work:
left (top): A, D, F
right (bottom): B, C, E

steps.explain: E is not in a corner, so E is the MIDDLE office on the bottom row. B and C therefore take the two bottom corners. Since C is in a corner, D (opposite C) is also in a corner of the top row.
steps.work:
bottom row: corner, E, corner
D at a corner of the top row

steps.explain: E and F do not face each other, so F is not the middle office of the top row — F is in a corner. That means A is the middle office of the top row, with D and F in the two corners. F is further down the corridor than A, so F is the far corner and D is the corner by the entrance. C is opposite D.
steps.work:
top row: D, A, F
bottom row: C, E, B

keyPoints.text: Office E is not in the corner.
keyPoints.note: E takes the middle bottom office.

keyPoints.text: The offices of C and D face each other.
keyPoints.note: C (right side) is opposite D (left side).

questions.stem:
If we eat breakfast, then we will more likely have the energy to run.
If we have more energy, there is a greater likelihood that we will run very fast.
If we do not run fast, we may not be chosen for the relay team for our school.
To make it to the national athletics carnival, we must make it to the relay team.

Which one of the following outcomes in not possible?
options: We eat breakfast and do not make it to the national athletics carnival.
We don't eat breakfast but make it to the national athletics carnival.
We don't run fast and do not make it to the relay team.
We run fast and definitely make it into the national athletics carnival.
questions.hint: Look at the key words: 'more likely', 'greater likelihood', 'may not'. These describe chances, not certainties. The impossible outcome is the one that claims a certainty the rules don't give.

steps.explain: List the chain with the exact wording.
steps.work:
breakfast → MORE LIKELY energy
energy → GREATER LIKELIHOOD of running fast
not fast → MAY NOT be chosen for relay
carnival → must be in the relay team

steps.explain: A: we eat breakfast but don't make the carnival. Breakfast only makes energy more LIKELY, so this can happen ✓ possible.

B: we don't eat breakfast but make the carnival. Breakfast isn't required for a fast run or the relay team ✓ possible.  C: we don't run fast and don't make the relay team — the rule says we 'may not' be chosen, so this can happen ✓ possible.

D: 'we run fast and DEFINITELY make it into the carnival.' Running fast only improves the chance of being picked for the relay team; the rules never guarantee it. The word 'definitely' makes D impossible to promise.

keyPoints.text: we will more likely have the energy to run
keyPoints.note: 'More likely' = a chance, not a guarantee.

keyPoints.text: we may not be chosen for the relay team
keyPoints.note: 'May not' leaves room for exceptions.

questions.stem:
It has been shown that earthworms do not feed when the temperature is below 2°C. It has also been found that earthworms feed mostly at night by pulling leaves into their burrows. To find out what encourages earthworms to feed, a piece of lawn was caged off and leaves were put inside the cage. The temperature of the soil was taken each night. Each morning the cage was examined to see how many leaves had been pulled down into the burrows.

The results from a week's worth of observations are shown in the following table:

Gavin: “Earthworms do not feed in wet weather.”
Frank: “Earthworms feed most when the weather is cloudy and windy.”

If the information given is true, whose reasoning is correct?

questions.stem:
A piece of square paper is folded diagonally, and then folded in half diagonally again. The second fold is at right-angles to the first.

A small triangle is cut off from the corner of the folded paper. The paper is then completely unfolded.

Which one of the following is not a possible appearance of the unfolded paper? (The dotted lines represent the folds).
questions.hint: After two diagonal folds the paper is a small triangle with ONE right angle (at the centre of the paper) and two other corners. Count how many cuts each option would need.

steps.explain: Fold the paper twice. After the first diagonal fold it is a triangle; folding it in half again (at right angles) gives a smaller triangle. Its right-angled corner is the CENTRE of the paper; its other two corners come from the corners of the original paper.

ONE small triangle is cut off ONE corner of this folded triangle. Cutting the corner at the right angle (the centre of the paper) gives a small square hole in the middle after unfolding. That is picture A.
steps.work: cut at the right-angle corner → square hole in the middle (A) ✓

steps.explain: Cutting off one of the other two corners removes the paper's corners in pairs — two opposite corners (pictures B and D) ✓.
steps.work: cut at a sharp corner → two opposite corners removed (B, D) ✓

steps.explain: C shows ALL FOUR corners cut off. One cut at one corner of the folded paper only removes two opposite corners — four corners would need two cuts ✗.

keyPoints.note: The folded paper is a right-angled triangle.

keyPoints.text: A small triangle is cut off from the corner of the folded paper
keyPoints.note: ONE cut only — see what a single cut can make.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Lauren: “Water is road for the sailor, weapon for the firefighters and power to the engineer to create electricity.”

Which one of these statements, if true, most strengthens Lauren's argument?
options: Some people in third countries don't have enough clean water to drink.
The government is trying to provide clean water for everyone.
Farmers can collect large amounts of recycled water when it rains a lot.
Water is life itself to people dying of thirst.
questions.hint: Lauren says water is useful to MANY different people and jobs — it is an essential part of life. Which option adds one more example of how essential water is?

steps.explain: Find Lauren's claim: water is <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">a road for the sailor, a weapon for the firefighters, power for the engineer</mark> — water is essential to many people in many different ways.
A strengthening statement adds another example that water is essential.
A is about a shortage of clean water, B is about what the government is trying to do, and C is about farmers collecting recycled water — none of them says how essential water is ✗.
D: water is life itself to people dying of thirst — another example, the strongest one, showing that water is essential.

keyPoints.text: Water is road for the sailor
keyPoints.note: One example of how essential water is.
Add another example of water being essential.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
James and Sandra are making their own alphabetical system for their English project. They decide that every alternate letter starting from B in the English alphabet is written in lower case, and the rest are written in upper case.

For example, 'calendar' is written as 'cAlEndAr'.

How is the month 'September' written in the new alphabetical system?
questions.hint: Lower-case letters are B, D, F, H, … (every second letter starting from B: the EVEN-numbered letters). All the others (A, C, E, G, …) are upper case. Write down the position of each letter of SEPTEMBER.

steps.explain: Number the alphabet: A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, … Letters starting from B and then every second letter (2, 4, 6, …) are lower case. Odd-numbered letters are upper case.
steps.work: even position → lower case;  odd position → UPPER CASE
