questions.stem:
A survey wanted to determine how different sports affected an athlete's flexibility.
This is what was found:

• All swimmers were more flexible than all gymnasts.
• Some gymnasts were more flexible than some ballerinas.
• The most flexible person was a ballerina.

If the statements above are true, which one of these sentences is also true?
options: Many ballerinas were more flexible than gymnasts.
Some gymnasts were more flexible than some swimmers.
The least flexible person was a gymnast.
Some swimmers were more flexible than some ballerinas.
questions.hint: Build a chain: swimmers > gymnasts > (some) ballerinas. If A is above B and B is above C, then A must be above C.

steps.explain: First fact: EVERY swimmer is more flexible than EVERY gymnast.
Second fact: there are some gymnasts who are more flexible than some ballerinas. Call them gymnast G and ballerina B.
Join the two facts. Every swimmer is above gymnast G, and G is above ballerina B, so every swimmer is above that ballerina B.

So at least some swimmers are more flexible than some ballerinas: D is true. A is not certain (we only know SOME ballerinas are below some gymnasts). B contradicts the first fact. C is not given (the least flexible person might be a ballerina).
steps.work: A ✗  B ✗  C ✗  D ✓   →   Answer: D

keyPoints.text: All swimmers were more flexible than all gymnasts.
keyPoints.note: Every swimmer is above every gymnast.

keyPoints.text: Some gymnasts were more flexible than some ballerinas.
keyPoints.note: Connects gymnasts to ballerinas — build the chain.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Tim: “Australian highways, freeways and motorways should have speed limits increased to 130 kilometres per hour. This increase is in the interest of driver safety. An increase in safety is expected to correlate with an increase in speed due to fatigue reduction, greater concentration on driving and improvements in driver aid technology and car safety technology.”

Which one of these statements, if true, most strengthens Tim's argument?
options: Long distance travel takes a considerable amount of time and leads to fatigue and fatal crashes.
In Germany, about 60% of freeways have no speed limit with very low fatality rates.
Australia has one of the lowest speed limits in the world.
Permitting higher speeds on many roads will increase fatigue and the probability of crashes.
questions.hint: Tim's claim: higher speed limits will make roads SAFER. Look for real-world evidence of high speed limits and good safety together.

steps.explain: Find the claim: speed limits should go up to 130 km/h <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">in the interest of driver safety</mark>.
A strengthening statement should show that fast roads can still be safe.

A says long trips cause fatigue — it doesn't connect speed limits with safety ✗. C says Australia's limits are low — it doesn't show that higher limits are safe ✗. D says higher speeds increase crashes — that goes AGAINST Tim ✗.
B: in Germany about 60% of freeways have no speed limit and very low fatality rates — real evidence that higher speeds can go with high safety.

keyPoints.text: This increase is in the interest of driver safety.
keyPoints.note: The claim: higher limits are safer.
Look for real-world evidence supporting it.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Once students master the fundamentals of mathematics and difficult concepts are introduced, calculators need to be utilised. Calculators can help quickly add, divide, multiply and subtract.

Which one of these statements, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: Calculators are an extremely fast and accurate technological tool for students.
Calculators can make mathematics more enjoyable for students which can lead to a much more positive classroom environment.
It costs less for schools to buy graphing calculators in bulk.
Some calculators do not have the ability to calculate in the correct mathematical operational order.
questions.hint: The argument says calculators SHOULD be used because they quickly and correctly calculate. Which option shows a PROBLEM with using calculators?

steps.explain: Find the conclusion: <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">calculators need to be utilised</mark> because they can quickly add, divide, multiply and subtract.
To weaken it, show a drawback or limit of calculators.
A (fast and accurate), B (more enjoyable) and C (cheaper to buy) all give MORE reasons to use calculators ✗.
D: some calculators cannot work in the correct mathematical order of operations — they may give wrong answers to longer calculations, which is a real reason not to rely on them.

keyPoints.note: The conclusion to weaken.
Choose a drawback of calculators.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Ruby and Ruth have a special way of communicating. They use their own symbols instead of words.

For example,

Ruby is written as  >  +  −  <  and
Ruth is written as  >  +  Δ  ÷

Ruby asked Ruth what type of food she likes the most, and she answered with
∗  ∇  #  ?  $  &.

What is Ruth's favourite food?
questions.hint: Decode what you can: the examples RUBY and RUTH give symbols for R, U, B, Y, T and H. The answer has six DIFFERENT new symbols — so the food has six different letters and none of R, U, B, Y, T, H.

steps.explain: From RUBY and RUTH, find the symbol of each letter: R = >, U = +, B = −, Y = <, T = Δ, H = ÷.
steps.work: R > ,  U + ,  B − ,  Y < ,  T Δ ,  H ÷

questions.stem:
Contact lenses have many advantages over eyeglasses. You can participate in sports and outdoor activities without the fear of something getting in the way. But Peter believes that eyeglasses offer many benefits over contact lenses. He says that they require very little cleaning and maintenance, and you don't need to touch your eyes to wear them which could increase the risk of eye infections. If you have dry or sensitive eyes, glasses won't exacerbate the problem like contact lenses do.

Which one of these statements, if true, most strengthens Peter's argument?
options: Glasses are not fashionable as they cover your facial features.
Eye infections can be caused by various factors, not limited to contact lenses.
Eyeglasses are cheaper than contact lenses as you don't replace them as often.
Contact lenses don't get in the way when you play sports and exercising.
questions.hint: Peter's argument: eyeglasses are BETTER than contact lenses. Choose the statement that gives one more point in favour of glasses.

steps.explain: Find the claim: <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">eyeglasses offer many benefits over contact lenses</mark> (little cleaning, no touching the eyes, fine for dry eyes).
To strengthen it, add one more advantage of eyeglasses.

A says glasses are not fashionable — a disadvantage ✗. B says infections have many causes — that weakens the 'touching your eyes' point ✗. D says contact lenses don't get in the way of sports — an advantage of lenses ✗.
C: eyeglasses are cheaper because you don't replace them as often — another benefit of glasses.

keyPoints.text: Peter believes that eyeglasses offer many benefits over contact lenses.
keyPoints.note: The claim to support.
Add another advantage of glasses.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Four friends live on the same side of a street in four houses each of different colours. Each person has a different favourite drink. The following additional information is also known:

• Ethan lives in the red house.
• Issac drinks tea.
• Nathan lives in the first house on the left.
• The person in the second house from the right drinks milk.
• Nathan lives adjacent to the blue house.
• Steven drinks juice.
• Tea is drunk in the blue house.
• The white house is to the right of the red house.

Which of the following is not true?
options: Milk is drunk in the red house
Issac lives in the blue house
Steven lives in the white house
Nathan lives in the yellow house
questions.hint: Draw four houses in a row and fill in the clues one at a time. Then check each option: is it forced by the clues, or does the puzzle never say it?

steps.explain: Draw four houses from left to right. Nathan lives in the first house on the left.

steps.explain: Nathan lives next to the blue house, so the blue house is house 2. Tea is drunk in the blue house, and Issac drinks tea, so Issac lives in house 2 (blue).

The person in the second house from the right (house 3) drinks milk. The remaining people are Ethan and Steven: Ethan lives in the red house and Steven drinks juice (not milk), so Ethan is in house 3 (red, milk) and Steven in house 4. The white house is to the right of the red house, so house 4 is white.
steps.work:
house 3: Ethan, red, milk
house 4: Steven, white, juice

questions.stem:
Obesity is a serious health issue. It can also lead to various other diseases like diabetes, asthma and high blood pressure. Recent research has even found that obesity may cause some types of cancer. So, major health campaigns should be launched to increase the awareness about this disease and encourage lifestyle changes to help people fight obesity.

Which one of these statements, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: Obesity is associated with a higher death rate when looking at all causes of death.
Research has found that health campaigns are received better by the public than any other medium.
Obesity is the leading cause of diabetes and other diseases.
People should change their lifestyle to cure obesity, like reduce fast food consumption and overeating.
questions.hint: The conclusion is about HEALTH CAMPAIGNS: they should be launched. Which option says campaigns WORK or are well received?

steps.explain: Find the conclusion: <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">major health campaigns should be launched</mark> to raise awareness and encourage lifestyle changes.
The reasons given are all about how bad obesity is. To strengthen the conclusion further, show that health campaigns are an effective way of reaching people.
A and C add more bad facts about obesity — they are about the problem, not about campaigns ✗. D tells people what to do but says nothing about campaigns ✗.
B: health campaigns are received better by the public than any other medium — so a campaign is a good way to spread the message.

keyPoints.text: major health campaigns should be launched
keyPoints.note: The conclusion about campaigns.
Support the campaign idea itself.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Your smile can act on your body and mind in a variety of positive ways, offering benefits for your health, your mood, and even the moods of people around you. Smiling increases mood-enhancing hormones while decreasing stress enhancing hormones. It also reduces overall blood pressure. The muscles trigger your brain to produce more endorphins – the chemical that relieves pain and stress.

Which of the following statements most supports the information given in the box above?
options: There are 15 different types of smiles, all conveying different messages. So not all smiles are expressions of happiness.
Smiling can help you live longer because you become more optimistic in life.
Smiling may not come naturally, but this can change due to many factors such as lifestyle and personal development.
Research has found that smarter people smile more often because it is related to a person's critical thinking skills.
questions.hint: The passage lists POSITIVE effects of smiling on health and mood. Which option adds another positive effect on health or outlook?

steps.explain: Find the main idea: smiling brings <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">positive</mark> effects on your body and mind (health, mood, lower stress, lower blood pressure).
steps.work: idea: smiling → good for body and mind

steps.explain: A supporting statement should give one more good effect of smiling.

A is about the meaning of different smiles ✗. C says smiling may not come naturally ✗ (not about benefits). D says smart people smile more — it is about who smiles, not about the effects of smiling ✗.
B: smiling makes you more optimistic, which can help you live longer — a further positive effect on health.

keyPoints.text: Your smile can act on your body and mind in a variety of positive ways
keyPoints.note: Main idea: positive effects of smiling.

keyPoints.text: most supports the information given in the box
keyPoints.note: Pick another benefit of smiling.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Ms Wilson is giving out the end of year award. She gave one test for English and one test for mathematics. The scores from these two tests were added together to give the total score for the year. Kathy and Jane got the same total score this year.

Kathy: “If I got 5 points less than you in the English exam, then you must have gotten 5 more points than me in the mathematics exam.”

Jane: “And if you got a higher score than me in the English exam, then I must have gotten a lower score than you in the mathematics exam.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Same total score means: whatever one person is AHEAD in English, she must be BEHIND by the same amount in maths. Use that rule to test each sentence.

steps.explain: Write the rule: English + maths is the same for both, so the differences cancel.
Kathy: 'If I got 5 LESS than you in English, then you must have got 5 MORE than me in maths.' Kathy is 5 behind in English, so she must be 5 AHEAD in maths — Jane got 5 LESS in maths, not 5 more ✗.
steps.work: Kathy: −5 in English → +5 in maths for KATHY (Jane has 5 less)  ✗

steps.explain: Jane: 'If you got a HIGHER score than me in English, then I must have got a LOWER score than you in maths.' Kathy is ahead in English, so she must be BEHIND in maths — Jane got a HIGHER maths score, not lower ✗.
steps.work: Kathy ahead in English → Jane ahead in maths  ✗

steps.explain: Both sentences have the maths result the wrong way round. Neither reasoning is correct.

keyPoints.text: Kathy and Jane got the same total score this year.
keyPoints.note: Differences in the two tests cancel each other.
Check which way round the maths difference goes.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
The diagram below is the net of a shape.

Which one of the shapes below can be the solid that is folded from the net shown?
questions.hint: Look for a special face in the net — here a TRIANGULAR face (the end piece on the left). The solid must have a triangle among its faces.

steps.explain: Study the net: a long strip of rectangles in the middle, an L-shaped piece above and a rectangle below, and a small piece at the left end that is made of a triangle and a four-sided face.
When the net is folded, that triangle becomes one of the faces of the solid. So the solid must have a triangular face.
Look at the four solids: A is a block with a sloping top (its faces are pentagons and rectangles), C is an L-shaped block, D is a block with one sloping rectangle.
steps.work: A, C, D have no triangular face ✗

steps.explain: B is the step-shaped solid with a sloping triangular side — the only one that has a triangular face, so only B can be folded from the net.

keyPoints.text: The diagram below is the net of a shape.
keyPoints.note: A net shows every face of the solid laid flat.

keyPoints.text: Which one of the shapes below can be the solid
keyPoints.note: Match the faces of the net with the faces of the solid.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests
meta.note: Figure vectorised from the book page (orange hatch kept). Book solution: none of the other shapes has a triangular face.

questions.stem:
Joey goes to the card shop to buy Yu-Gi-Oh cards. He can buy each card pack for $15. When he gets there, he is told there are 3 other deals he can choose from to save money.

Deal 1: Bundle of 3 packs for $40.

Deal 2: The store owner offers he will add on another pack on top of his bundle of three packs for an extra $14.

Deal 3: The store owner offers he will add 2 packs on top of his bundle of three packs for a total of $65.

Joey carefully calculated and decided to go for the best deal.

How much does he save per pack if he chooses to go for the best value deal compared to the original price?
questions.hint: Compare the PRICE PER PACK of every deal: price ÷ number of packs. Careful: Deal 2 and Deal 3 are built ON TOP of the bundle of 3.

steps.explain: Write how many packs each deal gives. Deal 2 adds ONE pack to the bundle of 3; Deal 3 adds TWO packs to the bundle of 3.
steps.work: Deal 1: 3 packs;  Deal 2: 3 + 1 = 4 packs;  Deal 3: 3 + 2 = 5 packs

steps.explain: Find the total price of each deal. Deal 2 is $40 plus $14 extra.
Divide by the number of packs to get the price of ONE pack.

questions.stem:
Recent research has established a relationship between obesity and lack of sleep. Lack of sleep causes the body to release hormones and people start craving sugary and fatty foods in order to alleviate their tiredness. In addition, they lack the energy to exercise.

Melanie: “That tells us that all you need to do to lose weight is to get plenty of sleep. So we don't need the diet sheet.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Melanie has made?
options: She assumes lack of sleep and obesity are not effects of another factor.
She assumes losing weight is always a good thing.
Lack of sleep is a necessary condition for gaining weight.
There may be other reasons why people might gain weight.
questions.hint: The research says lack of sleep CONTRIBUTES to obesity. Melanie says sleep is ALL you need. What does she leave out?

steps.explain: What the research says: lack of sleep <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">causes the body to release hormones</mark>, leads to cravings and less energy to exercise — so lack of sleep is ONE cause of weight gain.
steps.work: lack of sleep → one cause of gaining weight

steps.explain: Melanie's jump: 'ALL you need to do to lose weight is to get plenty of sleep.' She treats sleep as the only thing that matters.
The mistake: there may be OTHER reasons why people gain weight (food choices, exercise, health...), so plenty of sleep alone may not be enough, and the diet sheet could still be needed.

A guesses about 'another factor' — nothing in the passage suggests that ✗. B is not what she assumed ✗. C is the wrong way round (it says lack of sleep is NEEDED to gain weight) ✗. D states the real gap in her reasoning.

keyPoints.text: Lack of sleep causes the body to release hormones
keyPoints.note: A cause — but not necessarily the only one.

keyPoints.text: Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Melanie has made?
keyPoints.note: Her mistake: 'all you need' ignores other reasons.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
27 sweets are shared among Paul, Mark and James so that for every 4 that Paul gets, Mark gets 2 sweets and James gets 3 sweets.

Mark: “That means Paul gets 2 more than me.”

James: “No that's not right, Paul gets the double amount of your share.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Share 27 in the ratio 4 : 2 : 3. First find how many parts there are, then the value of one part.

steps.explain: Add up the parts of the ratio Paul : Mark : James = 4 : 2 : 3.
Find the value of one part.
Each person's share.
Mark says Paul gets 2 more than him. Paul has 12 and Mark has 6 — 6 more, not 2 more ✗ (he mixed up the ratio numbers 4 and 2 with the actual sweets).
James says Paul gets double Mark's share: 12 = 2 × 6 ✓.

keyPoints.text: for every 4 that Paul gets, Mark gets 2 sweets and James gets 3 sweets
keyPoints.note: Ratio 4 : 2 : 3 (9 parts).
Compare the real numbers of sweets, not the ratio numbers.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Two friends encode the text messages they send to each other on their mobile phone so that no one else can read them. The encoding system used for each letter in the message is as follows:

Operation 1: Replace each letter by its equivalent with the alphabet reversed: so A becomes Z, B becomes Y, C becomes X, etc.

Operation 2: Replace each letter resulting from operation 1 by a two digit number according to its place in the alphabet: so A becomes 01, B becomes 02, etc.

What is the coded form of the word MOVIE?
questions.hint: Do Operation 1 first on every letter (the reversed alphabet pairs A–Z, B–Y, C–X, … M–N), then write the place number of each new letter with two digits.

steps.explain: Operation 1 reverses the alphabet: A↔Z, B↔Y, C↔X, D↔W, E↔V, F↔U, G↔T, H↔S, I↔R, J↔Q, K↔P, L↔O, M↔N. Apply it to M, O, V, I, E.
steps.work: M → N,  O → L,  V → E,  I → R,  E → V   (MOVIE → NLERV)

questions.stem:
The seven basic symbols in a Roman numeral system and their respective values are as follows:

I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500 and M = 1000

In general, the symbols in the numeral system are read from left to right, starting with the symbol representing the largest value.

• The same symbol cannot occur continuously more than three times.
• The value of the numeral is the sum of the values of the symbols.
  For example, XXVII = 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 27.
• An exception to the left to right reading occurs when a symbol is followed immediately by a symbol of greater value; then, the smaller value is subtracted from the larger.
  For example, XLVI = (50 - 10) + 5 + 1 = 46.

The numeral 1995 is written as a Roman numeral following the rules given above. Which one of the following correctly represents the value of 1995?

1. MCMLXXV
2. MCMXCV
3. MVD
4. MVM

questions.stem:
Lee is senior to John and earns more than Harry. Lachlan is junior to Mac and senior to Harry and earns less than Keith. Jack is senior to Nick and junior to Harry and earns less than Nick but more than Keith. Nick is senior to Lee and earns less than Harry.

Based on the information above, which of the following must be true?
options: Nick is senior to Mac and earns more than Jack.
John is senior to Lee and earns more than Jack.
Lachlan is senior to Nick and earns less than Nick.
Harry is senior to Nick and earns less than Nick.
questions.hint: There are TWO separate orders: seniority and earnings. Build each one from the sentences, then test every option against both lists.

steps.explain: Seniority (senior = higher). Collect the clues: Mac > Lachlan; Lachlan > Harry; Harry > Jack; Jack > Nick; Nick > Lee; Lee > John.
steps.work: Mac > Lachlan > Harry > Jack > Nick > Lee > John

steps.explain: Earnings (more money = higher). Clues: Lee > Harry; Harry > Nick; Nick > Jack; Jack > Keith; Keith > Lachlan.
steps.work: Lee > Harry > Nick > Jack > Keith > Lachlan

questions.stem:
In an essay writing exam, students have to write a response to a question they have never seen before.

Lucy: “In the last essay writing exam, I wrote five pages. I normally top writing tests. This means that I will be able to write at least five pages again in the next essay writing exam.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Lucy has made?
options: Lucy is sitting in a different part of the classroom for this exam.
Lucy will write more than she did last time.
Lucy feels nervous and unprepared for the essay writing exam.
Lucy's response depends on the question given to her.
questions.hint: The exam question is one the students have NEVER SEEN before. Lucy treats last time's result as a promise. What can be different this time?

steps.explain: Lucy's reasoning: last exam five pages, and she usually tops writing tests, so next time she will write at least five pages again.

The mistake: in an essay exam the question is a NEW one each time. How much she can write depends on the question, not only on her past results — a question she knows less about may give her fewer pages.
A (seat) and C (nerves) are things we don't know about and the passage doesn't mention ✗. B says she will write MORE — that isn't a mistake in her reasoning ✗.
D names the real flaw: her response depends on the question given to her.

keyPoints.text: a question they have never seen before
keyPoints.note: The new question is the key difference.

keyPoints.text: shows the mistake Lucy has made
keyPoints.note: She assumes the next exam will go the same way.

However, some of the results were not recorded properly and are unavailable at the time of judgement. The judges are given what is available, as shown in the table below.

How many results are needed to find out which car is to be removed?

questions.stem:
To be able to win the draw for a European holiday, the online application must be submitted by next Monday. There are a total of 5 prizes available, and these are randomly chosen.

Megan: “I've already submitted 2 weeks ago so I have a very good chance of winning the prize.”

Kate: “I couldn't submit the application today, so I won't be able to win the prize.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Two key facts: the winners are chosen RANDOMLY, and the deadline is NEXT MONDAY. Does submitting early help? Is Kate's chance really gone?

steps.explain: What the box says: applications must be in by <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">next Monday</mark>, and the prizes are <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">randomly chosen</mark>.

Megan: 'I submitted 2 weeks ago so I have a very good chance.' Since the winners are chosen at random, applying early doesn't give extra chances — everyone who applies by Monday has the same chance. Her chance is the same as anyone's, not 'very good' ✗.
Kate: 'I couldn't submit today, so I won't be able to win.' She still has until next Monday to submit, so she can still enter and win ✗.
Neither reasoning is correct.

keyPoints.text: must be submitted by next Monday
keyPoints.note: Anyone who submits by Monday can still win.
Early submission doesn't help.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
A school committee conducted a survey of some parents to find out whether they would prefer to start the school day 30 minutes earlier.

Nathan: “If school starts earlier, then we can finish 30 minutes earlier too. Everyone will be happy to finish early.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Nathan has made?
options: The school should survey the students, not the parents.
There may be other factors different people consider.
The survey did not ask parents whether they prefer finishing 30 minutes late.
The survey was not conducted using a random sample of parents.
questions.hint: Nathan says EVERYONE will be happy. Think about whether one reason (finishing early) is the only thing that matters to every family.

steps.explain: Nathan's reasoning: starting earlier means finishing earlier, and finishing early makes EVERYONE happy.
steps.work: earlier start → earlier finish → everyone happy

steps.explain: The mistake: he thinks only one thing matters. Different people consider different factors — parents' work hours, travel times, children's sleep, after-school care — so not everybody will be happy with the change.
steps.work: 'everyone will be happy' is too strong

steps.explain: A, C and D are about HOW the survey was done, but Nathan's mistake is about what he concluded from it ✗.
B says there may be other factors different people consider — that is exactly why 'everyone' will not be happy.

keyPoints.text: Everyone will be happy to finish early.
keyPoints.note: 'Everyone' is the over-reach.

keyPoints.text: shows the mistake Nathan has made
keyPoints.note: Look for what he ignored.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Children can acquire motor skills through many different activities. Motor skills help perform diverse tasks such as riding a bicycle, preparing dinner, typing a letter, etc. All these tasks require precision and timing of muscular movement. Children should be encouraged to develop their motor skills at an early age.

If the information in the box is true, which one of the following most weakens the argument?
options: Most adults don't know how to take advantage of their motor skills.
All adults know how to type a letter and ride a bicycle due to motor skills.
Preparing dinner involves fire and hot objects so children should avoid it.
Motor skills are developed more quickly when people are younger.
questions.hint: The conclusion: children should be encouraged to develop motor skills early (the tasks include preparing dinner). Which option gives a reason NOT to encourage one of these activities?

steps.explain: Find the conclusion: children <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">should be encouraged to develop their motor skills at an early age</mark>, through tasks like riding a bicycle or preparing dinner.
To weaken it, show a risk or a reason to avoid one of these activities.
A and B are about adults, not about whether children should do these things ✗. D says skills develop faster when young — that STRENGTHENS the argument ✗.
C: preparing dinner involves fire and hot objects, so children should avoid it — a danger linked to one of the activities that is supposed to build motor skills.

keyPoints.text: Children should be encouraged to develop their motor skills at an early age.
keyPoints.note: The conclusion to weaken.
Find a reason to avoid one of the activities.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
I have used 36 identical tiles to make a pattern on the floor. There is a white square on top of one tile so that only part of the pattern is visible.

Using the same orientation as the diagram above, what is the pattern that is covered by the white square?
questions.hint: The floor is 6 × 6 tiles of the SAME design, so the covered tile looks like the tiles around it. Check how the lines meet at each EDGE of the white square and pick the tile that continues them.

steps.explain: Notice that all 36 tiles are identical, so the pattern repeats in rows and columns. The covered tile is one tile (the white square).
steps.work: same tile everywhere → the pattern repeats

steps.explain: Look at the neighbouring tiles. Each tile has curved arcs in two corners and diagonal lines in the other corners; the arcs of neighbouring tiles join to make circles and ovals.
steps.work: arcs join across the tile edges

steps.explain: The missing tile must continue every line and arc that reaches its four edges. Compare the four choices: A, B and C each have an arc or diagonal line in a corner that would not join the neighbours (a break in a circle or an extra line).
D has the arc and the diagonal lines in exactly the corners where the neighbouring tiles need them — it fits the book's solution.

keyPoints.note: The design repeats — copy the surrounding pattern.

keyPoints.text: Using the same orientation as the diagram above
keyPoints.note: Don't rotate the tile choices.

questions.stem:
Mrs Walter wanted to investigate whether playing piano affected her students' running time. She decided to do an experiment.

She split the students into two groups according to the type of instruments they play. One group played piano, and the other group played violin.
For one whole month, students practiced their instrument every afternoon.
After one month, she asked the two groups to do a running test and measured the time of each person.

She found that on average, the students who are good at piano were 5 seconds faster than the students who are good at violin.
The fastest score was gained by one of the students who is good at piano.

Mrs Walter: “So it's true, playing piano improves the ability to run more than other instruments!”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Mrs Walter has made?
options: The students who play piano ran faster than the students who play violin.
The students may have already been fast runners before they started to practice everyday.
On average, the students who play piano ran faster.
To be a fast runner, it is better for a student to be able to play piano than other instruments.
questions.hint: To prove that piano CAUSES faster running, the two groups must have been equally fast BEFORE the experiment. Did Mrs Walter check that?

steps.explain: What Mrs Walter found: after a month of practice, the piano group was on average 5 seconds faster than the violin group.
steps.work: piano group faster after the month

steps.explain: Her conclusion: playing piano IMPROVES running ability. For that she needs to know that the piano group was NOT already faster before the experiment — she measured only AFTER the month.

The mistake: the students <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">may have already been fast runners</mark> before they started to practise, so the difference may have nothing to do with piano.
steps.work: faster group ≠ piano made them faster

steps.explain: A and C only repeat what she found ✗. D repeats her wrong conclusion ✗. B names the real gap in her experiment.

keyPoints.text: After one month, she asked the two groups to do a running test
keyPoints.note: Only measured after the month — no starting point.

keyPoints.text: shows the mistake Mrs Walter has made
keyPoints.note: Her conclusion goes beyond her evidence.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Victor's school surveyed year 5 children about their favourite TV programs.
In a survey of television viewers, everyone who liked sports liked entertainment.
Everyone who liked entertainment liked music TV, but no one who liked entertainment liked documentaries.

Victor: “If you see a person who likes sports, he or she must not like documentaries.”

Adam: “If you see someone who likes music TV, he or she must also like entertainment.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Write arrows: sports → entertainment → music TV, and entertainment → NOT documentaries. Arrows only run in ONE direction.

steps.explain: Turn the sentences into arrows.
steps.work:
sports → entertainment
entertainment → music TV
entertainment → NOT documentaries

steps.explain: Victor: sports → entertainment → NOT documentaries. So someone who likes sports must not like documentaries ✓.
Adam goes BACKWARDS: 'likes music TV → likes entertainment'. The arrow only goes from entertainment to music TV; someone could like music TV without liking entertainment ✗.
Only Victor's reasoning is correct.

keyPoints.text: everyone who liked sports liked entertainment
keyPoints.note: Arrow 1: sports → entertainment.

keyPoints.text: no one who liked entertainment liked documentaries
keyPoints.note: Arrow 3: entertainment → NOT documentaries.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Car pollutants cause both immediate and long-term effects on the environment. Car exhausts emit a wide range of gases and solid matter, causing global warming, acid rain, and harming the environment and human health. Engine noise and fuel spills also cause pollution. Car pollution is one of the major causes of global warming.

Which one of these statements, if true, most weakens the above argument?
options: Keep your vehicle well maintained with regular check ups.
Increasing public transport would solve traffic problems in city centres.
It is quicker to walk through the city in the rush hour than to drive through it.
Public transport is usually not on time.
questions.hint: The argument implies we should cut down on car use because of pollution. Which option makes cutting car use harder — a reason people keep driving?

steps.explain: Find the point: car pollution is a major cause of global warming, so the number of cars on the road should be <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">reduced</mark>.
A weakening statement gives a reason why people will keep using cars anyway, so the problem can't be solved by switching away from cars.
A (maintain your car) and B (public transport would help) support the idea of reducing pollution or car use ✗. C says walking is quicker than driving in rush hour — that is a reason NOT to drive ✗.
D: public transport is usually not on time, so people have a good reason to keep driving, and car pollution would not fall.

keyPoints.text: Car pollution is one of the major causes of global warming.
keyPoints.note: The reason given for cutting car use.
Find a reason people will keep driving.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Speeding is the leading cause of death and injury on our roads. Every year, more than 740 people are killed whilst speeding and more than 20 000 people are injured because of speeding motorists.

Patrick: “The speed limits on highways should be lowered in order to reduce the amount of car crash deaths due to speeding.”

Which one of these statements, if true, most strengthens Patrick's argument?
options: Speed limits would not greatly impact anyone's day-to-day lives.
Lower speed limits would result in greater travelling times.
Lower speed limits would result in less severe injuries and possibly saving lives.
Fines for speeding offences should be higher than they are now.
questions.hint: Patrick's claim: LOWER the speed limits so fewer people die from speeding. Which option shows that lower limits really would reduce deaths or injuries?

steps.explain: Find the claim: lower speed limits <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">in order to reduce the amount of car crash deaths</mark> due to speeding.
To strengthen it, give evidence that lower limits actually save lives.
A says limits don't affect daily life much — that is not about deaths ✗. B says lower limits mean longer trips — a drawback, so it weakens ✗. D is about fines, not speed limits ✗.
C: lower limits would result in less severe injuries and possibly saving lives — direct support for Patrick.

keyPoints.text: The speed limits on highways should be lowered
keyPoints.note: The proposal.
Pick evidence that lower limits save lives.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Melanie counted in the following way on the fingers of her left hand:

She started by calling the thumb 1, the index finger 2, middle finger 3, ring finger 4, little finger 5 and then reversed the direction calling the ring finger 6, middle finger 7 and so on.

She counted up to 178.

She ended counting on which finger?
questions.hint: Count the first few numbers on the fingers to find the repeating pattern, then divide 178 by the length of one full cycle.

questions.stem:
The number of customers visited and number of gifts sold at Gift For You was recorded daily from Monday to Friday.

• Wednesday had the greatest number of customers but the least amount of sales.
• Friday had less customers than Tuesday and less sales.
• Friday had more sales than Wednesday.
• Tuesday had more customers than Thursday, but less sales.

If all the above statements are true, which one of the sentences below cannot be true?
options: Monday had the highest amounts of sales.
Friday had more sales than Thursday.
Thursday had less customers than Wednesday.
Tuesday had more customers than Friday.
questions.hint: Make TWO separate lists: one for customers and one for sales. Build each list from the clues, then test the options.

steps.explain: Sales (highest at the top). Wednesday has the least sales. Friday has more sales than Wednesday but less than Tuesday. Tuesday has less sales than Thursday.
Customers. Wednesday has the most customers. Tuesday has more customers than Thursday and more than Friday.

questions.stem:
Ten new television programs started during December. Four of the shows were children's TV, two were audition contests, and four were comedy. By June the next year, only six of these new programs were still on air. Four of the shows that remained were children's TV.

Tom: “Nobody watched comedy so they were all cancelled.”

Which one of the following sentences shows the mistake Tom has made?
options: Television viewers prefer children's TV over audition contests.
The comedy shows remained on air.
The most favourite shows were children's TV.
One of the cancelled shows could be comedy.
questions.hint: Count which shows are accounted for: 4 children's shows stayed. How many places are left among the six remaining shows, and which of the other six shows could fill them?

steps.explain: Ten shows: 4 children's, 2 audition, 4 comedy. Six remained, and four of them were children's TV — so ALL four children's shows stayed.
The two other remaining shows come from the 6 others (2 audition + 4 comedy). So four of those six were cancelled, but we are not told WHICH ones.
steps.work: 6 others (2 audition + 4 comedy): 2 stayed, 4 were cancelled

steps.explain: Tom says the comedy shows were all cancelled. The information does not say that — a comedy show might have stayed on air, and one of the cancelled shows might have been an audition contest. We are not able to tell which shows were cancelled.
steps.work: which shows were cancelled is not known

steps.explain: The book's key is D: the information does not tell us which shows were cancelled, so Tom cannot be sure that all the comedy shows were the ones cancelled.

keyPoints.text: Four of the shows that remained were children's TV.
keyPoints.note: All four children's shows stayed on air.

keyPoints.text: Nobody watched comedy so they were all cancelled.
keyPoints.note: Tom's claim goes beyond the information.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests
meta.note: Option D as printed ('One of the cancelled shows could be comedy') is loosely worded; follows the book key D (which shows were cancelled is not determined).

questions.stem:
In a diving competition, a diver's score is calculated by the following method.

• Five judges give a mark out of 10.
• The highest and lowest of these marks are eliminated.
• The average of the remaining three marks is determined.
• The final score is the product of the average score and the degree of difficulty.

Steven scored the following marks from the five judges.

9.8     9.5     9.8     9.2     9.5

The degree of difficulty for his dive was 2. What was Timothy's score for this dive?
questions.hint: Follow the method step by step: cross out ONE highest and ONE lowest mark, average the three marks that are left, then multiply by the difficulty.

steps.explain: Put the five marks in order.
Eliminate the lowest mark (9.2) and the highest mark (one of the 9.8s).
Find the average of the three remaining marks.
The final score is the average multiplied by the degree of difficulty (2).

keyPoints.text: The highest and lowest of these marks are eliminated.
keyPoints.note: Remove only ONE highest and ONE lowest.

keyPoints.text: The final score is the product of the average score and the degree of difficulty.
keyPoints.note: Multiply, don't add.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests
meta.note: The printed question says 'Timothy' where the marks belong to Steven; the answer is the score for the dive described.

questions.stem:
Four loose shapes are on the table as shown below.

Which of the below figures show how the shapes above can be composed to make a square?
questions.hint: Describe the four loose pieces (one small square turned like a diamond and three L-shapes), then look for the figure that is built from exactly these four pieces.

steps.explain: Describe the pieces: one small square (standing on a corner) and three L-shaped pieces of different sizes.
The pieces must fit together without gaps or overlaps into a larger square (the white diamond shape in each option, drawn on the green board).

In each figure count the pieces and look at their shapes. The pieces in A, B and C do not make the same set — an L-shape is replaced by another shape, or two pieces are the same size when they should be different.
The fourth figure contains four pieces: one square and three L-shapes of the sizes given, so it is the correct composition.

keyPoints.text: Four loose shapes are on the table
keyPoints.note: Piece set: 1 square + 3 L-shapes.

keyPoints.text: how the shapes above can be composed to make a square
keyPoints.note: Use all four pieces, no gaps, no overlaps.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests
meta.note: Figures vectorised from the book page. Book solution: the fourth image contains four pieces with one square and three L shapes.

questions.stem:
Students who play sport regularly every week tend to have better perseverance, courage to overcome difficult problems and nurture better relationships with friends. They also have a lower likelihood of developing health problems such as asthma and catching a viral infection.

Harry: “Michael doesn't play sport, so he doesn't have good relationships with his friends at school.”

James: “Max plays sport every day, so will definitely endure any problem in his life.”

If the information in the box is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.hint: Find the key words in the box: 'tend to'. It describes a general pattern, not a certainty. Then look for strong words like 'doesn't' and 'definitely' in the speakers' sentences.

steps.explain: The box says students who play sport <mark style="background:#fde68a;border-radius:4px;padding:0 2px">tend to</mark> have better perseverance and better relationships. That is a general trend, with exceptions.
Harry: 'Michael doesn't play sport, so he DOESN'T have good relationships.' The box says nothing about students who don't play sport — they may have good relationships for other reasons ✗.
James: 'Max plays sport every day, so he will DEFINITELY endure any problem.' 'Tend to' is not a guarantee; 'definitely' and 'any problem' are far too strong ✗.
Neither reasoning is correct.

keyPoints.note: 'Tend to' = usually, not always.
Both speakers use certain words ('doesn't', 'definitely').

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem:
Peter, John and Nick to go tennis regularly. Peter goes on Saturday, Monday and Wednesday. John goes every second day, while Nick can only go once a week.

If they were all there on Monday, what is the minimum number of days before the three boys meet up again?
questions.hint: Write out the days each boy goes, starting from Monday (day 0). Peter has a weekly pattern, John goes every second day, and Nick can go only ONCE in each week.

steps.explain: Peter goes on Saturday, Monday and Wednesday every week. Counting from the first Monday (day 0): Mon 0, Wed 2, Sat 5, Mon 7, Wed 9, Sat 12, Mon 14 …
John goes every second day: all the even-numbered days.
Days when BOTH Peter and John go: 0 (Mon), 2 (Wed), 12 (Sat), 14 (Mon) …

questions.stem:
Identical cubes are arranged to make the following shape. Some are white cubes and some are blue cubes.

Some more blue cubes are added to this shape. The new views from the front and the side are shown below.

What is the minimum number of extra blue cubes needed to make the front and side views as they are shown above?
questions.hint: Compare the blue cubes you can see in the FRONT and SIDE views with the blue cubes already in the 3D shape. The extra cubes are only needed where the views show blue and the shape doesn't have it yet.

steps.explain: Look at the 3D shape: some blue cubes are already in place on the top and in the front rows. The new FRONT and SIDE views show MORE blue squares than the original shape can give.
steps.work: views need more blue than the shape has

steps.explain: Front view: the bottom row is white, the second row is all blue, and the third row has three blue squares in the middle. The three top blue squares and one more blue square in the second row are not provided by the original cubes.
Side view: a blue column on the left is already there, but two blue squares at the right end are shown. One of them is not provided by the original cubes.
Mark the cubes needed with a cross on the views: four on the front view and one on the side view.
The minimum number of extra blue cubes is 5.

keyPoints.text: Some more blue cubes are added to this shape.
keyPoints.note: Only blue cubes are added.

questions.stem:
Two blocks of solids are put together next to each other as shown below.

Which one of the below could be a view of the two solids together?
questions.hint: Look at the small triangular tip on the top outline of the picture. Check the angle of that tip in each option.

steps.explain: The two solids together form an outline with a small pointed tip at the top, a stepped left side and a sloping right side.
steps.work: outline: tip on top + steps on the left + slope on the right

steps.explain: C is a tall thin outline with no tip and no sloping side — it cannot be the view of these two solids ✗. D has a tip, but its left side has no steps ✗.
A and B look very much alike. The difference is the little tip at the top: the tip must be a RIGHT-ANGLED triangle, as in the solids shown.
steps.work: tip of the small triangle = right angle

steps.explain: Only B has the right-angled tip, so only B is possible.

questions.stem:
Jean is a tour guide at Denver Castle. Tours of the castle begin at the entrance every 15 minutes from 9:30 am to 5:00 pm daily. Each tour takes 35 minutes to complete.
A number of guides are employed on a part-time basis to lead these tours.
However, on a day when a guide does work, she is expected to lead a minimum of six guided tours.

What is the earliest possible time Jean can finish her work for the day if she starts at 9:30 am?
questions.hint: Tours leave every 15 minutes, but each lasts 35 minutes. After one tour ends Jean can only take the NEXT tour that starts at or after that time. Do this six times.

steps.explain: Tour 1 starts at 9:30 and takes 35 minutes.

The next tour Jean can lead leaves at or after 10:05. Tours leave at 9:30, 9:45, 10:00, 10:15 … so the next one is 10:15. It ends at 10:50. Then the next tour at or after 10:50 leaves at 11:00 (ends 11:35).
After 11:35 the next tour is at 11:45 (ends 12:20). After 12:20 the next tour is at 12:30 (ends 1:05 pm).
After 1:05 pm the next tour leaves at 1:15 pm and ends 35 minutes later. That is her sixth tour.

questions.stem:
In the following pair of images, the right-hand image is the result of applying a series of changes to the left-hand image. These changes are a difference in the order of the shapes and the application of rotations to two of the shapes.

Which of the following pairs of images shows the same series of changes applied to the left-hand image to produce the right-hand image?
questions.hint: Work out the rule from the example: where does each shape go, and which shapes are rotated? Then test each option with the same rule.

steps.explain: Name the three shapes in the example from left to right: 1st (triangle ◁), 2nd (a plus +) and 3rd (a box with an arrow-head inside). Find them on the right.
The triangle ◁ is now on the right-hand end (3rd) and points the other way: it was rotated 180°. The plus is now 1st. The box is now 2nd and looks the same.

Two shapes are rotated. The box visibly stays the same, so the second rotated shape must be the plus — turning a plus gives the same picture. So the rule is: 1st → 3rd and rotated 180°; 2nd → 1st and rotated 180°; 3rd → 2nd, not rotated.
Test the options. A: the corner Γ looks the same after moving to the end (not rotated) ✗.  B: the second shape ⊣ keeps its direction (not rotated) ✗.  C: the second shape ⌠ is not turned ✗.
D: ↙ moves to the end and becomes ↗ (rotated 180°); the three dots move to the front and are turned upside down (rotated 180°); the black square moves to the middle unchanged.

keyPoints.text: a difference in the order of the shapes and the application of rotations to two of the shapes
keyPoints.note: Two things happen: a new order, and two shapes are rotated.

keyPoints.text: shows the same series of changes
keyPoints.note: Apply the same moves and rotations to each option.

meta.source: Mastering Thinking Skills Book 2 · Selective and Scholarship Tests
meta.note: Figures vectorised from the book page. Book solution: rotations of 180° on the 1st and 2nd shape; positions 1st→3rd, 2nd→1st, 3rd→2nd.

questions.stem:
There are 4 shapes below. The shapes are put together with the corresponding letters to be joined as one side.

Which one of the following shapes can be made from the 4 shapes?
questions.hint: Each shape has letters on some sides. The sides with the SAME letter must be joined together. Join a with a, b with b and c with c.

steps.explain: List the lettered sides: the up-arrow has side a (its stem); the rectangle has side b (its left side) and side c (its top); the down-arrow has side a (its stem) and side b (the other side of the stem); the triangle has side c (its bottom).
steps.work: a: up-arrow & down-arrow;  b: rectangle & down-arrow;  c: rectangle & triangle

steps.explain: Join the pieces: the two arrows touch along their stems (a with a), the rectangle touches the down-arrow (b with b), and the triangle is attached to the rectangle (c with c).

Check the options. A, B and C place the arrows or the triangle so that a lettered side is not joined to the side with the same letter (for example the triangle is attached to the wrong side, or both arrows point the same way).
Figure D joins every pair of lettered sides correctly: it is the first arrangement turned round, as in the book's solution picture.

keyPoints.text: The shapes are put together with the corresponding letters to be joined as one side.
keyPoints.note: a joins a, b joins b, c joins c.

keyPoints.text: Which one of the following shapes can be made from the 4 shapes?
keyPoints.note: Rotate and flip pieces if needed — only lettered sides must match.

questions.stem:
Three students studied for an exam.

• Steven studied the most but got the least marks.
• Ivy did not study the least.

If all the above statements are true, which one of the following sentences must not be correct?
options: Aidan scored the highest in the exam.
Ivy scored the highest in the exam.
Aidan studied the second most amount.
Ivy studied the second most amount.
questions.hint: Make two rankings: one for how much each student STUDIED and one for MARKS. Fill in what the two bullets tell you.

steps.explain: Studying: Steven studied the MOST. The other two are Ivy and Aidan.
Ivy did NOT study the least, and she isn't the most (that is Steven), so Ivy studied the second most. That leaves Aidan with the least.
Marks: Steven got the LEAST marks. The two others share the top two places in either order.
steps.work: least marks: Steven;  Aidan and Ivy: highest / second

steps.explain: Test the options. A: Aidan scored the highest — possible ✓.  B: Ivy scored the highest — possible ✓.  D: Ivy studied the second most — true ✓.  C: Aidan studied the second most — but Aidan studied the LEAST. This must not be correct.

keyPoints.text: Steven studied the most but got the least marks.
keyPoints.note: Steven: most study, least marks.

keyPoints.text: Ivy did not study the least.
keyPoints.note: So Ivy studied the second most.
